sources.title: Closing a $12k/month agency client: performance-based pricing, benchmarks and culture-fit framing
sources.originalTitle: Closing A $12,000/Per Month Agency Client *LIVE Footage*
sources.summary: Iman walks through a live two-call close of an e-commerce client, showing how he pre-frames results and culture fit, sets a performance fee that only kicks in above the client's existing baseline, and uses a break for partners to decide. The closing talk covers why the structure keeps incentives aligned and protects against churn at high billables.

principles.text: Use a cheap first call to stall and gather info when unprepared; then make the offer on a second call.
principles.quote: this initial call is basically me stalling and just getting some preliminary information and then kicking that the can down the road.

principles.text: Pre-frame the sales call with two gates (results and culture fit) so prospects qualify themselves without cringe.
principles.quote: there's two things that need to be a green light. First of all, results front.

principles.text: Ask what success looks like and pin down numbers (revenue, spend, ROAS) to align expectations before pricing.
principles.quote: if you want to do it kind of maintaining your margins as is, uh you know, then it's definitely a conversation we can entertain.

principles.text: Set the performance fee to start only above the client's existing baseline, so you never take credit for what they already do.
principles.quote: I actually set a benchmark of what they're already accomplishing, so we actually don't, uh, in terms of our performance fee, it only kicks in at a certain boundary.

principles.text: Keep the base retainer low and make most pay performance-based, so incentives are aligned and the deal is a no-brainer.
principles.quote: we don't take a percentage of ad spend. We don't take a percentage of revenue. We take a percentage of what we're making you after ads on the campaigns.

principles.text: Use a 6-month minimum then rolling monthly, since high billables without a baseline structure invite churn.
principles.quote: it's a 6-month minimum. That's standard with us, so we we don't take clients on for anything less than that, um, these days.

sources.title: Iman Gadzhi's step-by-step SMMA sales call framework: from setup to closing and collecting cash
sources.originalTitle: Step-By-Step Guide To Close Clients For Your SMMA In 2024
sources.summary: Iman breaks down the closing process he taught thousands of agency owners: prepare your environment and research the prospect, choose a one-call or two-call structure, then run Rapport, Pre-frame, Discovery, Transition, Pitch and Close. The core ideas are leading the call with authority, making prospects sell themselves in discovery, and pitching a system rather than a service.

principles.text: Beginners should use a two-call close: discovery first, pitch second. The gap resets prospect energy and lets you tailor the offer.
principles.quote: prospects buy when they are interested and a lot of the time interest is linked directly to energy

principles.text: Pre-frame the call to take authority, show no desperation, and agree upfront on a clear yes or no to avoid "I need to think about it".
principles.quote: at the end of the call I just want a yes or a no let's avoid the maybe

principles.text: In every sales call one person leads with questions and the other follows. As the seller, you must hold the authority to keep the call on track.
principles.quote: in every single sales call there's one person that leads by asking questions and the other that follows by answering them

principles.text: Run discovery on current state, future state, gap, opportunity cost and doubt so the prospect talks themselves into needing you.
principles.quote: remember the key is in the fact that the client says it when you say it it means nothing but when they say it themselves is when your message is hitting

principles.text: Pitch your offer as a system, not a service. Owners see services as expenses and systems as investments, and confused buyers never buy.
principles.quote: business owners can view Services as expenses but they often view systems like Investments

principles.text: State your price with confidence, do not justify it, use silence, then collect cash on the call because a client is only a client once they have paid.
principles.quote: a client is only a client once they have paid

sources.title: How Iman Gadzhi closed $80K of SMMA retainers in 72 hours using anchoring, minimum terms and guarantees
sources.originalTitle: Closing $80,000 Of SMMA Clients In 72 Hours
sources.summary: Iman walks through four agency deals closed in one weekend. He explains how he anchors price, trades lower retainers for longer minimums to raise guaranteed value, and separates logistics questions from objections. He also covers collecting payment on the call and his guarantee.

principles.text: Set a price anchor before you quote: have the prospect guess your rate so a lower offer feels like a steal.
principles.quote: I wanted to set that benchmark because then once I told him, okay, look, we're going to charge you £2,500 a month with a 6-month minimum, it seems like a total steal.

principles.text: Longer minimum terms can matter more than a higher monthly fee, so judge deals by guaranteed value and lower churn.
principles.quote: I'm starting to think more in terms of like the guaranteed value of the client.

principles.text: Tell logistics questions apart from objections: logistics means the buyer is sold and needs the delivery explained.
principles.quote: Objection handling is, you know, they're not sold on it, so they're trying to test. Whereas logistics handling is they're sold on it, but they just need to wrap their head around the logistics

principles.text: Don't leave the call until payment is taken; no payment means no client.
principles.quote: I am not leaving that call until payment.

principles.text: Extra calls add friction and lose deals, so close in as few calls as possible.
principles.quote: Any sort of added friction really ruins the likeliness of the sale.

principles.text: Offer a guarantee and take on the risk yourself. It removes the buyer's downside and forces you to pick clients carefully.
principles.quote: we guarantee a return on ad spend. Um, so that's 1.5x. So that basically means it's physically impossible for you to lose money.

sources.title: How to prevent and overcome SMMA sales objections with a 5-step framework
sources.originalTitle: How to Close 75% More SMMA Clients (Objection Handling Tutorial)
sources.summary: Iman Gadzhi argues every sales objection is really a trust objection hidden behind a smokescreen. He teaches prevention (answer all questions, then a 1-10 tie-down before pricing) and a five-step process for any remaining objection: diffuse, reframe to the goal, tie down, isolate, overcome.

principles.text: A great closer prevents objections; a good closer only handles them.
principles.quote: a good closer knows how to handle objections but a great closer knows how to prevent them from ever even coming up

principles.text: Before pricing, make sure every question is answered; a confused buyer never buys.
principles.quote: a confused buyer never buys so if you have a prospect who has a bunch of questions then you shouldn't go straight into pricing before answering them

principles.text: Run a 1-10 tie-down before pricing and probe anything under a 9 to surface hidden doubts.
principles.quote: out of curiosity what's stopping you from being a nine or a 10 this will give you clarity about what their main concerns are

principles.text: Every objection is a trust objection disguised as a smokescreen (spouse, money, think about it).
principles.quote: every single objection is essentially a trust based objection they either don't trust you your agency or themselves

principles.text: Diffuse the objection by agreeing first, not getting defensive, so the prospect avoids fight or flight.
principles.quote: you want to avoid confronting them and make them feel their thoughts and concerns are valid at least for the moment

principles.text: Take a service-over-sales mentality: most buyers need your help deciding, so be firm from a place of authority.
principles.quote: one out of 10 are never going to buy one out of 10 are guaranteed to buy regardless but but eight out of 10 will need your help to decide

sources.title: How Iman Gadzhi finds SMMA prospects: networking, manual sourcing, software and freelancers
sources.originalTitle: Never Run Out of SMMA Clients Using These 4 Prospecting Methods
sources.summary: Iman breaks down four ways to build a prospect list for an agency: networking, manual lead sourcing, lead software, and outsourcing to B2B lead gen freelancers. He explains the quantity vs quality trade-off of each and how to pick a combination based on your network, time and money.

principles.text: Use your network first; warm contacts and referrals are the easiest way to land your first client.
principles.quote: in my humble opinion it's the easiest way to sign your first client

principles.text: Be honest that you're a beginner; business owners respect it, and ask every contact for referrals.
principles.quote: people really appreciate honesty and most business owners have been in the same position as you and they respect it

principles.text: Manual lead sourcing (Google Maps, LinkedIn, Instagram, directories) gives the best lead quality and costs $0, but is slow.
principles.quote: the advantage of manual lead sourcing is the quality of the prospect because you are finding everything yourself

principles.text: Lead software trades some quality for huge volume and time savings; clean the list and use verification tools.
principles.quote: the quality of the list does suffer a bit but is the trade-off worth it in my opinion 100%

principles.text: Outsource list building to freelancers like you outsource delivery, but test with the cheapest tier first and check reviews.
principles.quote: always buy the first tier even if each Prospect costs a little bit more because this will allow you to use the list and judge the quality of it

principles.text: Choose your prospecting mix by network, time and money; prospecting is ongoing, so keep the list big.
principles.quote: prospecting is an ongoing task so build the habit of always keeping your prospecting list as big as possible

sources.title: How to start an SMMA in 2026 with $0: the shadow operator model for micro creators
sources.originalTitle: How To Start SMMA For Beginners In 2026 With $0
sources.summary: Iman lays out a 9-step SMMA roadmap, contrasting the traditional local-business route with a "shadow operator" model. In it you partner with micro creators (20k-100k followers), use AI instead of contractors, and take a revenue split instead of selling retainers. Covers niche, offer, outreach, sales, pricing and launch.

principles.text: Pick unsophisticated buyers: if they already do the service at 6/10, you must beat that; if they do nothing, a 4/10 still wins.
principles.quote: Pick unsophisticated businesses where the business owner has no idea how to do the service that you offer.

principles.text: Niche down to simplify: one niche means the same prospecting, outreach, sales, delivery and offer, instead of running several businesses at once.
principles.quote: When you have multiple niches, it's literally like running multiple different businesses at one go.

principles.text: Target micro creators who already have the audience; skip the hardest problem of getting eyes on a product nobody knows.
principles.quote: They already have the eyes and the attention. They just don't have the back-end strategy to launch the product and monetize that attention.

principles.text: Charge a revenue split instead of selling retainers: no upfront ask means no risk for the creator, and the sale becomes an opportunity pitch.
principles.quote: You're not convincing them to pay you any money upfront. No, no, no. There's a very big difference here.

principles.text: Automate the split at the moment of sale so the partner never feels like they're paying you; every manual payment invites a reconsideration.
principles.quote: Every recall is a reframe. Basically, every time someone needs to remember to pay you, they reconsider if it's worth it.

principles.text: Set a non-negotiable daily outreach floor (the bare minimum) plus a stretch target, and keep the first message short, personal and ending in a question.
principles.quote: BAM stands for bare ass minimum. This is the number of outreach messages you will do every single day, no matter what.

sources.title: How to start an SMMA from scratch: Iman Gadzhi's 9-step blueprint to $10k/month
sources.originalTitle: The Ultimate Guide to Start SMMA From Scratch In 2026
sources.summary: Iman explains why agencies are the best beginner model (low capital, high margins, high demand, easy fulfillment) and walks through nine steps: niche, service, setup, offer, prospecting, outreach, sales calls, onboarding funnel, and outsourced delivery. He also pitches a micro personal brand as the easiest way to get inbound clients.

principles.text: Judge beginner business models on startup capital, profit margin, demand and fulfillment ease.
principles.quote: the most beginner friendly models always have the following low startup Capital High profit margins high demand and easy fulfillment

principles.text: Niche down: one niche keeps complexity low, and complexity is what blocks scaling.
principles.quote: increased variation in your business results in increased complexity and increased complexity hinders your ability to scale

principles.text: Target businesses with high-ticket products so one extra sale pays back your fee.
principles.quote: if you get them one new job a month they've instantly made a 5x return on their investment if they're paying you $2,000 a month

principles.text: As a beginner, sell into unsophisticated niches where you can be the expert in the room.
principles.quote: as a beginner you're always better off selling your services to unsophisticated Nas because this allows you to be the expert in the room

principles.text: Agencies get paid upfront and pay contractors later, so hire cheaper skilled talent abroad (contractor arbitrage).
principles.quote: the client always pays UPF front but everyone knows salaries and team and contractors all that stuff they get paid at the end of the month this means that you never have cash flow issues

principles.text: Outreach is a numbers game: volume gives you wins and the data to refine your approach.
principles.quote: Outreach is a numbers game you have to send Outreach messages and make cold calls every single day and you must be consistent

sources.title: Iman Gadzhi's beginner guide to starting a social media marketing agency
sources.originalTitle: Social Media Marketing Agency Guide (Beginners)
sources.summary: Iman walks through starting a lean SMMA: pick one niche, build a small lead list, cold outreach to sell the meeting rather than the service, close with emotion then logic, and deliver paid social ads (outsourced if needed). He stresses simplicity, no free trials, and getting paid before starting.

principles.text: Sell the meeting, not the service; make it infinite upside and zero downside for the owner.
principles.quote: you are selling the meeting not the service so when you're reaching out to clients don't start talking about the benefits of your service

principles.text: People buy with emotion and justify with logic; future-pace their desired life, then back it with their numbers.
principles.quote: people buy with emotion and then they justify with logic

principles.text: Never offer free trials; they set a zero-price expectation and don't convert to paying clients.
principles.quote: never offer free trials ladies and gentlemen you need to understand the free trials never convert

principles.text: Keep the agency simple: one niche, one core service. Complexity kills profit.
principles.quote: the best agencies on earth are the ones that are the most simple and the most streamlined

principles.text: You don't need deep skills at the start; sell the service and use contractors to deliver results.
principles.quote: I just knew enough about Facebook ads to sell that to clients and then I had my contractor deliver those results

principles.text: A prospect isn't a client until they've paid; use invoicing to collect on the spot.
principles.quote: you have not closed the client until they've paid they are not a client until they have paid for the service

sources.title: Capital allocation for an agency: bank first, then software, then yourself
sources.originalTitle: Capital Allocation For An Agency
sources.summary: Iman explains why agency owners, with high margins and free acquisition channels, should put profit in the bank first, keep software lean, and invest in their own education. Cash reserves create a non-needy sales posture that wins higher-ticket clients, creating a flywheel.

principles.text: Bill clients upfront and let contractors get paid 30 days later, so team costs never strain cash flow.
principles.quote: whenever a client signs you build them straight away okay I always always always start work after a client has paid the invoice

principles.text: An agency's real costs are just software and team; keep software lean and bootstrap with free tools early.
principles.quote: really what makes up an agency is software is team members and that's really it that's the beautiful thing that is really at the the you know the profit margins are just through the freaking roof

principles.text: Early on, the best investment is your own education, because outreach is free and you are the main lever.
principles.quote: the best investment you can make as an agency owner is in yourself in your own education and in giving you that information to drive your agency

principles.text: At roughly 20-40k monthly profit, spend on paid traffic to grow social platforms or run case-study and webinar funnels for agency leads.
principles.quote: once you get to around 20 30 40 km on profit consistently my best piece of advice is spend money on paid traffic to either grow up your social platforms

principles.text: Cash in the bank improves sales: prospects smell neediness, and willingness to walk away signals the right person for the job.
principles.quote: if you put two scenarios through you know two people with the same skill level two people with the same sales level

principles.text: Banking profit creates a flywheel: more clients bring more cash, and more cash makes it easier to sign clients.
principles.quote: the more clients you sign the more money you can put in the bank the more money you can put in the bank the easier it is to sign clients

sources.title: Why age is an advantage in online marketing: reframe limiting beliefs into positioning
sources.originalTitle: Is Running An Agency Harder If You're Young?
sources.summary: Iman argues that being young is not a handicap when selling online marketing, because business owners want someone who grew up with the platforms. He gives a general rule: objectively test each limiting belief, and if it is a real disadvantage, spin it into a selling point (age, no degree, cheap cost of living).

principles.text: Objectively test a limiting belief; if it is a real disadvantage, spin it into an advantage.
principles.quote: no matter what you believe your limiting belief is objectively assess whether it is a disadvantage and most the time it's not and if it is a disadvantage just find a way to spin it

principles.text: Clients look for the generation that grew up with the skill, so young marketers are seen as the experts.
principles.quote: when they look at you they actually see that as an advantage not a disadvantage

principles.text: Practice what you preach: being on the platforms you pitch daily is a compelling sales argument.
principles.quote: I practice what I preach you know or eat eat your own cooking right

principles.text: No degree is easy to counter because marketing knowledge goes obsolete fast; daily learning beats a credential.
principles.quote: because I don't have any certifications in digital marketing or you know I don't have a marketing degree I'm learning every single day

principles.text: Pick fields where results beat track record: online marketing is early, so businesses are only now hunting for help.
principles.quote: online marketing at the moment is kind of like this eighth wonder you know it's kind of this thing where businesses are just starting in a catch up

principles.text: Turn a geographic or cost disadvantage into an offer: more dedication and lower price because you do not pay inflated rent.
principles.quote: you're not spending the on increased expertise or increased knowledge you're just spending that on their increased rent

sources.title: Iman Gadzhi: build an intentional micro personal brand and monetize it with 1:1 coaching
sources.originalTitle: How To Start A Personal Brand in 2026 (Step-by-Step)
sources.summary: Iman explains why everyone already has a personal brand and how to make it an asset. Work backwards from what you sell, pick one platform, attract a small high-quality audience with content that gets paid to acquire clients, then monetize through info and 1:1 coaching sold to a narrow niche.

principles.text: Work backwards: decide what you sell and who your perfect client is, then build the brand to attract them.
principles.quote: we work backwards. We knew we wanted to make more money and we found something to sell to make that money. [music] And then we figured out what our perfect client looks like and then we built an intentional brand to attract more of those clients through our content.

principles.text: Optimize for audience quality and profit per follower, not follower count; a thousand right followers can be enough.
principles.quote: You do not need millions of followers to get rich with a personal brand. You just need a thousand of the right ones.

principles.text: Build niche brands per audience segment, even if that means lower views, to attract only the prospects you serve.
principles.quote: you're going to notice that the views on the business channel are significantly lower, but do I care? No, I don't care because I'm attracting the audience I want.

principles.text: Pick the platform where your ideal audience already hangs out and that plays to your skills; don't master all at once.
principles.quote: you give yourself a huge head start if you create content where your ideal audience already hangs out, where they already spend their time.

principles.text: Organic content can achieve negative cost of acquisition: platforms pay you while content sells your offer on the back end.
principles.quote: content allows you to achieve something called negative cost of acquisition.

principles.text: Be authentic and take the audience on the journey; people resonate with the journey, not a hero.
principles.quote: An audience does not resonate with a hero, they resonate with the journey.

sources.title: How Iman Gadzhi went from broke teen to $100M: five years running a social media agency
sources.originalTitle: I made $100M online and recorded EVERYTHING
sources.summary: A year-by-year documentary of Iman's agency journey from a £95/week first client in 2016 to millions by 21. It covers pricing lessons (retainers plus performance fees, lifetime value over monthly price), sales habits, hiring mistakes, and investing agency cash flow rather than letting it sit idle.

principles.text: Optimize for client lifetime value, not monthly price: lower retainers kept longer beat high retainers that churn fast.
principles.quote: it's much better to have a clan that pays $25,000 a month and you keep them for 10 months rather than a clan that pays $5,000 a month and you only keep them for 3 months

principles.text: Charge a lower base retainer plus a performance fee, with longer minimum terms, to earn far more per client.
principles.quote: we would have much lower base retainers but because of our performance that we were delivering for our clients you know we were still building way more than five figures a month

principles.text: Never work with an agency that charges a percentage of ad spend or revenue, because incentives must be aligned.
principles.quote: if an agency ever charges you percentage of AD spend or percentage of Revenue just leave the meeting because here's the issue okay our incentives need to be aligned

principles.text: Price per client based on value and work involved, and don't sell packages without diagnosing the client's problem first.
principles.quote: I always tell people like don't do packages don't do packages and also your pricing should be different per client

principles.text: Don't qualify yourself to high-level people; act like you belong from the start of the conversation.
principles.quote: you act like you're here from the get-go it's a lot better of a dynamic to start the uh start the meeting off in that Way

principles.text: Agencies are cash-flow machines; send profits into an investment portfolio monthly and let compounding work.
principles.quote: when you have cash flow you invest it and then you let the compounding nature of time do its trick

sources.title: How Iman Gadzhi built a six-figure-a-month marketing agency from age 16 to 20
sources.originalTitle: From 0 to Millionaire at the Age of 20 (SHOCKING STORY)
sources.summary: A compiled four-year timeline of Iman's agency, from a £380/month first client in 2016 to $20k/month at 17 and $100k monthly profit by 2019. Covers niching down, retainers plus performance pay, retention, and the habits and mindset behind it.

principles.text: Find a high-income skill: if you deliver 100 units of value and charge 20, buyers hire you.
principles.quote: I found a high income producing skill right so I found something where if I learn this skill I am worth a lot of money I am worth a lot of money to other people

principles.text: Specialize in one service and a sweet-spot niche as you scale instead of offering everything.
principles.quote: once you hit that 7even fig year mark you're really going to need to specialize in on one service offering

principles.text: Grow through traction, not by adding extra services.
principles.quote: the real power in business is traction not addition um it's not adding extra [ __ ]

principles.text: Add a performance percentage on top of retainers; flat retainers alone left money on the table.
principles.quote: pretty much every single one of our deals these days does have a percentage of row as so basically a performance Kickback within that

principles.text: Maximize retention: a few clients staying 12-18 months can carry large monthly profit.
principles.quote: if you've got Clan staying on for for 12 months 18 months you really don't need many of them to consistently be clocking in 100 200k months profit with the agency

principles.text: Don't qualify yourself in meetings; act like you belong from the start and turn your age into an advantage.
principles.quote: don't qualify yourself

sources.title: How to build and sell digital products fast: validate, ship an MVP, and get traffic via influencer arbitrage
sources.originalTitle: Copy This Method To Make $2,700/Week with Digital Products
sources.summary: Iman Gadzhi lays out a step-by-step playbook for digital products: pick and validate a topic using proof of existing demand, build the store page first, ship a cheap ebook MVP with AI, then drive traffic through commission-only influencer deals, paid ads and organic content. The core idea is rapid, low-risk testing with unlimited "spins".

principles.text: Pick topics people have already proven they'll buy, not what you think they want.
principles.quote: They create something that they think people want instead of something people have already proven to buy.

principles.text: Go a level deeper than market and niche so buyers feel the product was made just for them.
principles.quote: The deeper you go and the more specific you get, the better? Because this will make your product truly stand out.

principles.text: Validate demand by checking competitors' ads: long-running ads and many creative variations signal profit.
principles.quote: You need to understand that people wouldn't keep spending money if they weren't making money back.

principles.text: Ship an imperfect MVP fast to get proof of concept, then double down on what works.
principles.quote: stop focusing on perfection and start focusing on progress.

principles.text: Build the store page before the product; writing the pitch tests whether the topic is worth pursuing.
principles.quote: creating a store page forces you to really think about what you're going to sell and whether or not it's something you want to do.

principles.text: Get first sales via commission-only deals with micro influencers who can't monetize their audience, so there's no upfront risk.
principles.quote: Typical commission rates are 30 to 60% of each sale. And the reason that you can do this is because there are no cost of goods for digital products.

sources.title: How Iman Gadzhi builds a $10k/month online coaching business: UVZ, offer, acquisition
sources.originalTitle: Give me 33 minutes & I’ll Show You How To Make $10,000/pm with Online Coaching
sources.summary: Iman lays out a four-step path to $10k/month coaching: find a narrow unique value zone, build a high-ticket offer around problem, specific result and a named mechanism, acquire clients via outreach, referrals and organic content, then deliver with a structured call format. He stresses specialization as the source of pricing power and coaching as a way to learn your market.

principles.text: Go one layer deeper than niche: pick a unique value zone (e.g. weight loss for postpartum moms) so you can specialize and charge more.
principles.quote: having a uvz allows you to specialize and charge more

principles.text: Specialists command premium prices; generalists compete on price. Specialization creates perceived value.
principles.quote: Specialists command premium rates generalists compete on price clients pay more when they trust your expertise

principles.text: A coaching offer needs three parts: a core problem, a specific measurable result in a time frame, and a unique named solution.
principles.quote: there are three key parts to your coaching offer that you absolutely need to nail number one is the core problem

principles.text: Sell the outcome, not the coaching. Give your method a name; naming what you already do is enough to create a unique mechanism.
principles.quote: people do not buy coaching coaching is the vehicle in which to get them an outcome

principles.text: Don't run paid ads until you've hit $10k/month organically; you haven't validated the market or refined messaging yet.
principles.quote: stay away from Paid ads until you've surpassed at least $10,000 a month through organic methods first

principles.text: Coaching teaches you your market fast: recurring words and problems from calls become your offers, messaging and sales angles.
principles.quote: it's crazy how quickly you become expert in a market by actually coaching people cuz you start to spot the patterns

sources.title: Facebook Ads for Beginners: setup, testing structure and optimizing for ROAS
sources.originalTitle: Facebook Ads for Beginners (2024 Tutorial)
sources.summary: Iman walks through the full Facebook ads setup (page, business manager, pixel, domain) and how his agency structures campaigns: separate testing and prospecting budgets, broad targeting, and creatives as the main lever. He also covers the three metrics behind ROAS and how to size budgets and kill losers fast.

principles.text: Creatives are the biggest lever in paid ads; spend about 80% of your focus on making and testing more of them.
principles.quote: a great creative can work with bad targeting bad campaign structure bad campaign optimization and bad bidding strategies

principles.text: Split budget between prospecting (70-80%) and testing (20-30%), and promote winners from tests into prospecting.
principles.quote: ideally you should set around 70 to 80 percent of your budget to prospecting campaigns and 20 to 30 to testing

principles.text: Broad, large audiences usually beat micromanaged targeting because the algorithm knows who to show ads to; small audiences raise frequency and CPMs.
principles.quote: one of our historically best performing audiences across all industries is broad targeting this means no segmentation at all

principles.text: Size test budgets relative to product price (at least 0.5x, ideally 1x) so the platform has a realistic chance at a sale.
principles.quote: never go below 0.5 x product price

principles.text: Diagnose ROAS through CPC, conversion rate and AOV together, fix the weakest bottleneck, and kill clear losers fast.
principles.quote: don't let clear undeniable losers run for longer than they should this is what kills the overall performance of your ad account

principles.text: Winning ads stop the scroll, earn the click through curiosity, and look like a native post rather than an ad.
principles.quote: it shouldn't look like an ad nowadays we get bombarded with so many ads that by default we have the banner blindness

sources.title: Iman Gadzhi's CLEAR method: ranking 5 AI side hustles (UGC, websites, clipping, voice agents, digital products)
sources.originalTitle: 5 Proven Ways To Make Money With AI (No Experience)
sources.summary: Iman breaks down five AI side hustles with pricing, retainer math and pros and cons, then scores each with his CLEAR framework (competition, longevity, effort, autonomy, recurring). AI digital products rank first because income decouples from hours. Voice agents rank second because a steep learning curve thins competition and clients stay sticky.

principles.text: Analysis paralysis is the real blocker. People who pick one option and start beat those who keep researching.
principles.quote: the people who just picked one, they're already ahead. Not because they were smarter than you, but simply because they stopped scrolling, and they just started.

principles.text: Score any business idea with CLEAR: Competition, Longevity, Effort, Autonomy, Recurring, five points each out of 25.
principles.quote: It's called the CLEAR method. CLEAR is an acronym and it stands for competition, longevity, effort, autonomy, as well as recurring.

principles.text: A low barrier to entry is a double-edged sword. It makes starting easy but floods the market and pushes people to compete on price.
principles.quote: when everyone can do the same thing, people start competing on price. And normally, that's a race to the bottom that you don't want to get into.

principles.text: Prefer monthly retainers over one-off projects. Recurring revenue means you don't start at zero every month.
principles.quote: the real money is in the retainers, okay? A brand pays you a flat fee every month for a specific batch of videos.

principles.text: A harder skill is a moat. Fewer people push through the steep learning curve, so competition stays manageable and the service pays more.
principles.quote: I would say this one has the steepest learning curve, but that's also exactly why it pays the most. Fewer people push through the barrier.

principles.text: Sell by showing the cost of the problem, not by persuading. When the ROI is obvious before the pitch ends, selling gets easy.
principles.quote: instead of trying to convince them, instead you're showing them what it's already costing them not to have it.

sources.title: How to build a $10K/month one-person business as a beginner: simple, niche, productized
sources.originalTitle: Build A One-Person Business As A Beginner (From $0 To $10K)
sources.summary: Iman Gadzhi lays out a stripped-down path to a solo $10K/month business: pick a simple business model, niche down hard, productize with digital products, use AI as leverage, build an audience organically, ship imperfect work, and don't scale before product-market fit.

principles.text: Start with a simple, validated business model; prefer productized digital products over custom service work.
principles.quote: building something once and having the ability to sell it forever.

principles.text: Niche down to a hyper-specific audience and promise; specificity beats a bigger addressable market.
principles.quote: Don't be a fitness coach, please. Instead, be the guy who helps busy dads in their 30s lose their beer belly in 90 days without giving up weekend beers.

principles.text: At $10K/month, run one funnel, one core offer, one clear outcome; double down on what works before expanding.
principles.quote: One funnel, one core offer, and one clear outcome. You find one thing that works, and you double down on it until it's generating consistent revenue.

principles.text: Monetize problems people need solved, not your passion; the market pays for what it needs to learn.
principles.quote: The market does not pay for what you want to teach. It pays for what it needs to learn.

principles.text: Build an organic audience on one platform first; ads can't fix a broken offer or build an audience from scratch.
principles.quote: trying to use ads to fix a broken offer or to build an audience from scratch is just an expensive mistake.

principles.text: Don't scale or hire before product-market fit; perfect the offer, systems, and unit economics first.
principles.quote: Scaling a broken business will just break it faster and cost you more money.

sources.title: Iman Gadzhi's "growth marketer" model: partner with micro creators and build their digital products with AI
sources.originalTitle: Best Online Business to Make $10k+/month In 2026 (Beginner Friendly)
sources.summary: Iman pitches a beginner business model: partner with micro creators (10k-100k followers) who have audiences but no products, win them with a free "monetization game plan", build the product with AI, and launch via a 14-day Instagram story sequence for a revenue share. He also gives a six-metric framework for judging how beginner-friendly a business model is. The video is a long funnel for his paid consulting program, so treat the income claims with caution.

principles.text: Judge any business model on six metrics before committing: unit gain, startup capital, speed to first dollar, skill needed, fulfillment complexity, scalability.
principles.quote: Unitary gain, that's how much you make per transaction. Startup capital, that's how much money you need to start. Speed to first dollar, that's how fast you can make your first sale.

principles.text: A beginner-friendly model needs a handful of sales to reach 10K/month, near-zero capital, a first dollar in 14 to 30 days, and low skill and fulfillment burden.
principles.quote: For speed to first dollar, you want it fast. Ideally, 14 to 30 days so that way you see results quickly because if it takes too much longer than that, the likelihood of you quitting goes through the roof.

principles.text: Don't start on the hardest difficulty. Pick a model realistically attainable for beginners instead of one with a higher ceiling but a brutal learning curve.
principles.quote: Making this mistake is kind of like playing a new video game on the hardest difficulty instead of working your way up.

principles.text: Target micro creators (10k-100k followers, one specific topic) who have trust and audience but no product to sell.
principles.quote: They are called micro creators, creators with anywhere from 10,000 to 100,000 followers that talk about a very specific topic.

principles.text: Never cold pitch with a generic ask. Lead with a custom, give-first deliverable showing exactly how they can monetize their audience.
principles.quote: What if instead of asking for something, you gave them something valuable first, so that you show you can help them by actually helping them.

principles.text: Make the first deal a no-brainer: offer a 70/30 split in the creator's favor and renegotiate later once you have proof.
principles.quote: The creator keeps 70% of all the revenue, you keep 30%, and that's because when you're first starting out, you want to make this as much of a no-brainer for them as possible.

sources.title: Iman Gadzhi's 17 laws of success: lessons from the top 1% he knows
sources.originalTitle: The 17 Laws of Success
sources.summary: Iman shares 17 lessons from the wealthy people he knows. They cover buying assets with windfalls, doing the practical thing over the sexy one, discipline over motivation, small circles, radical responsibility, and compounding years of private work. Most of it is mindset and wealth habits rather than tactics.

principles.text: When a big sum of money lands, buy hard-to-sell assets so you can't spend it. In your first decades you are your own biggest liability.
principles.quote: you are a massive liability to yourself if you make a lot of money there's a high chance a high probability that you will spend it

principles.text: Make money in boring, practical businesses. Find inefficiencies and do something a few percent better, not a billion-dollar unicorn.
principles.quote: they just find areas in the market where there's inefficiencies or where they can just do something even three percent better and because of that they get more of the market shares

principles.text: Never be the first to name the price in a negotiation; talking less means fewer mistakes and more listening from others.
principles.quote: you should never ever be the first one to say the price when you're negotiating a deal

principles.text: Copy what successful people did at the start, not what they do now. Success is about doing things in the right order.
principles.quote: don't look at what a real estate agent is doing in their 15th year as being a real estate agent no look at what they did when they first started

principles.text: Rely on discipline, not motivation, because motivation is fleeting like a runner's high.
principles.quote: motivation is great sometimes you're gonna get it but it's fleeting you need to rely on discipline instead

principles.text: Winning is continuous: keeping and multiplying wins is harder than getting them, so don't rest on a win.
principles.quote: if you sleep on a win you're gonna wake up with a loss

sources.title: Why timing, speed, and a "minimum viable business" get beginners to their first $1,000
sources.originalTitle: It's Boring, But Will Make Even Beginners Millionaires in 2026
sources.summary: Iman Gadzhi argues success is mostly timing: market timing plus matching the business to your career stage. Beginners should skip the "million-dollar business" trap, start a simple minimum viable business to reach $1,000, and move fast through optimization cycles. He also pitches his Digital Launchpad course.

principles.text: Success needs market timing plus career timing; match the business to your current stage.
principles.quote: those decisions only happen when Market timing meets career timing and when you understand this concept and you apply it one simple right decision will outweigh all of the wrong decisions you've ever taken

principles.text: Climb in steps: aim for the next income tier (zero to $1,000, then $10,000), never skip steps.
principles.quote: if you're at zero and you've never made any money online before ... your goal should be make $1,000 just $1,000 not $10,000 not $100,000 not a million just $1,000

principles.text: Start a minimum viable business: simple, cheap, solo, and almost impossible not to make money with.
principles.quote: a very very simple business that's easy to learn easy to implement and doesn't require you to invest any money or hire anyone to get started it's something that you can do by yourself

principles.text: Pick work for practical, real-world results, not passion; passion grows from succeeding.
principles.quote: the only thing you should ask yourself is this does it generate practical real life results that's the only thing that matters

principles.text: Speed of implementation wins: more test cycles in the same time beats fewer, even if the fewer all work.
principles.quote: if one person tests five new things in a certain time frame and another person tests 20 new things during the exact same time frame guess what the person who tested 20 new things wins every single time

principles.text: When public perception swings too far to one side, move the opposite way (e.g. 'you must start a million-dollar business').
principles.quote: usually when it's skewed way too much on one side your best move is to move the opposite direction

sources.title: 17 Money Lessons: Iman Gadzhi on opportunity cost, cash flow, and investing in yourself
sources.originalTitle: 17 Money Lessons (I Wish Someone Had Told Me)
sources.summary: Iman Gadzhi talks to his younger self about money mistakes: inaction and comfort cost more than any purchase, cash flow beats revenue, and early income should be reinvested in yourself and tools. He also covers lifestyle creep, geographic arbitrage, buying used, and why passive income is not passive.

principles.text: Opportunity cost, the businesses and side hustles you never start, is the biggest expense in your life.
principles.quote: the biggest expense in your life will be opportunity cost.

principles.text: Focus on cash flow and profit first; revenue is vanity. Chase enterprise value only later.
principles.quote: revenue is vanity, profit is sanity, and cash flow is reality.

principles.text: Treat tools and software as investments that stack competitive advantages, even as a solopreneur.
principles.quote: investing in your business tools isn't a cost it is an investment to have a competitive advantage

principles.text: Early income should be reinvested in yourself, since you are the company's whole output.
principles.quote: when you're making your first few thousands and your first few tens of thousands, that should all be reinvested in yourself

principles.text: Don't let lifestyle creep follow income; save and invest most of what you earn early on.
principles.quote: if I doubled my income, I didn't all of a sudden double my expenses.

principles.text: Wealthy people ask how much a purchase will lose, not what it costs; buy used and let others eat depreciation.
principles.quote: Truly wealthy people do do not ask how much does it cost. They ask how much will I lose?

sources.title: Iman Gadzhi: The three dark sides of running an agency and how to handle them
sources.originalTitle: 99% of Agency Owners FAIL unless they DO THIS
sources.summary: Iman covers the emotional rollercoaster, constant client churn, and the fact that you can't hide from people when running an agency. He argues for three-month minimums, treating retention as the biggest profit lever, and doing sales yourself, drawing on four years of agency experience.

principles.text: Sign every client on a three-month minimum so you have time to get results before they panic.
principles.quote: every single person watching this should be signing clients on a three-month minimum like that should just be a a given

principles.text: Retention is the biggest lever in an agency; it is easier to keep a client than to sign a new one.
principles.quote: it is much easier to keep a client than it is to sign a new one

principles.text: Raising average retention from about 7 to 10-11 months lifts profit around 50% with zero new clients.
principles.quote: i will literally make 50 more profit so hypothetically as an example i would go from 400 000 pounds a year from the agency to 600 000 pounds by signing no extra clients

principles.text: Accept churn as part of the model, since even clients getting great results can leave. Fight it with better results and incentives for longer contracts.
principles.quote: you could be getting clients incredible results and they'll still leave you right and it just comes with it it comes with having an agency

principles.text: Don't outsource sales. Do the call math; a couple of calls a day is a small price for driving revenue yourself.
principles.quote: you can outsource everything as an agency owner except for sales

principles.text: Treat the emotional swings as seasons: stop labeling things good or bad and remember this too shall pass.
principles.quote: it's really important to disassociate from or disassociate and stop labeling things as this is good this is bad it's all part of the process

sources.title: Iman Gadzhi's 7 productivity hacks: protect attention, plan the night before, cut daily decisions
sources.originalTitle: 7 Productivity Hacks That Made Me a Millionaire
sources.summary: Iman Gadzhi argues productivity comes from guarding attention and removing decisions, not from elaborate routines. He covers treating YouTube and books as entertainment, planning tomorrow tonight, uniform clothes and meals, deleting TikTok, muting Instagram, and a short three-step morning routine.

principles.text: Learning only counts when it is intentional and tied to a problem you know you must solve; passive consumption is entertainment.
principles.quote: the only thing that I would consider proper learning is when you know exactly what you need to do and you're educating yourself on how to do it

principles.text: Strip algorithmic feeds (home feed, sidebar, comments) and keep only subscriptions to protect attention and focus.
principles.quote: you need to be extremely diligent with where you put your attention

principles.text: Plan tomorrow the night before with just three to five tasks so you start the day with intention.
principles.quote: just very simply write three to five things down tonight before tomorrow starts and you'll see your brain starts working overnight and you go into tomorrow with real intention

principles.text: Remove repeat decisions: wear a simple uniform, meal prep the same food for the week, lay out clothes the night before.
principles.quote: the worst thing in the morning that you can have is the decision fatigue of deciding okay what am I going to wear today

principles.text: Treat food as fuel so it doesn't consume your life; save enjoyment for holidays and restaurants.
principles.quote: make sure food does not take up a crazy amount of your life meal prep at the beginning of the week and just make sure it's the same food for the entire week

principles.text: Keep the morning routine to three steps and under about 90 minutes; long routines are fluff.
principles.quote: just make sure it's a three-step morning routine no 10-step or 12 step and nothing that takes four hours

sources.title: Iman Gadzhi's 2025 lessons: own stakes, work with people you love, keep the chip
sources.originalTitle: Future Billionaire Shares Expensive Life Lessons From 2025
sources.summary: Iman reflects on 2025: why he now prefers owning 5-20% of big companies over building his own, why who you build with matters more than the mission, and why he keeps some businesses as pure passion projects. He also explains why a chip on your shoulder is still useful after success.

principles.text: Own 5-20% of strong companies rather than building every business yourself; ownership compounds.
principles.quote: I like to buy anywhere from 5 to 20% of a company. Anything more than 20% and I just don't really want to be involved in the changing of a CRM or like really the minutia.

principles.text: Early on think short-term and take cash, but learn the long-run value of equity as you grow.
principles.quote: no one teaches you the value of ownership. And of course, that's not to say if you have a bad company that offers you you know, 20% of nothing is still nothing.

principles.text: Who you build with matters more than the mission; a small, well-served problem is enough.
principles.quote: To me it's not what you do in life it's who you do it with

principles.text: Life is too short to work with people you don't respect; no ego and clear roles make work fun.
principles.quote: Life's too short to work with people you don't love and respect.

principles.text: Keep passion businesses separate from how you make money, and don't chase scale tactics you don't want to do.
principles.quote: I've always been very good at keeping my passion away from like how I make my money.

principles.text: Keep a chip on your shoulder as a driver even after big wins.
principles.quote: I actually think you need to keep that chip on your shoulder.

sources.title: Change Your Life in 6 Months: action-based goals and picking a money skill
sources.originalTitle: Change Your Life in 6 Months (My 5-Step Process)
sources.summary: Iman argues you should replace result goals with measurable daily-action goals, then pick one monetizable skill using four filters (ease of learning, perceived value, barrier to entry, personality fit). He shows how to turn copywriting, cart-recovery sales or viral TikTok e-commerce into a concrete action count, and notes that most people fail because they lack a proper execution plan. The video ends in a pitch for his courses.

principles.text: Set action-based goals, not result goals. Results become a byproduct of consistent actions.
principles.quote: you have to stop setting result oriented goals because these types of goals more often than not hurt more than they help

principles.text: A good goal is measurable by volume of work, so you know exactly where you failed and what to fix.
principles.quote: if you fail to execute on an action based goal you know exactly where you failed you know exactly how far away you were from the goal and what you need need to improve on

principles.text: Choose a money skill by four parameters: ease of learning, perceived value, barrier to entry, and personality fit.
principles.quote: we're going to have to use four parameters the first one is ease of learning

principles.text: Personality fit is the most overlooked factor. Pick a skill that plays to your strengths, not a one-size-fits-all method.
principles.quote: you have to choose something that plays to your strengths rather than your weaknesses

principles.text: Learn as you earn: write free spec work for target brands, send the best pieces, and convert responders to retainers.
principles.quote: the amount of paying clients you get is directly related to the amount of copy that you write and send to these M clients

principles.text: A risk-free, commission-only offer is easy to say yes to, such as recovering abandoned carts for a cut of recovered sales.
principles.quote: there's literally zero risk for them because they only pay for the sales that you recover which would be sales that they wouldn't have gotten otherwise

sources.title: Monk Mode: how Iman Gadzhi clears distractions and builds a custom focus protocol
sources.originalTitle: Monk Mode - What It Takes To Win.
sources.summary: Iman argues focus comes from starving distraction: block feeds on your computer, strip your phone, optimize your workspace, then run a time-boxed "monk mode" with a few non-negotiables plus your own variables. He favors a flexible protocol over rigid challenges like 75 Hard and starts beginners at 21 days.

principles.text: Focus is mostly starving distraction; remove clutter instead of adding productivity apps.
principles.quote: most people just have too much [ __ ] in their lives when they try to go online and learn a new productivity system you know they try to download a new app and what they do is they add even more clutter to their lives

principles.text: Use systems, not willpower: hard-block distracting sites during focused work.
principles.quote: it's not enough to say that you're not going to go on youtube or facebook etc you have to put systems in place to ensure it doesn't happen

principles.text: Keep the phone off and minimal in the morning; track screen time and treat lowering it as a challenge.
principles.quote: from my experience you lose 50 of your focus instantly right

principles.text: Use YouTube intentionally with a note-taking app open; most of it is procrastination disguised as learning.
principles.quote: if you do use youtube you want to use it in a very intentional way right so if you have a topic that you want to learn about look it up add it to your watch later

principles.text: Reward early profits with tools that make you more productive (desk, chair, computer, headphones) rather than status purchases.
principles.quote: when you're first making money spend it on making your life more pleasant and easier not buying gucci to impress people who you don't even care about

principles.text: Run monk mode with three non-negotiables plus two custom variables, starting with 21 days, because rigid protocols don't fit entrepreneurs.
principles.quote: i think 21 days for the first cycle in a case where you may not have the strongest discipline i think is a very very good idea to begin with

sources.title: Iman Gadzhi's 7 habits to $10M by 21: skills, character, investing
sources.originalTitle: 7 Habits That Made Me A Multi-Millionaire By 21
sources.summary: Iman lists seven habits he credits for reaching $10M liquid by 21: weekly reading, high-income skills, an abundance mindset, daily meditation, high-value skills, character over tactics, and early investing. He says to build the business first, then let investments compound.

principles.text: Learn high-income skills early, even without a clear payoff; they compound later.
principles.quote: even if you don't know how a high income skill will help you in the future just learn it regardless

principles.text: Stack complementary skills (copy, social growth, creative) into one offer.
principles.quote: those three high income skills came together to form my creative agency and that's how i was a 17 year old pulling in 25 000 months from my agency

principles.text: After high-income skills, build high-value ones you aren't paid for directly, like hiring and keeping talent.
principles.quote: i'm incredibly incredibly good at going out there finding convincing attracting talent and then also keeping them with me for years and years and years

principles.text: Ask who you need to become, not which tactic to use; tactics follow character.
principles.quote: always focus on who you need to become in order to reach your goals not on what tactic or trick to use

principles.text: Emotional control drives wealth; meditation exposes unconscious triggers behind spending and habits.
principles.quote: half of building wealth is maintaining emotional homeostasis

principles.text: Build the business first, then invest; investments make wealth long-term.
principles.quote: your business is going to make you rich but your investments will make you wealthy long-term

sources.title: Iman Gadzhi on beginner-safe businesses, intentional personal brands, and why content rewards beat ads
sources.originalTitle: Why I Struggled With Money, Focus, and Fame | Iman Gadzhi
sources.summary: Iman Gadzhi explains why beginners should pick digital products or services where failure is cheap, how to build a personal brand around a specific business goal, and why intensity must give way to patience and rigid routines give way to new interests. He also shares his case for WAP's content rewards as an advertising channel.

principles.text: Beginners should pick businesses where failing costs little: digital products or services, not inventory or ad-heavy models.
principles.quote: I like businesses where you can fail for 6 months, 12 months. And by the way, I don't view anything as a failure. I view it as you're getting closer and closer

principles.text: Start with simple services or cheap products to get a foot in the door; don't copy the end-stage moves of someone far ahead.
principles.quote: So, I started off by doing simple services for local businesses. So, yeah. Is are these opportunities going to make you a multimillionaire? No. But it's it's your foot through the door.

principles.text: Be intentional with a personal brand: define the business benefit you want, and don't equate views with success.
principles.quote: number one mistake is not being intentional

principles.text: Match content to the buyer: split into niche channels so advice for a specific audience reaches that audience and funnels to the right back-end offer.
principles.quote: the more niche the advice the more niche the market.

principles.text: Content rewards (paying clippers and creators) can deliver reach at a fraction of Facebook ad CPMs while paying your fans instead of the platforms.
principles.quote: you're accomplishing advertising at like a, you know, 10% or 5% the CPM of what it would cost on Facebook.

principles.text: Hold urgency in the short term and patience in the long term; intensity gets you off the ground, but plateaus break when you loosen the routine and add interests.
principles.quote: short term you have to have this feeling of urgency but then in the more medium term you have to have this understanding that like you are young.

sources.title: Iman Gadzhi on CEOCAST: competitive advantage, service businesses and personal brand
sources.originalTitle: IMAN GADZHI: Future Billionaire's Ultimate Guide To Make Money Online & Build Wealth
sources.summary: Iman explains how his approach changed from 7/10 to full throttle: only enter businesses where he holds an edge, use his personal brand to feed them, and hire operators over thinkers. He also lays out why low-risk service businesses sold to other businesses are the best beginner path.

principles.text: Only start or buy businesses where you hold a real competitive advantage, ideally one your audience can feed.
principles.quote: I've built my businesses synergistically so I've I don't get into business unless I know I have a competitive advantage

principles.text: Pick a beginner business where you can fail for a year and not get wiped out.
principles.quote: I can't think of many businesses in the world where you can start it for 18 months you can fail fail fail fail fail and it won't bankrupt you

principles.text: If you sell a service, sell it to businesses rather than broke consumers.
principles.quote: if you're going to sell a service you might as well serve it sell the service to not broke people and not broke people are businesses

principles.text: Service arbitrage works because clients pay upfront and contractors get paid after delivery, creating positive cash flow.
principles.quote: we're getting paid up front and then the contractor is getting paid once the work gets delivered so you have that little positive uh Arbitrage play and you have that cash flow play

principles.text: Everyone should build a personal brand because it lifts whatever business they run.
principles.quote: anyone should build a personal brand because there will there is a correlation to whatever it is that they're doing in their business

principles.text: Hire operators to run the company, not visionaries who duplicate the founder.
principles.quote: there's certain people that are operators there's certain people that are thinkers and this I'll be honest there certain people that are very good at thinking but sometimes you don't want a thinker in that position in the company

sources.title: How Iman Gadzhi went from dropout to $2M with an SMMA: outreach, retainers, systems
sources.originalTitle: IMAN GADZHI: How A 17-Year-Old Dropout Made His First $2 Million From His Laptop! (SMMA)
sources.summary: Iman recounts building a social media agency from a £300/month soccer club client to six figures a month. He covers the fake audit cold outreach, the Expedia-style contractor model, why results-based services beat content retainers, and the founder discipline that kept him scaling.

principles.text: Cold outreach: use a fake video audit with a play button so replies show who is ready.
principles.quote: I just take a photo of their home screen add a little play button so it looks like it's a video even though it's on the email

principles.text: Pitch business owners on 'leaving money on the table' and a mismatch between their brand and their size.
principles.quote: your social media isn't congruent to the size of your business

principles.text: Sell services and hire contractors to deliver, so you're a business owner, not a glorified contractor.
principles.quote: I realize I am the headless chicken you know I'm client I'm delivering these services for my clients I'm doing it myself I'm not a business owner

principles.text: Work on the business, not in it: build systems, test them, then move to the next one.
principles.quote: you need to work on the business not in it

principles.text: Hire passionate contractors from niche communities like Facebook groups, not gig marketplaces.
principles.quote: the best place to look is actually Facebook groups

principles.text: Use a three-month minimum contract so day-30 emotional decisions don't kill the client.
principles.quote: just making sure that you do a three month minimum for all of your agency clients just allows you that breathing room

sources.title: How Iman Gadzhi runs 1M+ registrant launches: mass-market messaging, short-form reach, offers built on objections
sources.originalTitle: Iman Gadzhi's Unfiltered Business Strategy | Russell Brunson Interview
sources.summary: Iman Gadzhi explains how his team runs quarterly challenges with 1.2M registrants. He covers speaking to the four audience tiers, using short-form purely for reach to cut ad costs, building offers around objections, and baking in refunds. He also stresses profitability over revenue and building on existing competitive advantages.

principles.text: There are four markets; pick which one you serve. Mass market needs very different language and mindset work than beginners.
principles.quote: There's actually four markets. There's beginner, mid-market, advanced, and then, uh, mass market.

principles.text: Use short-form purely for reach, with no CTAs. Familiarity with your face lowers later ad costs.
principles.quote: Like we have no CTAs in any of our short form ever.

principles.text: Put ego aside and optimize for profit, not vanity revenue.
principles.quote: I think one thing that we've been able to do quite well over the years is put our ego to the side and focus on profitability rather than revenue.

principles.text: Design offers by starting from the buyer's objection, then license or build whatever solves it in advance.
principles.quote: the first thing that we do is we think about what's the objection and then we reverse engineer from there.

principles.text: Evaluate opportunities by your competitive advantages and build an ecosystem around your core, not new unfamiliar domains.
principles.quote: I'm just looking at what are my competitive advantages what are our competitive advantages and like how can I build on that

principles.text: Bake a refund cost into the business and refund generously to avoid complaints and regulator attention.
principles.quote: no matter what business you're in, I would just bake in a get tax where it's like you're you're you're acknowledging that you are being rinsed.

sources.title: Iman Gadzhi on info business: chase profit and organic brand, skip revenue vanity and low-ticket recurring
sources.originalTitle: Iman Gadzhi Exposes The Info Industry & How He Made $100m With It (BRUTAL Interview)
sources.summary: Iman argues info is a roughly 3/10 difficulty business where margins, organic traffic and a personal brand beat revenue bragging and paid ads. He explains why low-ticket recurring info fails on LTV math, how to treat YouTube like an ad platform, and why your business should follow your life design.

principles.text: Judge an info business by profit and margin, not revenue. Take less revenue for higher margins and less complexity.
principles.quote: I would rather make technically 50% less money I'd rather make 2 million rather than 3 million but with higher margins and less headache and less complexity

principles.text: Organic customers beat paid-traffic customers: they trust you more, refund less and forgive hiccups.
principles.quote: you're getting customers from pay traffic which are not quality customers in comparison to organic customers they're customers that are going to have a higher refund rate a higher dispute rate

principles.text: Avoid low-ticket recurring info offers. Work backwards from LTV and customer count, not MRR.
principles.quote: the issue is info and recurring don't go hand inand cuz imagine you bought a book today and in 4 months they're still charging you for it

principles.text: Treat YouTube like an ad platform: the thumbnail is the creative, the title is the hook, the concept is the targeting.
principles.quote: I view YouTube like I've actually just view like an ad platform I look at the thumbnail as a creative and the title as the hook

principles.text: Optimize for lead quality, not virality. Build a micro-niche brand that attracts actual buyers.
principles.quote: don't focus on trying to go viral you just want to build a Micro Niche personal brand

principles.text: Design your life first, then choose a business model and scale that fits it. Don't chase bigger numbers for ego.
principles.quote: if you don't create a life design you'll be living by someone else's design

sources.summary: Iman Gadzhi explains how he stacked self-education, health, social skills and wealth in order, runs 6 months of monk mode followed by months of play, and why he teaches agencies as the lowest-risk path to 10k a month. principles.text: Stack skills in an order that compounds; ask if a skill still pays off if the current business disappears.
principles.quote: let's say if that business goes away, is that something that's will still you know um give me dividends for decades to come.

principles.text: Immerse intensely in a habit, then back out and integrate it sustainably.
principles.quote: I get really immersed in it and then I sort of try to integrate.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Iman walks through a live two-call close of an e-commerce client, showing how he pre-frames results and culture fit, sets a performance fee that only kicks in above the client's existing baseline, and uses a break for partners to decide. The closing talk covers why the structure keeps incentives aligned and protects against churn at high billables.

chunks.heading: How Iman structures a performance-based e-commerce deal (live two-call close)
chunks.text: **Context:** Iman closes an e-commerce brand (Swedish store, run by two founders aged 23) for his Facebook ads agency. They spent €60k on ads and generated €200k revenue in their first month. The founder was running ads himself 4-5 hours a day. The first month billed 7,144 pounds (about $12,000 including the base retainer). Iman expected the second month's performance fee to land around 15,000 pounds.

chunks.heading: The two-call close and stalling
chunks.text:
- Iman had just traveled about 36 hours and hadn't watched the demo call recording. He told the client directly that he couldn't make an offer that day.
- He used the first call as a stall: gather preliminary information, say "no pressure", and pencil in a second call. He called it "a prime example of me stalling" since he "basically knew nothing about the client going into it".
- He now uses Zoom's waiting room feature to avoid two-call closes: put the prospect in the waiting room, confer with his media buyer Danny for a few minutes, then reconvene.
- On the second call, the two founders asked to talk privately. Iman had them mute and call each other, rather than kicking the decision to a later date. They came back and said yes.

chunks.heading: Questions to qualify and set expectations
chunks.text:
- Asks what success looks like in 6 months. The client answered 500k to 1M a month at a 2.5-3 ROAS.
- Asks whether they mean total business revenue or revenue the agency brings. He pushes for a specific number "so we can just gather expectations", since "500k a month at a 7x ROAS" wouldn't be realistic.
- Pulls real numbers: spend, revenue, best-selling product share (70% from one LED spotlight), and margins (bought for about $6, sold for about 30 euros).
- Asks why they want an agency. Answer: to stop managing ads all day and focus on warehouse, stock, and expansion into other countries.
- Asks about past agency experience. The client's prior agency got hacked and lost their business manager and ad money.
- Pushes expansion: a UK client of his, told to advertise in the US, saw US ads reach 3x the business's entire prior volume within 2.5 months. He frames it as "maybe you're thinking a little too small".

chunks.heading: Pre-framing results and culture fit
chunks.text:
- Early in the call he states two things must be a green light: results, and culture fit. He calls this a way to "get them to qualify themselves in a way that's not cringey".
- Results get a green light because the client fits his mold: a store doing 100-150k a month wanting 500k.
- He asks the culture question directly: "Why do you think you would be a good fit for our agency culture?" and gives an example of declining Hodinkee (about 15k a month retainer, a dream client) because "one person had to approve it with another person who had to approve it", which isn't how his agency works.
- Culture is "more important to us than anything": long-term partnership, "a relationship", not a car-salesman transaction.

chunks.heading: The pitch positioning
chunks.text:
- Results-based: "not based on impressions, not based on clicks". The offer only works if the agency improves on what the client does.
- Lean team (himself, Danny, Kieran, Louise), no office since 2018, so the retainer pays for value rather than "an espresso addiction" or a "swanky office".
- Differentiator vs one-dimensional agency owners: he has spent 5-6K a day of his own money on ads, has run a 100,000-person email list (6-7 emails a week), and has negotiated Stripe fees.
- Fully end-to-end after onboarding: the agency does creatives and copy; the client only supplies assets. The client translates the copy to Swedish (done in two minutes, and they add the final touch).
- Over-communicate (weekly Looms, updates) while never chasing the client for creatives.
- Admits upfront "we're expensive", framed as "zero risk, infinite rewards".

chunks.heading: The offer structure (performance above a benchmark)
chunks.text:
- Base retainer of 1,600 pounds a month (about $2,200), described as "tiny".
- Performance fee of 5% of "return on ad spend" (revenue minus ad spend), but only above 100k per month.
- Example: spend 100k, get 300k back = 200k net, 100k above the threshold, so fee is 5% of 100k = 5k. Another: spend 100k, bring back 350k = 250k net, fee on 150k.
- Rationale for the 100k threshold: the client already did about 140k net (200k minus 60k), so he won't "take credit for what you've already done", but 140k "could have been a fluke", so he leaves a margin of safety.
- Rule of thumb: for a client starting from scratch he charges a flat 5% with no stipulation. For a client already doing a decent amount, he sets a baseline and only charges above it. Charging 5% of an existing 200k/month "for doing literally nothing" would be a bad deal.
- A fixed baseline also helps retention: a client already paying 20k+ often starts thinking "we could have a team and an office for this", which he has seen cause churn. Setting a baseline means clients can't say they could have done it themselves.
- Terms: 6-month minimum, then rolling month by month, leave anytime. He introduced the 5-6 month minimum only around 9 months before this recording.
- He doesn't take on clients under about 4,000 pounds a month in billables. The base retainer is "inconsequential" to him; the aim is to push clients toward 400-500k a month, where the money gets "interesting".
- Incentive alignment: no percentage of ad spend or revenue, only of profit after ads. Additional channels (Google, YouTube, Pinterest) cost no extra since the fee is on net outcome. SEO is out of scope (paid traffic only).
- Clients can keep running parallel campaigns and testing their own products.

chunks.heading: Closing and onboarding
chunks.text:
- After the "yes", next steps are immediate: send the invoice, collect company details (registered name, address, VAT ID) on the call, create a Slack channel, send the onboarding link (45 minutes to complete, so the team doesn't chase logins for 3 weeks), then book the onboarding call.
- The cofounder Kieran (background in law) adds contract amendments, delivered within 30-60 minutes.
- Result he shares: first-month bill 7,144 pounds, expected second month around 20-25k dollars total billable, and he sees potential for 40k. The client reported a day of about 350,000 Swedish crowns (about $35,000) in sales while the agency managed 10 ad accounts for them.

chunks.heading: Scaling Facebook ads at $12k/day (e-commerce account walkthrough)
chunks.text:
A second segment (a media buyer walking through a client account; Iman shares it as part of his program) covers a client spending about $12,000 a day across 6 ad accounts, over $1M in 30 days. Before the agency, they spent no more than $2,000 a day.

- Campaign structure: CBOs treated as assets, never edited once live; underperformers are killed and relaunched. Over 400 campaigns across six accounts historically, budgets $50 to $600 a day. ($12,000 at $40 per ad set would be 300 ad sets, which is unmanageable.)
- Mostly CBO, one-day attribution window (tested vs seven-day click), kill on a one-day window.
- Scale aggressively the same day something works; kill less aggressively than you launch, because turning off too fast seems to hurt the pixel.
- Test about four creatives a week per product, pay attention to video ads.
- Funnel benchmarks cited: click to page view over 85% (account at 88%), page view to add to cart about 9% (5% still good), add to cart to checkout over 90%, checkout to purchase about 65%, store conversion about 5%.
- Facebook performance is "not linear"; launching more assets reduces the role of luck, then you kill the losers.
- Inspiration: the Facebook Ads Library. Scroll for ads running for months (they're working) and ads with multiple versions; check it isn't retargeting.
- Reporting: build ads reporting pivot tables with a standardized attribution setting (needs at least two ad accounts selected) to see totals across accounts.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Iman breaks down the closing process he taught thousands of agency owners: prepare your environment and research the prospect, choose a one-call or two-call structure, then run Rapport, Pre-frame, Discovery, Transition, Pitch and Close. The core ideas are leading the call with authority, making prospects sell themselves in discovery, and pitching a system rather than a service.

chunks.heading: Pre-call setup: tech, environment and presentation
chunks.text:
- Iman says the most important skill in an agency is selling, and "99% of beginner agency owners have absolutely no idea how to sell." The system below is what he has taught to thousands of agency owners over 6 years.
- **Zoom:**
  - Use a paid Zoom Pro account. The free plan caps meetings at 45 minutes, and a 10-minute countdown appears at the top of the screen after 35 minutes. He calls that a terrible first impression, and Pro costs roughly $16 to $20-something a month.
  - Set up meeting reminders. The call may be the most important thing in the agency owner's day, but for the prospect it could be one of nine meetings.
