  - Change the display name from "Zoom user" to your full name, and add a profile picture (a headshot or the agency logo, never blank).
  - Turn on the waiting room so you can get your notes in order and let the prospect in when ready.
- **Look like a business owner:**
  - No bed in the background and nothing that looks like a bedroom.
  - A clean white wall works. So does a tidy office with books, lighting or a hobby collection.
  - No clutter. He keeps one side of his desk "clean pristine" for calls.
- **Audio:** bad audio kills professionalism. He uses a Shure SM7B-type mic (or the cheaper MV7), and used a Blue Yeti earlier. When travelling he uses $20-25 wired Apple EarPods, and notes that many of his wealthiest friends do the same.
- **Lighting and camera:**
  - Use a softbox, or face a window for natural light.
  - A good laptop camera (e.g. MacBook) is fine. You can also use an iPhone as a camera through Zoom, and later buy a dedicated camera.
- **Personal presentation:**
  - Be showered and groomed.
  - Wear a simple collared shirt or well-fitting t-shirt (smart casual or semi-formal).
  - No hoodies, oversized prints or three-piece suits.
- **Internet:** lag throws off the rhythm and raises doubts about professionalism. Upgrade your connection or take calls from a co-working space.

chunks.heading: Researching the prospect before the call
chunks.text:
Iman says to prepare like for a job interview. The research lets you assume familiarity, look professional and build "ammo" for objections. Learn:

- **Scope of product or service:**
  - What they sell, who their target market is, their price points, and services in their field they don't offer.
  - This shows whether they fit your niche, and lets you show knowledge without making them explain everything.
- **Locations:** whether they are a local family-owned business, a franchise or a global e-commerce business, and how wide their market is.
- **Current marketing:**
  - Whether they run ads, are active on social media, or are on lead-gen sites (his examples: Zillow for real estate, Checkatrade for home renovation).
  - This helps you handle objections and craft the angle for why your service adds more value than what they do now.

chunks.heading: One-call close vs two-call close
chunks.text:
Iman used both over the years. Early in his agency career he aimed for one call; later he used two.

- **One-call close:**
  - Discovery through close happens in a single call.
  - It suits more seasoned owners, because you must think on your feet, handle objections quickly and keep energy high.
  - Pros: saves time and removes second-call no-show risk.
  - It works best when the offer varies little between clients, e.g. a simple offer for real estate agents or gym owners.
  - Downside: you have to build the offer on the spot, with no time to crunch numbers.
- **Two-call close:**
  - Call 1 is discovery. Call 2 is the tailored pitch and close.
  - He recommends it for beginners.
  - His agency's deals were complex: performance-based, working with e-commerce and info-product owners. His CMO ran discovery, and then both joined the closing call.
- **Why two calls work better:**
  - **Energy:** prospect energy, attention and interest drop as a call runs longer, and so does close likelihood. He compares it to a big shopping day, where by hour 4 or 5 you can't be bothered to try things on. Two 30-minute calls beat one 60-minute call, and the gap resets energy.
  - **Preparation:** the break lets you review the first call and tailor the presentation to their needs.
  - **Crunching the numbers:** if the prospect isn't at the level you expected, you can tweak the offer (e.g. for a lower-level client). By call 2 he was "70% dead set" on the offer.
- **If new info forced an offer tweak on call 2:**
  - He didn't schedule a third call.
  - He put the client in the Zoom waiting room and talked to his CMO about minimum term, price, and how much should be base versus performance.

chunks.heading: Sales call framework: rapport and pre-frame
chunks.text:
The order is: rapport, pre-frame, discovery, transition, pitch, close.

- **Rapport (2 to 3 minutes):**
  - Break the ice naturally and ask a question or two about them.
  - Avoid weather small talk.
  - Speak with confidence, as if you've done this a thousand times.
  - If you share a commonality (a city, a product), he doesn't mind chatting about it for 2 to 3 minutes.
- **Pre-frame:**
  - Shift tone from casual to business.
  - Every call has one person who leads by asking questions and one who follows by answering. The seller must hold that authority, otherwise "you will get interrupted continuously and the call will inevitably go nowhere."
- **Pre-frame outcome 1: gain authority.** Say you've done this many times and typically know how these calls go. Say you'll be transparent about whether you can help, and ask for the same transparency from them.
- **Pre-frame outcome 2: show no desperation.**
  - Use a line like "If I believe that we can help you at the end of the call we will make you an offer, but if not we're going to try to point you in the direction of someone that can."
  - This puts the prospect at ease and draws them in, since "people want what they can't have."
- **Pre-frame outcome 3: agree an outcome.**
  - Say you just want "a yes or a no, let's avoid the maybe."
  - This heads off "I need to think about it" and "I need to speak to my wife" later.

chunks.heading: Discovery: the five elements
chunks.text:
Iman calls discovery "arguably the most important part of any call." The aim is to highlight the problem so the prospect mentally sells themselves.

1. **Current state:** what they do, what they charge, average monthly sales, profit margins and monthly profit (you can work it out), and how they currently get clients.
2. **Future state:** financial goals, how client acquisition must change to hit them, and the timeline.
3. **Gap:** how many extra sales or clients they need per month. Judge whether your service can fill it. Also ask what their plan was if you hadn't approached them, and politely challenge them if they have none.
4. **Opportunity cost:**
   - Ask whether having your promised outcome would bring them closer to their goals.
   - Ask whether what they're doing now will get them there.
   - "When you say it, it means nothing, but when they say it themselves is when your message is hitting."
5. **Doubt:**
   - Ask why they haven't tried something like this before.
   - Ask whether it's their first time hearing about it, whether they've had bad agency experiences, and whether they doubt agencies bring value.
   - Surfacing this lets you manage objections before pitching.

chunks.heading: Transition into the pitch
chunks.text:
The transition is the bridge from discovery to pitch. It shows you listened and gets buy-in to hear the offer.

- **Last chance to add info.** Example wording: "Thank you for all the information. Is there anything I missed or any information you'd like to share in order for me to understand your current situation better?"
- **Confirm synergy and fit.** Example: "Now that I have a good understanding of where you're at and where you're looking to get to and the gaps that currently exist, I think we could definitely help you get to your goals."
- **Permission to pitch.**
  - Offer two options: they ask a few questions, or you run them through the whole system from A to Z.
  - Always give the A-to-Z option second, because 99% of prospects won't know what to ask and nearly all will pick it.
  - Example: "…or alternatively what I can do is just run you through the process on how we help XYZ type of client, and you can ask me questions along the way. How would you prefer to do this?"
- **Final outcome agreement.** Example: "My goal is to make sure that you have complete clarity… by the end of today's call would it be out of this world to say that we could get you started today?" This surfaces third-party decision-maker objections early.

chunks.heading: The pitch: system, guarantee, testimonials, price
chunks.text:
- **Pitch a system, not a service.** Business owners see services as expenses and systems as investments, so a tangible system raises perceived value. Keep it simple: "confused buyers never buy."
- **Guarantee:** if you have one, use it. Showing you bear the risk makes the offer a no-brainer because the prospect has nothing to lose.
- **Testimonials:**
  - Get them from clients as soon as you can.
  - Other people vouching shows the offer works, and credibility is why sales get easier over time.
- **Price:**
  - State it with confidence after they understand the system, guarantee and proof.
  - Do not justify the price, because justifying "radiates desperation."
  - Use silence after stating it, whatever their reaction.
  - He generally doesn't recommend offering multiple price options.

chunks.heading: Closing, collecting payment and onboarding
chunks.text:
- **Agree on the close:** get a solid yes.
- **Contract and invoice:** have both ready before the call. Send them as soon as the prospect agrees, and push them to sign on the call, giving them a few minutes to read.
- **Collect cash on the call:**
  - "A client is only a client once they have paid."
  - Push for the full first-month fee.
  - If contract terms cause confusion, take a deposit for now. A deposit shows they are on board, and without payment nothing stops them ghosting.
- **Onboarding:** once paid, send the onboarding funnel, briefly explain the process, and say you and your team will help with any issues.

chunks.heading: Mindset principles for agency sales
chunks.text:
- **Sales is problem solving.** A strong discovery makes the prospect aware of their problems, so they see the solution sitting in front of them.
- **Confidence is everything.**
  - How the prospect feels talking to you drives trust.
  - Nervousness creates objections and doubts.
  - Confidence comes from experience, which comes from preparation and reps: book as many meetings as possible and do mock calls with other agency owners.
- **Businesses buy into you.**
  - Many people sell marketing services, and the biggest differentiator between agencies is the owner, not the service.
  - Present well, speak with confidence and earn trust.
- **Failure isn't final.**
  - Review calls that didn't close to find what to improve.
  - In business, unlike formal education, failing a test is a chance to improve for the next one.
- His stated target: implementing these steps and improving them should get you to a "$10,000 a month agency by the end of the year."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Iman walks through four agency deals closed in one weekend. He explains how he anchors price, trades lower retainers for longer minimums to raise guaranteed value, and separates logistics questions from objections. He also covers collecting payment on the call and his guarantee.

chunks.heading: How Iman prices and structures SMMA retainers (October 2020)
chunks.text:
- **Standard pricing:** minimum set retainer of £4,000/month, rising to about £12,000/month, with a percentage of return on ad spend (ROAS) added in the past. Case study or webinar funnel builds are charged £15,000-£25,000 upfront.
- **New approach:** he blends the funnel build into the retainer. He charges less per month but locks in a longer minimum, so the guaranteed contract value stays similar. Everything rolls month by month after the minimum.
- **Deals in one weekend:**
  - £2,500/month, 6-month minimum (£15,000 guaranteed)
  - £4,000/month, 5-month minimum (£20,000)
  - £3,500/month, 5-month minimum (£17,500)
  - £2,500/month, 6-month minimum (£15,000)
  - He sums these to roughly $80,000 of guaranteed contractual income (his total in the video does not match the line items, so only the "~$80,000" is reliable), with no new team members needed.
- **Why longer minimums:** "churn is not a fun thing at any agency." Longer client lifetime value beats chasing whales. His goal is an average retention of 12-18 months.
- **Guaranteed value over headline price:** he compares an £8K/month client on a 3-month minimum (£24K) with a £4K/month client on a 6-month minimum (£24K). He now thinks in terms of the "guaranteed value of the client."
- **Extending an existing client:** he dropped a 15% ROAS fee for a client paying £3,000/month plus 15%, in exchange for a 6-month extension. That put the client on at least 10 months total.
- **When to take percentage of ROAS:** only for info product businesses without a phone call funnel (a direct purchase on a sales page) or for e-commerce. Phone call funnels are "a nightmare" to track for a percentage.
- **Cost of lower-margin deals:** he accepts smaller deals when the team can deliver cheaply. A case study funnel takes his team (Kieran and Danny) about a day, so it costs little of his time. He would not take a £4,000/month, 3-month deal on that basis.

chunks.heading: Anchoring price with a guess and the "machine" framing
chunks.text:
- **Anchoring:** on one call he asked the prospect to guess the agency's price. The prospect guessed "at least 4K per month," which was right. Iman then quoted £2,500/month with a 6-month minimum, so it "seems like a total steal." He says this is not part of his normal script.
- **Cost-replacement framing:** the prospect was paying about $4K/month in commissions to closers. Iman framed the agency as replacing that: "a machine never wants a raise," works 24/7, and is never sick.
- **Value framing:** the client was making multiple five figures a month and shouldn't be running his own ads at that scale. Iman told him, "you're fired" from ads so he could focus on CEO work.
- **Guarantee:** at that time he guaranteed 1.5x return on ad spend, with a refund of service fees if missed. He had refunded only once in the agency's history. He says the guarantee puts all the risk on him, which is why he needs to trust his team on every deal.

chunks.heading: Logistics handling versus objection handling
chunks.text:
- **The distinction:** objection handling is for prospects who are not sold. Logistics handling is for prospects who are sold but need to understand how the service works.
- **Example:** a prospect with a working system feared Iman's team would replace it with a new funnel and cut his income. Iman explained the sequence: take over and improve the current system, build the new funnel in parallel, run ads to it, and only retire the old system once the new one outperforms it. After that the deal closed.
- **Tonality:** the prospect sounded unenthusiastic, but Iman read it as a logistics concern, not a lack of interest.
- **Taking payment:** he does not leave a call until payment is taken. "Unless I take payment, they ain't a client." Even £1 with a card on file counts as a commitment.
- **Billing friction:** invoicing took 22 minutes of a 47-minute call because of a European client's credit limit. He found German, Swiss and Dutch clients commonly have this problem, and US and UK clients less so. He prefers automatic billing over manual invoicing.
- **Easing payment:** he invoices on the call, asks for company details in the Zoom chat, and sets up Slack and the strategy session right away. With one client he considered offering PayPal to close faster but decided against it.

chunks.heading: The demo call plus close structure
chunks.text:
- **Setup:** his CMO Danny runs a 15-minute demo call to qualify prospects. At the time they were doing 2-3 demo calls a day. About 50% of demos were qualified, though the latest ones were nearly all qualified. Iman then takes the 45-minute discovery and close.
- **Delegating the decision:** Iman does not take deals he is unsure about. Danny can push for a lower-priced deal if he is confident he can run the account without it becoming a burden. Iman needs trust in him first.
- **Friction and call count:** a third call nearly lost one deal. One prospect was 8 minutes late because of a time zone mix-up. "Any sort of added friction really ruins the likeliness of the sale." He prefers a one-call close, but will do two calls when needed and says a second call is fine if it is guaranteed to happen.
- **Not a tactic:** a prospect said he noticed Iman's "I need to talk to Danny" tactic. Iman said it was not a tactic: the guarantee means he really must check that the account is viable before agreeing.
- **Goal:** the last thing he wants to remove himself from is sales. Once he does, he will have a "totally automated agency."

chunks.heading: Which clients to take (and which niches to avoid)
chunks.text:
- **Info product businesses are hard:** about 80% of his clients are info product businesses, and about 50% of deals require extra work such as building a case study funnel or cleaning up automations and emails. He calls it "the hardest niche in the world."
- **Advice for beginners:** don't run ads for info product businesses at first. Start with local businesses or e-commerce. E-commerce is "a hell of a lot easier," but still harder than local businesses.
- **Deals he turns down:** he nearly turned down a £4,000/month deal because of the complexity of the funnel build, and he declines B2B all-in-one platforms because the agency does not do B2B. In one case he considered referring a prospect to a strategic referral partner.
- **B2B check:** for a B2B prospect he asked for the client's lifetime value and how much they would pay to acquire a customer. He reasoned from his own B2B agency numbers: he is comfortable spending about £6,000 to acquire a client against an average retainer of about £6,000 per month. The prospect's number fit his estimated cost per scheduled call. The deal was £2,500/month, 6-month minimum, with no guarantee, using deliberately pessimistic assumptions (a 15% close rate versus the prospect's actual 80%).
- **Cost to serve:** he keeps complexity low internally and with clients, which he says is why the agency gets such good results.

chunks.heading: Margins, business buckets and team
chunks.text:
- **Agency:** 75-90% margins, which he calls his "lifestyle business." He never lets it dip below 75% (he later says 65%, so treat the floor as roughly 65-75%). His stated goal is $150K/month profit, after hitting $100K/month the previous year.
- **Education company:** 25-35% margins. Costs include around £30,000/month on advertising, £4,000/month on software, £35,000/month on staff, schools in Nepal, and events. He won't let it fall below about 20%.
- **Clothing line (Gadzhi):** about 60% margins. He is willing to scale it to seven figures in revenue at zero profit, because it is a passion project and he reasons about each business in a separate bucket. Plan: an influencer manager and 10-20K/month on influencer promotions, rather than scaling to 300K/month through ads.
- **Hiring:** he cut 150 performance marketer applicants to seven, then three final interviews. Candidates had spent more than $20 million on ads. Rather than paying a recruiter £4-8K, he passed the strong runners-up to his students.
- **Rhythm:** after months focused on other companies, he spends the next several months on agency growth. He expects the agency to stay in maintenance mode while he works on others.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Iman Gadzhi argues every sales objection is really a trust objection hidden behind a smokescreen. He teaches prevention (answer all questions, then a 1-10 tie-down before pricing) and a five-step process for any remaining objection: diffuse, reframe to the goal, tie down, isolate, overcome.

chunks.heading: Prevent objections before pricing
chunks.text:
Iman says a good closer handles objections but a great closer prevents them, and the goal is the prospect pulling out their credit card, not objection handling. He wants closing to be as easy as possible. Before discussing price on any SMMA sales call he does two things:

- **Answer every question first.** "A confused buyer never buys," so if the prospect still has questions, don't go into pricing.
- **Run a 1 to 10 tie down.** He asks: on a 1 to 10 scale, with 1 being "get me off this call right now" and 10 being "this is exactly what I've been looking for," where do you fall?
- This gauges interest and surfaces doubts. If they say 8 or lower, follow up with: "gotcha, appreciate you sharing that with me. Out of curiosity, what's stopping you from being a nine or a 10?"
- The answer shows their main concerns, lets you address them, and moves them toward a 10 so they're sold on the offer by the time price comes up.

He says that if discovery calls are run correctly there should be few or no objections to handle.

chunks.heading: Every objection is a trust objection hidden behind a smoke screen
chunks.text:
Iman argues every objection is essentially trust-based: the prospect doesn't trust you, your agency, or themselves. Nobody says "I don't trust you and I think you're lying," so they use "smoke screens" that feel socially acceptable and let them exit without feeling forced to buy.

- Typical smoke screens: "I need to speak to my spouse," "I need to run the numbers and think about it for a day or two," "it's too expensive and I might not afford it."
- His test: if your agency were guaranteed to work and hit their goals, would they need to think about it, would money be a problem? No, they'd get creative to find a solution.
- His analogy: if you were diagnosed with a terminal illness and a guaranteed cure cost $100,000, you'd borrow, sell assets or take loans to get it.
- The aim is for prospects to trust your agency can deliver so completely that money, time and other objections "melt away."
- So the real issue is never that they lack money or need to consult someone; they don't yet trust you to get them to their goals.

chunks.heading: The five categories of objections
chunks.text:
Iman says every objection, however unique it seems, falls into one of five categories:

1. Think about it
2. Business partner or spouse
3. Finances
4. Doubt
5. Logistics (his favorite)

Knowing the categories lets you build a framework for each and handle any objection thrown your way.

chunks.heading: The five-step framework, steps 1 and 2: diffuse and reframe
chunks.text:
**Step 1: Diffuse.** Beginners treat objections as rejections and get defensive, which is the last thing to do. Instead, avoid confronting the prospect and make their concerns feel valid for the moment.

- Lines: "I can respect that," "I totally understand that," "yeah, that's not a problem at all."
- Why: the prospect has effectively said no and expects you to push back. Pushing triggers fight or flight and the sale is lost for good.
- His analogy: a 10-year-old told by mom to brush their teeth who says no, knowing a fight is coming. Prospects feel the same, so show you're on their side.

**Step 2: Reframe to the goal.** Using Covey's "begin with the end in mind," shift focus from the objection to the end goal they want.

- Line: "Just so I know, before you think about this, do you actually feel like we can get you to your goals? Because for me personally that's the only part that really matters."
- This reminds them why they considered the service, makes the call outcome-focused, and reveals how convicted they are.
- Listen to tonality. Some say yes just to be polite. If your gut says something is off: "From your tonality just there I can sense maybe something is missing. If you're not being honest with me, maybe you're just being polite, I'd rather know what's on your mind. If it's not the right fit, it's not the right fit. So to go back, do you really feel like we can get you to your desired goal?"
- Doing this effectively jumps you to isolating the objection (step 4).

chunks.heading: Steps 3 to 5: tie down, isolate, overcome
chunks.text:
**Step 3: Tie down.** If they sound confident you can get them to their goals, use a tie down, a micro commitment that gets a yes or agreement and shows they're following along.

- Benefits: feedback on where the prospect is, control of the call, "yes momentum," and a sense of how close the deal is.
- Get them to say why your service can help: "Okay cool, why do you feel like that's the case?" Keep it natural, like a friend supporting a friend in a decision.
- Having them verbalize the reasons strengthens their commitment and reduces doubt.

**Step 4: Isolate the real objection.** Once they've said you'll get them results and why, ask: "Yeah, got you. Now when you think about it, what specifically do you feel like you need to think about, just so I have an understanding and maybe I can help?" This surfaces the actual objection, whether financial, time or something else.

**Step 5: Overcome it** with analogies, logic and reframes, chosen to fit the type of prospect.

- He quotes Sun Tzu: know your enemy and know yourself. The better you understand the prospect, the better you choose analogies and reframes.
- Be confident and firm, which is not the same as rude. You have the client's best interest at heart and are helping them see this is the right decision.

chunks.heading: Service over sales mentality
chunks.text:
Iman's mindset for the final step is "service over sales." His rule of thumb: of 10 prospects, one will never buy, one will buy regardless, and eight need your help to decide. Helping them decide from a place of authority is what wins them.

- Treat firmness as service, not pressure.
- Most closes are decided by how well you guide the undecided majority.

chunks.heading: Using word tracks and the objection playbook
chunks.text:
Iman offers an objection playbook (linked in his video description) with word tracks.

- Everyone's sales style differs, so the exact scripts may not suit you; use them as inspiration and add your own twist.
- He says the knowledge has helped thousands of students in his Agency Accelerator program prevent and overcome objections. He cites student Jacob signing clients month on month, and student Aiden reaching $12,000 after 4 weeks servicing real estate agents, with lead sales coach Scott Bruning.
- He points to his separate video on a step-by-step guide to closing clients for your SMMA in 2024 for running discovery correctly.
- His practice advice for learning this: pen and paper, phone on airplane mode, no distractions.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Iman breaks down four ways to build a prospect list for an agency: networking, manual lead sourcing, lead software, and outsourcing to B2B lead gen freelancers. He explains the quantity vs quality trade-off of each and how to pick a combination based on your network, time and money.

chunks.heading: Prospecting is building a contact list of businesses in your niche
chunks.text:
- Iman defines prospecting as "simply building a list of businesses within your Niche businesses that will want to buy from you."
- Example: for kitchen and bathroom remodelers, build a list of every remodeler he can find.
- The list holds whatever contact info the outreach method needs. Cold calling needs a phone number, not an email.
- He teaches four methods: networking, manual lead sourcing, software, and B2B lead generation specialists.
- Each has pros and cons, so he recommends combining them to cover all bases.
- He says these are the methods he used in his agency over 6 years and taught to thousands of students in Agency Accelerator.
- Prospecting is ongoing. He says to build the habit of keeping the prospect list as big as possible.

chunks.heading: Method 1: Networking (best for the first client)
chunks.text:
- If you have a competitive advantage, "use it unapologetically." Friends and family who work in your niche are "absolute gold."
- They can buy from you and also spread the word about your services.
- Tactic: ask for a chat in person, or by Zoom or phone, then break down your service and value proposition.
- Be open that you are a beginner getting your first clients and case studies. He says people appreciate the honesty, and most business owners have been in the same position.
- Two possible outcomes, both wins:
  - They are interested and buy.
  - You ask if they know anyone who would be interested and leave with referrals.
- Disadvantage: volume. Your network is only so big.
- Advantage: when you are starting out, it gives warm, qualified prospects. In his words, "the easiest way to sign your first client."

chunks.heading: Method 2: Manual lead sourcing (free, high quality, slow)
chunks.text:
- Manual lead sourcing means looking for leads online. Search your industry plus location on Google, jump from site to site, and save details into a CRM.
- Google Maps: search an industry and location, then copy phone numbers and emails from the left-hand panel into your list. It is the easiest route for local businesses.
- LinkedIn: search niche keywords. For remodelers, that means terms like contractor, remodelers, builders. LinkedIn Sales Navigator adds advanced search and lead recommendations.
- Instagram: business owners follow each other there. Find one good prospect, go through their followers or following, and keep going down the rabbit hole to build the list fast.
- Online directories: sites where businesses register their contact details. He calls them a "game changer" and "truly underrated."
  - Common for service businesses such as plumbers, electricians, roofers and remodelers.
  - UK example: Checkatrade. Most countries have similar directories.
- Advantage: quality. You find everything yourself, so you know the contact details are correct and active. It costs $0.
- Disadvantage: very time-consuming and tedious.
- He calls it a great place for beginners to start.

chunks.heading: Method 3: Prospecting software (most efficient, lower list quality)
chunks.text:
- Lead generation software lets you enter niche, location, size and revenue, and it pulls thousands or tens of thousands of leads quickly.
- You then import the list into your sales pipeline. His own agency software, Floy, has an import function for this.
- What to look for: it should be user-friendly and give you lots of leads quickly. Compare a few alternatives found by searching "lead generation software."
- Trade-off: quantity over quality. The list will not be perfect, and most tools can't tell whether a prospect is still active.
  - Skim the list and delete irrelevant prospects.
  - Use lead verification software, which flags dead leads when you run a list through it.
- Advantage: time saved and sheer volume. Asked whether the quality hit is worth it, he says "100%."

chunks.heading: Method 4: B2B lead generation specialists (outsourced prospecting)
chunks.text:
- This is the advanced method. It applies his "contractor arbitrage" idea (outsourcing service delivery) to prospecting.
- Hire freelancers on Upwork or Fiverr by searching "B2B lead generation." Hundreds will build lead lists for a small fee.
- Risk: some charge for a subpar service and send random, unqualified businesses, sometimes outside your niche.
- Mitigation:
  - Check client reviews and proof of work, which both platforms show.
  - Buy the lowest package as a low-risk test.
- Package tiers: freelancers usually offer three tiers.
  - The cheapest tier has the highest cost per lead.
  - The top tier is the most expensive overall but has the lowest cost per lead and the most prospects.
- His advice: always buy the first tier, even though each prospect costs a bit more. Judge the list quality. If it's good, buy the top tier. If it's bad, find someone else.
- Advantage: a huge number of qualified leads. Downsides: cost, and risk if you aren't careful.
- His recommendation: if you have extra money to invest in your agency, give it a shot.

chunks.heading: Choosing the right mix: three questions
chunks.text:
- **Have you used your network as much as possible?** If you have an unfair advantage, use it.
- **How much time do you have?**
  - With a demanding job that leaves about 2 hours a day, automate lead sourcing as much as possible.
  - Manual sourcing gives high-quality leads but is too time-consuming in that case. Lean on B2B lead generators and prospecting software.
  - Someone with a day job likely has enough cash to bankroll this for a few weeks without signing clients to pay the bills.
- **How much money can you invest?**
  - Early on there are two ways to grow: time investment (you do the tasks) or capital investment (you pay software or others to do them).
  - With money, invest in software or B2B lead generation experts.
  - Without money, do manual lead sourcing. It takes more effort but gets the same result.
- Whichever you pick, he says to use a combination of methods, since each has advantages and disadvantages.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Iman lays out a 9-step SMMA roadmap, contrasting the traditional local-business route with a "shadow operator" model. In it you partner with micro creators (20k-100k followers), use AI instead of contractors, and take a revenue split instead of selling retainers. Covers niche, offer, outreach, sales, pricing and launch.

chunks.heading: Two ways to run an SMMA in 2026: traditional vs. shadow operating
chunks.text:
Iman says SMMA "still remains one of the best business models for 2026," but argues the way most beginners plan to do it is wrong. He gives two routes and says both work.

- **Traditional:** sell marketing services to local businesses for retainers.
- **New way (shadow operating):** partner with micro creators and take a percentage of what they make from their own audience.

He picks the agency model because it has no big upfront cost, little risk and high margins. It also doesn't require being "a dancing monkey online." He says it is the model where beginners learn the most. He notes that many of his friends with eight- and nine-figure net worths started with an agency or service business, himself included. His first agency was "IG Media," which he calls a terrible name, especially once he moved to paid traffic.

- Agency setup is an admin step you do once and move on from. He says "your agency setup doesn't make money. Prospecting and outreach do."
- Name: keep it simple and don't overthink it. "No one cares about your name as much as you do."
- Domain: if the first choice is expensive, pick a variation or a different TLD such as .io or .org.
- Logo: use Canva or an AI tool. A nice logo won't make the difference between failing and succeeding.
- Google Workspace for a professional email, Zoom for calls, and a website that is optional. He made $20,000 a month before he had one.
- For shadow operating, add a cleanup of your social profile because creators see it first. That means a clean photo, a clear bio, and at least nine posts so the grid is full. He says you don't need a Lamborghini in Dubai, just to look like "someone who has their life together."

chunks.heading: Traditional route: niche selection and service selection
chunks.text:
Iman says to niche down for two reasons, specialization and scalability. His analogy is that you'd trust a brain surgeon over a general practitioner, and the specialist can charge more. With one niche, prospecting, outreach, sales style, delivery and offer all stay the same. With several niches it is "literally like running multiple different businesses."

**Example:** his client Bobby sold to authors who publish on Amazon. He scaled to $150K a month with 100+ clients by repeating the same prospecting, outreach and delivery.

**Criteria for picking a niche:**
- Profit: look for businesses making at least $10,000 a month in profit, not revenue. Otherwise paying you $2,000 feels expensive.
- Ticket size: it is easier to help a solar company that earns $10,000 per job get one more sale than to help a shop with $5 profit per t-shirt.
- Growth: avoid dying industries, such as DVD rental versus info businesses.
- Market size: home renovation has millions of businesses, while Italian wedding dress designers number maybe 50 in a country.
- Sophistication: as a beginner, avoid sophisticated markets such as e-commerce owners who already run ads. If you offer a "4 out of 10" service to someone doing nothing, it beats nothing. If they're already at 6, you must get them to 8.

He says 90% of people get stuck on niche selection and overanalyze it for weeks.

**Service selection:** services are either convenience or ROI.
- ROI services are easier to sell: paid traffic, email marketing, copywriting, SEO, lead generation.
- Convenience services save time: social media management, videography, video editing, reputation management, web design.

To pick one, ask two questions: what is the biggest problem businesses in my niche face, and what is the most efficient way to solve it? Then weigh four factors:
- Skill set: can you deliver it yourself? If so, use it. He started with a creative agency because he was good at creating content.
- Scalability: this mostly comes down to location. He switched from a content agency to an advertising agency because paid ads let you manage 20 clients from a laptop, while video production needs you on-site.
- Upfront cost: copywriting needs a laptop, while videography needs camera gear. Match the service to your current resources.
- Income variation: project-based (for example $4,000 for a website) versus recurring (for example $2,000 a month for 6 months).

chunks.heading: Shadow operating: why micro creators are the target
chunks.text:
Iman says there are an estimated 150 million+ micro creators with 20,000 to 50,000 followers. They have audiences that "know, like and trust" them but earn only a few hundred dollars from brand deals or affiliate links. They are good at content but don't know how to package and sell.

He gives three tiers:
- **Nano (1,000 to 10,000 followers):** too small, with limited monetization potential.
- **Micro (10,000 to 100,000 followers):** the target. Elsewhere in the talk he gives the range as 20,000 to 100,000.
- **Macro (150,000+ followers):** avoid as a beginner, since they already have agents and managers.

**Why this lowers difficulty:**
- You skip niche selection because the creator's niche is already built.
- You don't need to be the expert, because the creator is the expert on fitness, finance, parenting or whatever it is.
- You skip the hardest part of agency work, which is getting attention for a business nobody knows. The audience already exists.
- Creators are unsophisticated buyers. They started from passion, not business, so they are easier to help.

**Example:** a divorced-single-moms account with 40,000+ followers and 10,000+ views per reel on average. The bio has a collab email and a few affiliate links but no product of her own.
- Selling a $50 product to just 1% of her audience would mean about $20,000.

**Proof of demand:** a TikTok creator with 100,000 followers (inner healing) DMed him asking for "AI shadow operators." She said the business and tech side was her challenge. He points to Congo Brands (Prime, which owns 60% of the business) and the Shahiti twins building Happy Dad with the Nelk Boys as examples of shadow operators. He says he met many creators' behind-the-scenes partners at the WAP office.

chunks.heading: Offer creation and pricing
chunks.text:
**Traditional:** an offer is niche + service + pricing model. It bridges the gap between the prospect's current state and desired state. Five components:
- **Promise:** a tangible outcome plus a time frame, such as "30 qualified booked appointments in 90 days" or "four long-form YouTube videos in 60 days."
- **Methodology:** keep it simple. For example, run ads, leads fill a form, qualified ones get booked.
- **Pricing model:** monthly retainer, pay per project, pay per lead, or a percentage of ROAS, plus an optional setup fee.
- **Contract duration:** at least 3 months for recurring services, so you have time to optimize and get results.
- **Free value:** audits, resources, lead reactivation.

**Pricing:** the more money you make for clients, the more you can charge. Start at a price you're comfortable with and test it. If every prospect says yes with no pushback, raise it. If everyone says it's too high, lower it.

**Guarantees:** he is "not the biggest fan" for agency services because they send the wrong message.

**Shadow operator:** there are no fees. You earn a percentage of sales, so the more you make them the more you make.
- Starting splits: he suggests 90/10, 80/20 or 70/30 in the creator's favor, to make the partnership attractive until you gain confidence.
- Free value: a "creator audit" is a document covering who they are, who their audience is and their pain points. He suggests a 2-minute Loom walkthrough.

chunks.heading: Prospecting and outreach
chunks.text:
**Traditional prospecting:**
- Manual: Google Maps, directories and social media.
- Software: Apollo, Leadswift, Leads Gorilla.
- Hire lead generators on Upwork or Fiverr.

**Traditional outreach:** cold calls, cold emails or cold DMs, chosen by where the business owner lives (calls for home renovation owners who are on the move, email for SaaS). It is a numbers game and some prospects will ghost you.

**BAM and Reach:**
- BAM ("bare ass minimum") is a daily number of outreach messages you do no matter what.
- Reach is the stretch number you strive for.
- He attributes much of his agency success to this consistency.

**Shadow prospecting:** find micro creators on Instagram, YouTube, Twitter, TikTok or LinkedIn, and DM them on Instagram, where they're most active.
1. Search niches such as fitness, personal finance, productivity, self-improvement, parenting, relationships, career and mental health.
2. Keep accounts in the 20,000 to 100,000 follower range.
3. Note content type, audience, average reel views, posting frequency, and likes and comments.
4. Check on SocialBlade for an engagement rate of at least 2.5% to 3% (the transcript is garbled here).
5. Use the "suggested accounts" button to find similar creators and repeat.

**Challenge:** build a list of 100 creators. He offers a free prospecting tracker.

**Outreach messages:** short, personalized with their name, about them and not you, and ending with a question. Examples:
- "Hey John, I notice you have a very engaged audience who follows you. Are you currently monetizing your audience?"
- "Hey Sophia, do you currently sell any coaching or mentorship?"

**Goal of outreach:** you are "selling the meeting," not the service. When someone replies, lead with value (the creator audit).

chunks.heading: Sales: traditional call structure vs. shadow operator calls
chunks.text:
**Traditional call:** rapport (2 to 3 minutes), pre-frame, discovery, transition, pitch.
- Pre-frame script: "I'm going to ask you a few questions... all I ask for is transparency... if I believe we can help you, I'll make you an offer. Does that sound fair?"
- Discovery: find the current state, desired state, the gap, the opportunity cost and any doubts. Example questions:
  - "How many clients do you get on average per month?"
  - "How much profit do you want to be making in 6 months?"
  - "Where would you be today if you had a solution 6 months ago?"
  - "Why have you never tried a solution like ours before?"

**Shadow operator (two calls, no pitch):**
- **Call 1:** only gather information. Ask:
  - Their 6 to 12 month goals and income targets.
  - What holds them back.
  - Their audience's biggest problem and frequent questions.
  - What transformation the audience wants.
  - What they've sold before.
  - Their vision (coaching, course, community).
  End by saying you see opportunities and will put together a plan.
- **Call 2:** present the plan and the numbers.

**Worked math (30,000 followers, $95 product, 2.5% conversion):**
- 750 sales × $95 = $71,250.
- 50/50 split: about $35,000.
- 70/30 split: about $21,000.
- 90/10 split: about $7,000.
- All of it is pure profit with no employees.

He stresses this has no upfront cost and no risk to the creator, so there is nothing to overcome.

**Auto revenue split:** he says every recall is a reframe, meaning each time a client remembers to pay you, they reconsider. Creators manually sending a share to a partner creates friction. He says he is a co-owner of WAP, a platform processing almost $200 million a month in payments. His team built an auto revenue split feature. For a $100 sale at 70/30, the creator gets $70 and the operator gets $30 at the moment of sale, so the creator never feels like they're paying you. He compares it to Uber.

chunks.heading: Service delivery: contractor arbitrage vs. AI arbitrage
chunks.text:
**Traditional:** the agency model gets paid upfront, so you stay cash-flow positive when paying contractors.
- Contractor arbitrage: hire skilled people in places like Brazil, South America or Serbia for around $500 per client per month, while you charge the client $2,000.
- Find them on Upwork, Fiverr, Facebook groups or OnlineJobs.ph.
- You still need to know the basics, so you can sell confidently, manage them and quality check.

**Shadow operating:** he says "contractor arbitrage is getting replaced by AI arbitrage." The creator is the expert, and AI tools produce the marketing assets: sales copy, landing pages and course outlines.
- Tools named: Ghostwriter OS (he says he uses it daily and that it produced the story sequence for his own launch) and Synthesize AI for program outlines.
- He says AI doesn't take sick days or raise prices, and does in minutes what took a contractor a week.

**Build on WAP:**
- Mentorship plus community: create the account, product and store page, then add the calendar bookings app and the forums app.
- Video course: same setup but with the courses app. The creator records modules and sends them to you for upload.

chunks.heading: Launching with the Instagram story sequence
chunks.text:
He gives a rule to build anticipation before the product goes in front of the audience. He says there are 15 launch frameworks but recommends starting with the Instagram story sequence. He says it is the same strategy he uses, and that he has "broken the WAP records twice this year."

**Why stories work:**
- Story viewers are the most engaged followers.
- Stories feel intimate, like a conversation.
- They disappear in 24 hours, which creates urgency and FOMO.
- A first-ever product has pent-up demand.

**Format:** a 14-day sequence with three phases: warm-up, pre-launch, open cart. The creator posts 5 to 10 stories a day using a Hook, Story, CTA structure.
- Day 1: "Something's been on my mind lately," then a story about the audience's problem, then "Can you relate to this?"
- Day 7: reveal what you've been building, then "doors open tomorrow at 10:00 a.m."
- Day 14: "Last chance, cart closes in 2 hours," with final testimonials and "link in bio before it's gone."

He says you don't need to be a copywriter. The creator knows the audience's problems and language, and you structure it from what they tell you. After the first launch you can refine, repeat and launch again.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Iman explains why agencies are the best beginner model (low capital, high margins, high demand, easy fulfillment) and walks through nine steps: niche, service, setup, offer, prospecting, outreach, sales calls, onboarding funnel, and outsourced delivery. He also pitches a micro personal brand as the easiest way to get inbound clients.

chunks.heading: Why SMMA is the best beginner model
chunks.text:
- Iman started with a social media marketing agency (SMMA) in 2016 and ran it for six years, until 2022. He calls it the business that "paved the way for the rest of my career": his first $10,000 a month, moving out at 17, and supporting his mom.
- Gomez (founder of Lemlist), Sam Ovens (founder of Skool), Alex Hormozi (founder of Gym Launch) and Andrew Wilkinson (founder of Tiny) all started with service businesses or agencies.
- He judges a beginner business model on four metrics: startup capital, profit margin, demand and fulfillment. The best beginner models are low capital, high margin, high demand and easy to fulfill.
- Dropshipping scores badly:
  - Startup cost is $1,000-$5,000, mostly for testing ads.
  - Margins are 10-60% (he says 60% is too high) after ads, chargebacks and refunds.
  - Demand is low because the products are trendy gimmicks.
  - Fulfillment has lots of admin from logistics, refunds and support.
- Agencies score well:
  - Startup cost is $50-$100 (a domain and Google Workspace).
  - Margins are 65-98%.
  - Demand is high because you solve real business problems.
  - Fulfillment is easy when done the way he teaches.
- Iman says he closed his last agency program, Agency Accelerator, at the end of 2024. He made this video as a free blueprint for getting to $10,000 a month.

chunks.heading: Niche selection: specialize so you can charge more and scale
chunks.text:
- There is "no such thing as the best niche". The goal is the most suitable niche for your situation.
- Specialists beat generalists on trust and price. His analogy is a brain surgeon versus a general practitioner: "people always gravitate towards specialists over generalists", and specialists charge more.
- One niche means one way to find prospects, one outreach method, one delivery process. Multiple niches mean different channels (Instagram DMs vs LinkedIn) and a new delivery setup for every client, which Iman compares to running multiple businesses. "Increased variation in your business results in increased complexity and increased complexity hinders your ability to scale."
- Example: a friend scaled to over $150,000 a month with 100+ clients at peak by working only with real estate agents.
- Niche checklist:
  - **Revenue and profit:** the business should make at least $155,000 a month in profit before it will comfortably pay $2,000 a month. A $50,000-a-month business barely notices $2,000.
  - **Product ticket:** pick businesses with expensive products. A coffee shop paying $2,000 at $2 profit per cup must sell 1,000 extra cups to break even. A roofer earning $10,000 profit per job gets a 5x return from one extra job a month. It is easier to promise one extra sale than a thousand.
  - **Growth and stability:** avoid dying industries. His example is newspaper printers (dying) versus info businesses (growing).
  - **Market size:** home renovation has millions of businesses. Asian-themed wedding dress designers are so rare you'd need a near-100% close rate to reach $10,000 a month.
  - **Competitive advantage:** past work in the niche, knowing the language, or a family or network with warm leads.
  - **Sophistication level:** as a beginner, sell to unsophisticated niches so you're "the expert in the room". E-commerce owners have often run ads for years. Real estate agents almost never have. Even 2-8 weeks of focused study puts you ahead of them.
- His difficulty key:
  - Advanced: SaaS, law firms, cybersecurity, fintech, e-commerce.
  - Intermediate: solar, accountants, chiropractors, med spas, real estate, car detailers.
  - Beginner: HVAC, pest control, roofing, painters, pool installation, landscapers.

chunks.heading: Service selection: find the problem first
chunks.text:
- There are two types of service:
  - **Convenience** services save time: social media management, videography, video editing, reputation management, web design.
  - **Return-on-investment** services make money: paid traffic, email marketing, copywriting, SEO, lead generation. These are usually easier to sell because the client sees an investment with a monetary payoff.
- To avoid analysis paralysis, ask two questions: what is the biggest problem businesses in my niche face, and what is the most efficient way to solve it? Research by talking to business owners and reading online.
- Example: roofers' biggest problem is not being at client capacity, so they need more clients. SEO, paid traffic or email marketing could all deliver that.
- Choose among candidate services using four considerations:
  - **Skill set:** use skills you already have. He started as a creative agency because his background was photo and video.
  - **Scalability:** location-bound services cap your client count. Videography means one client at a time. Paid traffic lets you manage many ad accounts from home. This is why he switched from a creative agency to an advertising agency.
  - **Upfront cost:** videography needs thousands in equipment. Copywriting needs a laptop. Keep upfront costs minimal as a beginner.
  - **Income variation:** project-based work (e.g. $8,000 for a website) is lumpy. Recurring work (e.g. $2,000 a month for 6 months of paid traffic) is stable.

chunks.heading: Agency setup: don't overthink it
chunks.text:
- **Name:** his was "IG Media" (his initials). It stopped making sense within a year when he became an advertising agency, and he still made hundreds of thousands a year. If you're stuck, use Namelix.
- **Domain:** buy on Namecheap. If the name is expensive, pick a new name or a variation. Prefer .com and avoid .edu and .org.
- **Logo:** make it in Canva (the free version is fine). A nice logo won't decide success or failure.
- **Personal socials:** clean up your personal profiles, because prospects will look at them. No party or drinking photos, but don't be "a corporate robot" either. "People want to do business with people who ooze authority."
- **Email:** set up Google Workspace for a professional address and for Slides, Docs, Sheets and Gmail.
- **Email warm-up:** new accounts have low deliverability and land in spam at volume. Use a warm-up tool (he names Lemwarm); it takes 3-4 weeks, so start immediately.
- **Website:** optional. He made close to $20,000 a month, if not more, before he had an agency website. He mentions his own software company, Floy, as an all-in-one agency hub (website builder, CRM, proposals, invoicing, onboarding funnels, client space), but says any tool works.
- **Other tools:**
  - Stripe for payments (Payoneer if Stripe isn't available in your country).
  - Zoom, upgrading to Pro once you start booking sales calls, because the free plan's 45-minute limit looks amateur. Google Meet is free.

chunks.heading: Offer creation and pricing
chunks.text:
- An offer is your niche plus service plus pricing model, plus how you package it. Two agencies with the same niche, service and pricing can have very different offers because packaging changes perception.
- The goal of an offer is to bridge the gap between a prospect's current state (unsolved problem) and desired state (problem solved).
- Components of an offer:
  1. **Promise:** a tangible result in a time frame, e.g. "30 qualified booked appointments in 90 days" or "four long-form YouTube videos in 60 days".
  2. **Methodology:** a brief outline of the steps. Example: you run social ads to the target market, leads fill in a form, and qualified leads are booked into the client's calendar.
  3. **Pricing model:**
     - Monthly retainer.
     - Pay per project.
     - Pay per lead.
     - Percentage of ROAS (return on ad spend: what you brought in minus ad cost, taking a percentage of the difference).
     - A setup fee can be added to any model except pay per project.
  4. **Price:** research what other agencies charge, start somewhere you're comfortable with and aligned with the market, and undercut slightly. If every prospect jumps at it with no pushback, raise the price. If everyone says it's too high, lower it.
  5. **Contract duration:** a minimum term, never more than 90 days. Three months gives enough time to optimize and get results, and protects you. The client doesn't have to leave at the end; terms are renegotiated.
- Bonuses to go the extra mile: free website audits, value resources, lead reactivation.
- Guarantees: Iman is generally not a fan. They "do more bad than good" and signal that you're begging for business. The one he'd use in a tough negotiation is a pro-rata guarantee. Example: you promise 20 appointments for $2,000, so each is worth $100; if you deliver 18, refund $200 instead of the full amount. He holds it as a fallback, not a headline offer.

chunks.heading: Prospecting and outreach
chunks.text:
- Prospecting means building a list of businesses in your niche with contact details. Ideally collect name, location, email, number and social media.
- Three methods:
  - **Manual:** highest quality, slow, free. Use Google Maps for local businesses, Checkatrade for blue collar, Zillow for real estate agents, LinkedIn for corporate professionals.
  - **Software:** fast and cheap, with lower quality, but worth it for the volume. He names Apollo, LeadSwift, LeadGorilla and Clay.
  - **Lead generators:** contractors on Upwork or Fiverr who build lists for you. Most expensive but hands-off. Buy a small, cheap list first to test quality before buying a bigger one.
- During outreach "you aren't selling your service". You are pitching the meeting only.
- Pick the outreach method to match how the niche works: cold calling, cold email or DMs. Home renovation businesses are on the move, so calls beat email. SaaS companies are active on email, so the opposite is likely true.
- Every message needs three elements:
  - Highlight the pain point.
  - Emotional buy-in (the result of the pain being gone).
  - A no-brainer offer: the meeting plus a bonus such as free resources, SOPs or templates.
- Outreach is a numbers game. Monthly thresholds to sign clients regularly: bronze 2,000, silver 3,000, gold 4,000 outreaches. Volume matters most early on because you have no credibility yet, and more data shows what to change in method and copy.
- Better path: inbound through a personal brand. He says he turned down about 90% of the businesses that wanted to work with his agency without running ads or doing cold outreach. He started with a micro personal brand: an audience of a few thousand where everyone is interested in what you share and sell. He pitches his company Monetize for this, which was closed to enrollment and reachable by DMing him "personal brand" on Instagram.

chunks.heading: Sales call structure
chunks.text:
- Prep for calls: Zoom Pro, a clean professional background (no bed), and fast, stable Wi-Fi.
- Call structure: rapport, pre-frame, discovery, transition, pitch.
- **Rapport:** the first 2-3 minutes, an icebreaker so the call isn't awkward.
- **Pre-frame:** ask permission to move to business, then set the agenda. His script: you'll ask a few questions about the business, you ask for transparency, you'll make an offer if you believe you can help, and if not you'll try to connect them with someone who can. "Does that sound fair enough to you?" Delivered with confidence, it lets you lead the call instead of the prospect taking over.
- **Discovery** is the most important part, in five parts:
  1. **Current state:** clients per month, profit per client, how many clients they could handle, what they're doing now to solve it.
  2. **Future state:** profit they want in 6 months, extra clients needed, what life looks like if they hit it. Keep it tied to finances.
  3. **The gap:** break down the numbers and ask what concrete plan they have if they hadn't jumped on this call. Most don't have one, which they realize on the call.
  4. **Opportunity cost:** where would they be today if they'd had a solution 6 months ago, and where will they be in 6 months without one. Answering aloud raises problem awareness.
  5. **Doubt:** surface objections early. Ask why they've never tried a solution like yours, and what went wrong if they used another agency.
- **Transition:** summarize what you learned and ask what you missed. Then offer two options: answer more questions, or break down how you can help. About 99% of the time they ask for the breakdown.
- **Out-of-this-world frame:** before pitching, ask "if I break everything down and it makes sense how we're able to help you, would it be completely out of this world for you to get started today?" It weeds out financial objections early.
- **Pitch:** explain the methodology in their language, since "confused buyers never buy". Keep getting verbal agreement with "does that make sense?". Finish with "where would you like to go from here?", which leads them to ask for the price.

chunks.heading: Onboarding and service delivery
chunks.text:
- Onboarding is collecting payment, getting information and granting access. Send a small onboarding gift for a good first impression.
- Avoid manual onboarding over Zoom, email or WhatsApp; it's slow and looks amateur. Use an onboarding funnel link, ideally with a video on each page. Order:
  1. **Contract and payment:** a downloadable, e-signable contract (stating payment terms and length) and the first invoice. Collect payment at the end of the sales call, then let the client continue on their own.
  2. **Welcome video:** you welcoming them, covering your mission and values, past results and expectations, with a "get access" button.
  3. **Client space access:** plus a Loom walking through how to use it.
  4. **Strategy call booking:** a call to cover anything still needed and plan the next few months.
- **Contractor arbitrage:** Iman is a Content expert, not an ads expert, when he moved to advertising, so he hired someone to run the ads. Agencies get paid upfront and pay the team at month-end, so there are no cash-flow problems. Experts in places like Brazil, South Africa and Serbia can earn well on $500 per client per month while you charge, for example, $2,000. At five clients that is $2,500 a month for them, which is a strong local salary.
- He found his first contractor in a Facebook group. Other places: Discord, Fiverr, Upwork. Run a real interview process; Upwork and Fiverr let you post specific job roles.
- Still learn the basics of the service you sell. It makes you more confident selling, helps you spot talent in hiring, and lets you manage the team better.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Iman walks through starting a lean SMMA: pick one niche, build a small lead list, cold outreach to sell the meeting rather than the service, close with emotion then logic, and deliver paid social ads (outsourced if needed). He stresses simplicity, no free trials, and getting paid before starting.

chunks.heading: Starting a social media marketing agency: why it works and who it suits
chunks.text:
- Iman started his agency at 16 and, by early 2017, earned more than his principal and teachers. He then dropped out of school, though he says he doesn't recommend that for others.
- Pros: more free time, a much higher income ceiling than a nine-to-five, and location freedom. He was working from Cape Town, two hours off London time.
- Cons: more responsibility, no guaranteed income, and more mental strain because you answer only to yourself.
- Results vary with luck and timing. Some students who work hard land a client in month six, while some who work less land one in month one.
- He says many people don't want millions. They want to replace a salary or add $2,000-$5,000 a month. He cites students making $65,000, $25,000, $18,000 and $10,000 a month in profit.
- "You're one client away." One or two clients can replace a nine-to-five income. He advises keeping your job and building the agency on the side.
- Getting started is the hardest part. He describes a student who prepared mentally for three months, then on January 10th began outreach and signed his first client 24 days later. That one client paid as much as a graduate nine-to-five.

chunks.heading: What a social media marketing agency is, and what you don't need
chunks.text:
- It is a service business that sells services to clients, with no hack or trick. It can be run from anywhere for clients anywhere. He holds all sales calls and client check-ins on Zoom and never meets clients in person.
- He says a small town is not a reason to hold back, because remote work removes the local-lead limit.
- You don't need an office, employees, a legal corporation, a degree, or deep marketing knowledge.
- Contractor arbitrage: he began with a creative agency (video and photo content), then moved to a Facebook Ads agency when he "really wasn't very good at Facebook ads." A contractor delivered the results while he knew just enough to sell. After about five clients, he turned a contractor into a full-time employee.
- He doesn't recommend business partners at the start, because it makes it "twice as hard to make the same amount of money."
- He operated as a sole trader from his first client (August 2016) until April 2018, tax-registered but with no company. His registered business still has a different name from his agency.
- Setup list: laptop, email, social media account. For about $1 a year (domain) plus roughly $5 a month (Google G Suite), you can email from your own domain, which looks more serious and gets better replies.
- Keep the agency simple. He has seen full-service agencies at $20,000 a month revenue take home only $3,000-$4,000 in profit because they ran ten niches and ten services plus upsells and downsells. "The best agencies on earth are the ones that are the most simple and the most streamlined."
- A website isn't required. He suggests a simple one on ClickFunnels, which he also uses for case study funnels and onboarding.

chunks.heading: Finding clients: niche, lead list and outreach
chunks.text:
- A client is "anyone who needs more customers."
- Pick one niche you know and have lead ideas for. You can switch later, but don't try to serve everyone. Market size is not a problem: the US alone has about 38,000 gyms, 200,000 dentists and 600,000 restaurants.
- Build a small local lead list of 20-30 businesses in a Google Sheet, doc or on paper. Record name, phone, email, website, and Facebook and Instagram pages, so outreach can be personalized.
- Pick a channel: cold call, cold email, or Instagram DM. Most of his first five to eight clients came from cold DMs.
- His early DM approach was a short note with one to three tips: "I just saw your page and noticed a couple of places I think you're leaving money on the table." He held back the best material for a one-on-one coffee meeting. If nothing came of it, the prospect still got a free audit to use as they liked.
- Basic script: "Hey, my name is Iman and I help restaurants get new customers. I've looked at your website and noticed you're leaving a lot of money on the table. I have some great ideas. Would you like to discuss them?"
- Set a daily outreach target and book follow-up meetings.
- "You are selling the meeting, not the service." Don't pitch your service in outreach. Frame the meeting as "infinite upside with zero downside," because owners are busy and need a win-win.

chunks.heading: Running the sales meeting: dig, emotion, logic, close
chunks.text:
- Meetings can be on Zoom. Sign the client there and then, send an invoice, and agree a start date.
- Structure the meeting in four phases:
  1. Dig: learn the ins and outs of their business and get numbers.
  2. Emotion: "People buy with emotion and then they justify with logic." Business owners want more money for a reason, such as a bigger house or a Rolex. Future-pace what life looks like once your service delivers.
  3. Logic: use the numbers from the dig phase to show why it's a no-brainer.
  4. Close: if the first three are done well, the close is not a hard sell.
- Tips:
  - Sync Zoom with Google Calendar so invites auto-create a Zoom link.
  - Never offer free trials. They don't convert, because going from free to $1,000-$3,000 a month feels like a new cost. He says he has trained thousands of agency owners and saw this repeatedly.
  - Best clients are independents with high margins and a small team in charge, not chains.
  - Use invoicing software and get paid immediately: "They are not a client until they have paid."
- Once you deliver, clients refer others, and referrals grow over time. Repeat the cycle.

chunks.heading: Choosing and delivering the service: paid social
chunks.text:
- Convenience offers (content creation, social media management) versus results-driven offers (paid social ads, email marketing, SEO). He recommends paid social advertising: clearest ROI, easiest to learn, no software cost (you advertise directly on Facebook), and usually the best retention.
- Delivery options: outsource (easier to scale) or do it yourself (easier to start).
- Start on Facebook because it has the most users, the most targeting, is the most user-friendly, and has native lead generation. Other channels include Google, YouTube, Snapchat, LinkedIn and TikTok.
- Setup: create a Facebook business account, request access to the client's page through Business Manager, and create an ad account.
- Client pays for ad spend: "You never ever ever want to charge ad spend." You charge only your service fee. The client attaches their own card in Business Manager so Facebook bills them directly. Handling client ad money is "a nightmare."

chunks.heading: Building the ad campaign
chunks.text:
- Choose the lead generation objective in Ads Manager.
- Set audience by location, age and gender. For a gym, you can target a postcode or a street plus one mile. The client supplies assets (images) and demographic info, while you write the copy and tweak targeting.
- Copy: write compelling long-form copy, which he says works better than snappy slogans.
- Images: avoid stock images and use lifestyle content. Test: would you post it on your own timeline?
- Top tip: "If the person looking at it can tell it's an ad, you've done it all wrong." It should look like an organic post from a friend, and iPhone images often outperform polished camera or stock images.
- Use a desirable offer for a strong call to action. Leads can be followed up by phone, email or in-person visits.
- Automate by exporting leads from Business Manager so the client is notified of each lead. Zapier handles this, including SMS follow-up to leads. ClickFunnels can host custom lead forms. Outsourcing saves time and can get clients better results.
- His free resources: a five-page cold call plug-and-play, 90 minutes of live footage of his old sales rep closing three of ten calls, a short sales script, and a six-page click-by-click guide to running ads for local businesses.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Iman explains why agency owners, with high margins and free acquisition channels, should put profit in the bank first, keep software lean, and invest in their own education. Cash reserves create a non-needy sales posture that wins higher-ticket clients, creating a flywheel.

chunks.heading: Agencies get paid up front, so the bank balance is the real lever
chunks.text:
Iman argues that an agency's finances are unusually simple. The client pays first, the team gets paid later, and software is the only real recurring cost. That leaves the owner free to put cash into the bank and into themselves.

- He compares agencies with gyms and e-commerce brands, which carry employees, payroll and ad spend that drive the business.
- He describes agency profit margins as "ridiculous" because the product is a service, not a physical product or commodity.
- His advice applies at any size: ten employees, five, or just the owner.
- Capital allocation means deciding where the money goes, and he says you first need money to allocate.

chunks.heading: Bill on day one, pay contractors on day 30
chunks.text:
Iman's rule is to bill the client up front and start work only after the invoice is paid.

- Example: he signs a client on January 1, collects payment, onboards them, and the contractor bills him around day 30.
- Contractors are often paid per client per month; his example is roughly $700 per client per month for email marketing, Facebook Ads or Google Ads.
- This gives a roughly 30-day "float", meaning positive cash flow with the client's money in hand before the team cost is due.
- He compares the float to why Warren Buffett has extra capital to invest from a business like Geico, and he skips going deeper.
- Because staff get paid after the client does, team cost is never a place you need to "allocate" cash.
- He says an agency's costs boil down to software and team members. The gym owner by contrast lives with payroll stress and can't pay staff a share of memberships.

chunks.heading: Keep software spend small
chunks.text:
Software is the one ever-present expense, and it stays tiny relative to revenue.

- Iman's agency was doing about $40-45K a month in profit (his figure) and about $50K a month in revenue, with software around $300 a month.
- His stack: Typeform (about $24/month, which he says does the same thing as Google Forms and he just likes the style), ClickFunnels, Loom Pro (he admits he doesn't need it), and a tool for running ads and making new ad variations.
- When bootstrapping, he suggests free options: Google Slides, Canva, Google Forms, ClickFunnels free trial.
- Upgrade software only as the agency scales.

chunks.heading: First money goes into the bank
chunks.text:
Iman's first priority for profit is cash reserves, and he repeats it emphatically ("please please please put some money in the bank").

- Story: a private consulting client was making around $15-25K a month and told Iman he had only about $7,500 in the bank. Iman was "blown away" and called it "not a healthy business."
- His point: you can't decide where to put money most effectively if you've put none away.
- Cash in the bank is also a sales tool. Two equally skilled salespeople pitch the same client, one with $30K in the bank and one with $3K; the one with $3K needs the deal more, and prospects can tell.
- He cites this as one reason he keeps landing high-ticket clients when pitching $5K-10K/month retainers: his case study funnel makes it plain he doesn't care whether any single prospect signs, because he has money in the bank.

chunks.heading: "The hungry don't get fed"
chunks.text:
Iman uses this phrase to explain why scarcity hurts sales.

- Example: people pitch Gary Vee all the time with free work and "value", though he is the person who least needs it. Nobody does that for an ordinary person just starting an agency.
- Prospects "smell" neediness "from a mile away"; abundance attracts more abundance. He calls this simple psychology and social proof, not mysticism.
- Desperate owners after a dry month start signing clients who aren't a fit. They chase prospects, trip over their words and handle pushback badly.
- The right posture is willingness to walk away at any moment: if you lose this client, you have tons more. Prospects then read you as the right person for the job.
- Background he shares: the only tattoo he has says "my cup runneth over", meaning "I have more than I need". He ties it to his childhood and to his mother, the youngest of seven children from the Soviet Union, who taught him to "take everything you have because you never know when you're gonna get more". His view is that in a first-world country with lots of opportunity, you need to drop that scarcity mindset.

chunks.heading: Invest in yourself early, then in paid traffic
chunks.text:
Iman says the best early investment for an agency owner is self-education.

- Reasoning: an e-commerce business needs paid traffic, which needs cash in the bank. Agency lead generation (video outreach, email outreach, cold calling, LinkedIn, personal brand with inbound leads) costs almost nothing.
- So at the start, "the only person driving you forward" is you, the main lever of the agency. Improving yourself is the highest-return spend.
- Once profit is consistently around $20-40K a month, he recommends spending on paid traffic in one of two ways:
  - Growing your own social platforms with ads. He points to Gary Vee spending millions on social ads, which then lets him command retainers of $200-500K a month.
  - Building an auto-acquisition funnel, such as a case study funnel or webinar funnel. He says there are four or five ways to get agency clients through paid traffic.
- He warns that funnels are hard to get right at first, and you will probably lose a couple of thousand dollars initially.
- He uses a case study funnel for his own agency.

chunks.heading: The flywheel: cash makes sales easier
chunks.text:
Iman's summary ties the points into a loop. He references Jeff Bezos's book on Amazon and Jim Collins's "Good to Great" for the flywheel idea.

- More clients lead to more money in the bank, which makes it easier to sign clients, because you walk into meetings not needing the deal.
- Priority order for agency profit: 1) put money in the bank (it improves your sales and gives security), 2) invest in yourself, 3) later, spend on paid traffic once profit is solid.
- The agency stands out from a gym or e-commerce brand because margins are high and the main driver of the business is the owner, whereas for e-commerce it is paid traffic.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Iman argues that being young is not a handicap when selling online marketing, because business owners want someone who grew up with the platforms. He gives a general rule: objectively test each limiting belief, and if it is a real disadvantage, spin it into a selling point (age, no degree, cheap cost of living).

chunks.heading: Age is an advantage in online marketing, because clients look for people who grew up with it
chunks.text:
- Iman says a common limiting belief among new agency owners is "I'm 16, 17, 18, 19, 20, even 25, why would business owners take me seriously?" He calls it "cancerous" because it stops people from building six and multi-six-figure businesses.
- His test is to assess the belief objectively rather than just assert that age doesn't matter. The analogy: if he needed a document produced on a typewriter, he would look for someone 50 to 80 who grew up with typewriters, not a teen.
- Business owners hunting for help with online marketing think the same way: they look for the generation that grew up with it. Most of them did not grow up with social media, and many did not grow up with the internet, so a young operator reads as an advantage.
- He says this plays out in practice. Corporate clients have referred him onward as a "wonder kid" or "wizkid" of marketing, and his age helped him rather than deterred him (he says he hates being introduced that way).
- He has seen 11 and 12 year olds closing a couple of grand a month in social media marketing, so he sees "genuinely no excuse." He allows that at 11 to 13 it may be a struggle, but not much.

chunks.heading: Why online marketing is unusually open to young people
chunks.text:
- Iman describes online marketing as an "eighth wonder": a field businesses know they need but don't know how to do, which is where the agency comes in.
- Contrast with fields like accounting or advising on company mergers, where a 22-year-old has no track record. He doesn't think teens or people in their 20s can get away with a very successful business in those.
- Businesses are only now starting to realize how much money they leave on the table by not doing it. Once they see the opportunity cost (competitors doing it and winning), they search for who can fix it, and they look for people "almost bred" to do this.
- He started at 16 and closed his first couple of clients then. He says he didn't really struggle with it, and he didn't realize at the time that it was a real business model; he "stumbled upon" it.
- His takeaway: "there has never been a better time to get into digital marketing," because it breaks down age and experience barriers.

chunks.heading: The pitch to a client who says "you're young, what do you know?"
chunks.text:
- Iman's answer was that he knows a lot because he grew up with the platforms. He is on Instagram and YouTube every single day, including the platforms he pitches on.
- He frames this as "eating your own dog food" or "eat your own cooking": practicing what he preaches.
