- He notes his agency now only sells paid traffic services, so he no longer uses that exact pitch, but he calls it a "very compelling pitch" when he did.
- For age, you "play it off as an advantage." If you're young, you're the person who grew up with this, it's all you think about, and you're seen as the expert.
- If you're older (he mentions 40, 50, 60), the same lever works the other way: you have traditional marketing and business experience and you also know online marketing, SEO, ads, whatever you're selling.

chunks.heading: Handling the "you never went to university for marketing" objection
chunks.text:
- Iman calls this a "very simple objection to squash."
- His answer: online marketing knowledge goes obsolete within roughly 6, 12 or 24 months. Anything he'd have learned in a marketing degree three years ago would be obsolete now.
- Because he has no certification or degree, he is learning every day, whereas a chief marketing officer may think they know everything.
- He argues a degree gives "a false sense of entitlement," a feeling of having accomplished something when you've only read about it.

chunks.heading: Turning any limiting belief into an advantage
chunks.text:
- His rule: "just choose to believe whatever favors you." Objectively assess whether the belief is actually a disadvantage (most times it isn't), and if it is, find a way to spin it.
- Worked example for living somewhere with a low cost of living, such as Brazil, when a US client asks why they'd hire you:
  - Admit it plainly: "yeah you're right, I do live in Brazil, and I'm not gonna lie, there's not much to get up to here, so that's why I do this 24/7."
  - Contrast with a well-paid US hire doing it 8 hours a day because it's just a job, who has more distractions and is less passionate.
  - Make the price argument: that person might cost the client $4,000 a month because of their cost of living, whereas Iman could do it for $2,000 a month. The extra $2,000 "isn't going on increased expertise," just on their rent.
  - His illustrative figures: his dream apartment would cost about $500 a month versus about $3,000 for them.
- He says living abroad can be an advantage for exactly this reason, not a disadvantage.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Iman explains why everyone already has a personal brand and how to make it an asset. Work backwards from what you sell, pick one platform, attract a small high-quality audience with content that gets paid to acquire clients, then monetize through info and 1:1 coaching sold to a narrow niche.

chunks.heading: Why a personal brand matters and what it is
chunks.text:
- Iman says everyone already has a personal brand: "the world's perception of you." The only question is whether it helps or hurts you (jobs, college, private clubs, Rolex waitlists, dating).
- He says the one thing he'd credit most for 10+ years of success and $100M+ in earnings is an intentional personal brand, not the biggest one. He calls it the most valuable asset anyone can build.
- He also says it is not a business model. It is an asset that makes whatever you do easier: it is the "petrol and fuel" for his software companies, info business and eyewear brand (his smallest business, still a couple of million dollars a year in profit).
- Your brand should serve you, not the other way around. The goal is to get rich, not to get famous.
- His examples of brand-driven value:
  - George Heaton (Represent): the brand was struggling 5-6 years ago, then grew to hundreds of millions in value after he started posting founder-led content. He has only a few hundred thousand Instagram followers.
  - Guillaume (Lemlist): bootstrapped to a multi-hundred-million valuation with zero outside funding, mostly through LinkedIn content.

chunks.heading: Step 1: Clarify your intention and work backwards
chunks.text:
- Decide what you sell first, then define your perfect follower, then plan how to attract more of them.
- Examples of intentional brands:
  - Nico Leonard: luxury watch retailer, built his brand around luxury watches.
  - Ryan Serhant: luxury real estate, built around luxury real estate.
  - A pastry shop owner who showed off his pastries to bring people into the shop.
- His own case: at his agency IG Media he built a marketing/SMMA brand to attract clients.
- Questions to answer: who is my perfect follower, and how do I attract more of them?

chunks.heading: Micro personal brands: audience quality over size
chunks.text:
- "You do not need millions of followers to get rich with a personal brand. You just need a thousand of the right ones."
- Track profit per follower, not vanity metrics. A thousand followers at $150 each beats a thousand at $1 each.
- Example: a friend with about 4,000 YouTube subscribers and 5,000 Instagram followers makes multiple five figures a month from coaching.
- A real estate agent should attract a few thousand people looking to buy property. A female personal trainer should attract women who want to lose weight.
- He practices this himself. His main channel has about 5.5M subscribers and attracts beginners (titles mention "100,000", a common beginner goal). His separate Iman Gadzhi Business channel (about 10-15,000 subscribers, weekly uploads) targets owners making over $250K a year.
  - Titles are ultra specific, and thumbnails use terms like "cart abandonment" to deter beginners.
  - Views are lower on purpose. He licenses a business-to-business offer and only works with established businesses.
- He tells wrong-fit audiences, in effect, "I love you, I respect you, I just don't serve you."

chunks.heading: Step 2: Pick your platform with three questions
chunks.text:
1. Which platform matches your intention? Go where your ideal audience already spends time (corporate law services: LinkedIn over TikTok; photographer targeting influencers: Instagram over X).
2. Which suits your skills and hides your weaknesses? Writers should use X/LinkedIn; people who like video should use YouTube, TikTok or Instagram.
3. Faceless or front-facing?
   - Front-facing always wins because "people connect with people."
   - If faceless, his options are X (alias) or YouTube (walkthroughs without a face cam).
- It is fine to pick more than one, but do not try to master all of them from day one. "A jack of all trades is a master of none."
- His own path: he started on YouTube because he liked videography, not from strategy. He later added X and LinkedIn once he'd built copywriting skill, and now has about 12 million followers across platforms.
- "Confidence comes from competence." His 2015-2016 videos are still online and were bad. Reps fix it.

chunks.heading: Step 3: Content as negative cost of acquisition
chunks.text:
- Ads cost money per client. Content that sells on the back end means platforms pay you for views while you earn from sales. He calls this "negative cost of acquisition."
- Proof from one VSL on his YouTube channel:
  - About 10 million views.
  - YouTube AdSense paid him $266,000.
  - About 12-13,000 people bought a $1,500 info product at the end, roughly $20M in sales, with no acquisition cost.
- Consistency: 439 videos in 9 years, about one a week. But "consistency does not guarantee results"; the right strategy can grow an audience in months.
- Example: a channel called Callaway grew to 75,000 subscribers and 1.6M views in 4 months with 21 videos. Iman guesses it made at least $250K, possibly up to $1M, in that time.

chunks.heading: The three content pillars
chunks.text:
- **Authenticity:** be unapologetically yourself and don't emulate others.
  - He has dressed the same way for years. He made tens of millions before buying a car (a Range Rover, purely a utility vehicle). His first watch was a £20 Timex from Argos, and he spent millions on watches before buying a car.
  - He shared private voice notes from a time of crippling anxiety. "An audience does not resonate with a hero, they resonate with the journey."
- **Impact (value):** you don't need to be an expert.
  - Joe Wicks isn't a pro bodybuilder or chef but built about 5M Instagram followers and tens of millions in revenue by documenting his journey.
  - "Level one wants to learn from level five on how to get to level three." Being close to your audience's stage is your advantage.
  - Three angles: teach something, present new opportunities, share personal experience.
- **Intention:** make content that attracts the right audience, not a big one. A big audience may come, but it shouldn't be the goal.

chunks.heading: Content types, categories and ideation
chunks.text:
- Two types, and you need both:
  - Superficial content makes you known (tells your story, builds trust).
  - In-depth content makes you money (builds authority by educating).
- Four categories:
  - Actionable: show how, e.g. "the eight-step SMMA outreach process."
  - Narrative: tell a story, e.g. "I never followed my passion and neither should you."
  - Theoretical: explain why, e.g. "my five-step system to building a hundred-million-dollar team."
  - Attractor: share results.
  - Actionable and theoretical lean in-depth. Narrative and attractor lean superficial.
- Ideation:
  - Study what performs in every niche, not just yours.
  - Most good content is packaged as niche, problem, solution. Copy the packaging and swap in your own niche, problem and solution.
  - On YouTube, use VidIQ to find outlier videos. His example: a "make $10,000 as a student" video with a 13x outlier multiple, repackaged for another niche.
- Structure ("power of three"): big idea, three main points, three subpoints, a clear takeaway.
- Hooks: the first line of a video or copy. Include one of: bold claim, spark curiosity, promise value.
- Challenge: create 5 pieces of content in 10 days without posting, just to get reps in.

chunks.heading: Step 4: Monetize with information and one-on-one coaching
chunks.text:
- A brand can turbocharge a current business. Example: Dr. Alex, a US chiropractor who built a TikTok brand, is booked months or years ahead, serves celebrities and can price as high as he wants.
- If starting from a clean slate, he says to sell information. Everyone already pays for info (books, school, a tennis instructor, a boxing coach, a corporate lawyer). The only difference is the packaging: one-on-one coaching, group coaching, courses or a book (he doesn't recommend writing a book).
- Use AI to synthesize research into an actionable plan. His software company Synthesis AI does this. "You're not going to beat AI" at synthesizing information.
- Find a unique value zone (UVZ) using the "third layer theory":
  - Go down three layers from the market level to reach untapped but big enough markets.
  - Don't sell "health" or even "weight loss." Sell weight loss for new mothers (postpartum weight loss).
  - Selling to a UVZ makes sales much easier.
- Start with one-on-one coaching:
  - Charge roughly $3,000 to $20,000 per client.
  - You only need 3-5 clients a month, and about 1,000 right-fit followers can support a full-time income.
  - Product effort is minimal. He still does coaching himself.
- He rejects the "don't sell your time for money" idea. Taylor Swift on tour and the CEO of Google both sell their time. The point is to make your time as valuable as possible.
- He says a full coaching offer training is coming in a later video.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A year-by-year documentary of Iman's agency journey from a £95/week first client in 2016 to millions by 21. It covers pricing lessons (retainers plus performance fees, lifetime value over monthly price), sales habits, hiring mistakes, and investing agency cash flow rather than letting it sit idle.

chunks.heading: Starting a social media agency at 16 with no niche, no investment and no playbook
chunks.text:
- Iman signed his first agency client in 2016, aged 16, in the UK. He was too scared to charge monthly, so he charged £95 a week (£380 a month).
- For that fee he shot, edited and posted 30 Instagram posts, 30 Facebook posts and 4 YouTube videos a month. He calls it "basically minimum wage."
- In 2016 he did everything he now tells people to avoid: long proposals, in-person meetings, and burying the point of the conversation. He signed no more clients in the second half of 2016 and was rejected a lot.
- A 2016 goal was to make £15,000 in a year. He tracked it early: £489 in the first 11 days.
- He says he never made excuses for his age, school, or lack of rich parents. He bootstrapped everything with zero investment and zero guidance.
- His mindset advice: enjoy the tedious process (making channel art, talking to clients), because happiness doesn't arrive at the first 1,000 subscribers or the first million. "If you can find a way to do that then maybe you're doing the wrong thing" if you can't.
- His daily routine was gym, steam room, sauna, meditation, then 30 to 50 pages of a book. He aimed for a book a week and kept roughly a 90% track record for about 3 years.

chunks.heading: 2017: $25,000 months while doing everything wrong
chunks.text:
- By 2017 he was hitting $25,000 a month, which he calls the best period of his life. He says the first $100,000 does something "unexplainable" that later millions don't.
- He was making that while running a content creation agency with no niche. He also sold side services, did all the work himself, didn't auto-bill clients, and didn't keep cards on file for automatic monthly subscriptions.
- He hired his first employee in summer 2017. The person flew over from America and left within days because the deliverables-based work was boring. Iman says he lost about 50% of revenue around then.
- In August 2017 he lost 50% of his clients. He blames himself: he got complacent, stopped being a student, and let his ego and comfort take over.
- His lesson from that: "the problem with comfort is it breeds complacency." Staying a student and keeping your ego in check is what produced the success in the first place.
- Even with the money, he still felt young. He felt clients didn't respect him as a business owner, which became the focus for 2018.

chunks.heading: Selling to people far above you: don't qualify yourself
chunks.text:
- Iman's rule when talking to millionaires, influencers or boardroom execs is "don't qualify yourself."
- Qualifying means listing accolades or how much you've made to prove your worth. He says people at that level "see right through that."
- They hear that constantly from people trying to climb up to their level, and it reveals that you know you're below them.
- Instead, act like you belong there from the first minute. He says that sets a better dynamic from the start of the meeting or conversation.
- He ties selfworth to a purpose bigger than you. He told his mom a year before that he'd take her to Paris and then did it. He argues that if you do it only for yourself you will quit, but doing it for another person gives extra will.

chunks.heading: 2018: locking in a niche, the first five-figure retainer, and moving up the service ladder
chunks.text:
- In 2018 he finally locked in a niche. He signed his first five-figure-a-month client, a sleepwear brand (Oura-type product company he was already a customer of) that he calls a very cool moment. He hired his first proper full-time employee, who still works for him.
- In 2018 he stopped feeling imposter syndrome and bought his first Rolex at 18 for $155,000 with his own money. In 2016 he had set a 2017 goal of a $115,000 profit and blew past it.
- His service ladder:
  1. Social media distribution and growth plus some content: $5,000 to $6,000 a month.
  2. Higher-value services people pay more for: paid ads, funnel creation, email marketing, retargeting.
  3. Consulting: "come in, get paid a big fee, and get out."
- He charged $20,000 for a 2-day training (he says £15,000, roughly $19,500). He says he stopped selling packages and pricing should differ per client.
- Pricing analogy: if a doctor says "take this medicine" without hearing your problem, it feels like a scam. Quote per client based on their situation and the work involved.
- In a 45-day stretch he doubled his retainers to about $50,000 to $55,000 a month. In one day he signed a £4,000-a-month and a £7,800-a-month client. He did this without a website.
- He says being respected is a big perk of social media marketing, because owners tell him a workshop "literally changes everything" for their business.

chunks.heading: 2019 and 2020: retention, lifetime value, retainers vs performance fees
chunks.text:
- In 2019 he was signing five-figure monthly retainers "left, right and center," but found his client retention wasn't where he wanted it.
- His realization: there's a direct conflict between how much you charge and how long you keep the client. Charging a bit less keeps them substantially longer.
- He shifted to optimizing lifetime value instead of monthly value: a client paying $25,000 a month for 10 months beats one paying $5,000 a month for 3.
- In 2020 they signed more clients than in 2019, charged them less, and kept them longer, making much more money overall.
- Structure he moved to: lower base retainers, longer minimum terms (five or six month minimums), plus performance fees.
- His agency advice: get client focused, operations focused and sales focused. Track cost per conversion and return on ad spend, not cost per click. A better service than the agency next to you wins.
- About 70 to 80% of his clients were in the info product space. He ran paid ads for them, ran webinar funnels, and said retainer plus a percentage of return on ad spend is riskier but has far higher rewards. He wishes he'd done that sooner with more clients.
- He used retainers first because they gave predictable monthly cash flow, and he wanted operations simple and organized.
- He avoids retainer-only if incentives aren't aligned. He criticizes agencies that charge a percentage of ad spend or revenue: "just leave the meeting," because incentives need to be aligned.

chunks.heading: Deal examples and sales approach
chunks.text:
- Deal 1 (info product client): a £10,000 setup fee to build a case-study funnel plus a 30% performance fee on return on ad spend. He had done $35,000 to $45,000 a month in return on ad spend for the client's competitor. He estimated about $20,000 a month average over 6 months, so about £6,000 a month to the agency from the fee.
- On the sales call he wanted to close on the spot, but the client asked for a follow-up call. He chose to remove his ego and booked a 20-minute call for Tuesday. Soon after, the client emailed asking to pay £5,000 that day and £5,000 the next week.
- Deal 2: £2,500 base plus 15% on anything above 1.9x return on ad spend. He called this client "a certified whale" and expected the performance fee to be roughly £9,000 to £10,000 in the first month. The performance fee never falls below the base-level floor he described.
- His qualification bar for the agency: info product businesses doing at least $25,000 a month. He still takes sub-threshold calls because "that 45 minutes gives me reference experiences."
- He normally aims for a one-call close and rarely needs a third call. He is strict about taking only 100% fit clients, and he treats a no-show or stalling prospect as a sign they are less likely to sign.
- He uses a digital contract tool (HelloSign, or similar like PandaDoc) as part of the onboarding funnel after payment. Payment comes first, then the onboarding link and the contract.
- When he must stall for time on a first call, he uses Zoom's waiting room to pause and consult his CMO, then reconvene.
- He warns more decision-makers on the client side means slower, harder closes.

chunks.heading: Cash flow, investing and bandwidth (2020 to 2021)
chunks.text:
- At the end of 2020 the agency account held $1.5 million. He decided idle money was pointless and moved $1 million into investments: 70 to 80% crypto and the remainder watches.
- He calls the agency "such an amazing cash flow business." From then on he moved $100,000 a month from the agency into his investment portfolio and still does.
- His rule: when you have cash flow, invest it and let compounding do the work.
- In 2021 he made $9 million between agency profits and portfolio gains, and said the agency hit its record month in April 2021. He was only spending 5 to 10 hours a week on it because his CMO Danny ran it.
- He says he moved to Dubai for tax reasons, rents instead of buys at this stage ("it's more important to be mobile"), and had a roughly $10 million portfolio at age 21.
- His team ran about 20 clients at one point, with one client spending about $280,000 in a month across up to 10 ad accounts, which needed load balancing. His team burned out because he was slow to hire a new performance marketer, which he admits was a leadership miss.
- Bandwidth lesson: people overestimate what they can do in a year and underestimate 10 years. He said he had four companies plus a portfolio and needed to take on less.
- Abundance mindset: many people have "your foot on the gas but also on the brake" by believing rich people are evil. He says self-made entrepreneurs understand that money is a transfer of value, and you must provide value to the market to build a business.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A compiled four-year timeline of Iman's agency, from a £380/month first client in 2016 to $20k/month at 17 and $100k monthly profit by 2019. Covers niching down, retainers plus performance pay, retention, and the habits and mindset behind it.

chunks.heading: Starting out: first client, pricing, and rejection (2016)
chunks.text:
- Iman signed his first client in August 2016, his old football club, without knowing the words "retainer" or "social media marketing". To him it was "I'm doing this service for a client in return for a monthly fee."
- He quoted weekly because it "sounded cheaper": £95 a week, about £380 a month. Deliverables were roughly 4 YouTube videos, 30 Facebook posts and 30 Instagram posts. Effective pay was about minimum wage, but he cared more about landing more retainers, at higher prices.
- In 2016 he sent proposals and took many meetings, got rejected "again and again", and treated every rejection as a reference experience. Later he strongly discourages sending proposals.
- One early proposal (Skin Yoga, around October 2016) offered Instagram distribution and account management at £150 a week, plus £150 a week for content creation. It pitched December as the busiest growth month and urged building momentum for Q4.
- He says credentials mean nothing and experience means everything, and that school isn't important for what he's doing.

chunks.heading: Why social media marketing and agency work compound
chunks.text:
- By 2018 he describes social media marketing as "one of those financial vehicles that gets better over time". It doesn't get saturated, because you as a person become more valuable.
- Two years in he was signing five-figure monthly retainers, after starting at £380.
- He pitches age as an advantage: he understands the platforms better than a 30 or 40-year-old marketing graduate, since digital marketing has existed about 20 years and social media about 10.
- Acting like you belong in the room matters: "don't qualify yourself". Trying to prove you're worthy signals that you're beneath the people you're meeting, and high-level people "cut straight through that BS".
- Mindset framing: "you get what you think you deserve, not what you deserve." He uses affirmations, and prepares mentally for big meetings. He credits one multimillion-pound tech client, among his first five, to preparing his state the whole day before the meeting.
- His cut-off rule for ambition: write macro one-year goals down. In August 2016 he wrote eight, including making £15,000 in a year, which seemed crazy and then looked on track.

chunks.heading: 2017: the first breakthrough, and getting burned
chunks.text:
- He grew to $20,000 a month at age 17 while doing everything wrong: a creative agency with no niche, no auto-billing, sloppy onboarding, and doing the work himself.
- His first full-time employee, a videographer, lasted about three days (the video says three days, and a week in another place) before quitting because the work was too commercial.
- By August 2017 he lost around 40% to 50% of revenue (he cites both figures), which he blamed partly on himself. He had become complacent and stopped being a student, and he says comfort breeds complacency. Some of the loss was outside his control.
- August is a "shit month" for clients in any industry.
- By end of 2017 he felt burnt out and treated like "just any other contractor" rather than a respected business owner. He wanted that changed in 2018.
- His view of entrepreneurship: not endless networking events and deal closing, but sitting for hours building systems, watching them fail, rebuilding, and "think blocks" to check whether what you're doing works.

chunks.heading: 2018: niching down to paid traffic and landing whale clients
chunks.text:
- 2018 was when he gained full clarity. He moved from a creative agency, to a general full-service agency, to offering only paid traffic on Facebook and Google.
- His niche is about 80% info-product businesses and 20% e-commerce. He says the two have enough affinity to serve both. The niche locked in around April 2018, about 1 year 8 months in.
- Pricing step-ups: he describes quoting a huge agency $66,000 and realising he could have charged $10k to $15k more (the transcript is ambiguous on the exact figure). He started doing two-day trainings for $20,000 with expenses paid, including in New York.
- A "whale" client is $8,000 a month in retainer, roughly $100,000 a year in fees. He landed several in 2018.
- Valuation logic: if you're worth 100 units to someone, charge 20 units. A client explained he'd pay because it would take them about three years to build that skill in-house, and he didn't want to wait a year.
- He notes inbound beats outbound: clients came through his content and funnel (one converted six months after entering), and he gets no cold calls.
- A 2018 example: an ecommerce client (Oura-style ring brand) spent $4,700 on ads over two weeks and brought in $156,000, which he frames as about $151,000 of profit.

chunks.heading: 2019: ads for his own agency, whale clients, and retainer vs percentage
chunks.text:
- Around February to March 2019 he started running ads for the agency itself, and that brought 70% to 80% of clients for the rest of the year. He was comfortable spending $2,000 to $6,000 to acquire a client, since the first month's retainer covered it.
- Minimum retainer was £4,000 a month. Minimum term was three months, but average retention ran longer. He occasionally accepted £3,600 retainers when the back end (percentage of return on ad spend) was where the money would come from.
- July 2019 was the first month he hit $100,000 profit from the agency.
- In 2018 and 2019 he mostly avoided performance-based pay to keep cash flow predictable, and says he missed out on large upside when campaigns went well. He wishes he'd added percentage of ROAS earlier.
- Focus principle: "the real power in business is traction, not addition". He rejected adding services like Instagram management, email marketing or IP protection (each could be $2k to $12k a month), and chose to stay focused on one service.
- His specialisation rule: by seven figures you need to specialise in one service offering (lead gen, funnels, webinar funnels, etc.).
- A lesson in cash flow stress: when lead flow is low you get into a scarcity mindset and make worse decisions. He once refunded an $8,000-ish month, and the client pushed back, saying they appreciated his integrity.
- Payment rule: "until the payment has come through, they are not a client."
- Client filtering: he turned down a client whose ad performance made a 4x return on ad spend target unrealistic.

chunks.heading: 2020: restructuring and retention
chunks.text:
- By 2020 his agency was his most successful year. He added another media buyer to remove the capacity bottleneck that limited 2019.
- He revamped systems: new website, onboarding, custom reporting.
- Average monthly retainers were lower than 2019, but he signed five and six month minimums and made retention the priority. His logic: if clients stay 12 to 18 months, you need few of them to hit $100k to $200k months of profit.
- Nearly every deal now includes a percentage of ROAS performance component, so the agency earns more when the client does.
- His 2019 prices were high; by 2020 he deliberately had a different approach to pricing, which he says he covers in more detail elsewhere.

chunks.heading: What he says changes at 12 to 24 months, and the agency ladder
chunks.text:
- He claims something shifts around month 9 to a year, and it's most pronounced at 18 to 24 months, when owners feel "so much resolve". He says he sees this across thousands of students in his education business.
- Progression he describes for agency services: social media distribution and growth ($5k to $6k a month), then paid ads, funnels, email marketing and retargeting, then consulting (come in, charge a big fee, leave).
- Agency profit margin: he says about 20% to 25% on revenue after outsourcing, though doing the work yourself raises it. Time commitment can shrink: he'd automated parts of the agency to about 4 hours a week of real work.
- His reasons for why agencies win: most competitors report vanity metrics like cost per click, whereas for e-commerce and info clients the key metrics are cost per conversion and return on ad spend. Better service than the agency next door is enough to win.
- Mindset points he repeats: "two shall pass" (good and bad both pass), pendulums swing back as far, and don't let a bad month define you.
- He ends by promoting his Agency Incubator program and a free training, and says his agency also funded retiring his mother and buying a Rolex at 18.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Iman Gadzhi lays out a step-by-step playbook for digital products: pick and validate a topic using proof of existing demand, build the store page first, ship a cheap ebook MVP with AI, then drive traffic through commission-only influencer deals, paid ads and organic content. The core idea is rapid, low-risk testing with unlimited "spins".

chunks.heading: The core model: rapid-testing digital products
chunks.text:
- Iman argues drop shipping and Amazon FBA are not extinct but no longer offer first-mover advantage. Digital products (ebooks, PDFs, planners, templates, courses) still do, because AI has removed the technical and cost barriers.
- A digital product is created, delivered and consumed online, so after creation it can be sold infinitely with no inventory, shipping or storage.
- He frames it as a slot machine with unlimited spins: launch a minimum viable product (MVP) fast. If it sells, double down. If not, "spin again with a new idea." "The only way to lose is to stop spinning."
- He warns against the "perfectionism trap" of spending months building a course before knowing demand exists. His line: "stop focusing on perfection and start focusing on progress."
- His expectation: the first sale might take weeks or months, but "if you can get one sale, you can get 10."

chunks.heading: Step 1: Pick and validate a topic
chunks.text:
- **Option 1, your own skills:** ask about your interests, skills and spare-time activities. You only need to be a few steps ahead of the buyer, whether that is a level 10 helping an 8 or a level 3 helping a 1. Start with the audience, find their problem, and reverse engineer.
- **Option 2, let AI choose:** tools that scrape markets (he names Synthesize's "generate random ideas" feature) recommend topics based on what already sells.
- Ideas he says are working: AI prompt packs, website templates, lead magnet templates, social media automation tools (mass unfollow, lead scraping, DM automation setups), and white-labeled software (he names AutoDS and System IO as allowing rebranding).
- **Go a level deeper ("unique value zone"):** market, then niche, then specific angle. Example: digital planners, then wedding planner, then a wedding budget tracker for destination weddings. Buyers think "this was made just for me."
- **Manual validation methods:**
  - ClickBank: check the gravity score, which shows how many affiliates successfully sell a product.
  - Facebook Ads Library: count advertisers for similar products, how long ads have run (months suggests profitable), and creative variety (many variations suggests testing and profit). He mentions the Ad Sparrow Chrome extension.
  - Marketplaces like Etsy: sort by category and filter by most money made.
- Copy-and-improve tactic: find a seller like "Mr. Notion," read his reviews, see what buyers dislike, and make yours better.
- Synthesize AI cross-references ClickBank, the Ads Library and other sources to save hours of research.

chunks.heading: Step 2: Build the store page before the product
chunks.text:
- He recommends creating the store page first because writing the description, problem and audience forces you to see if the topic suits you. If not, pick another topic, since AI-made products are cheap to redo.
- Treat the page as digital real estate that must look professional and trustworthy.
- Platforms: Etsy, Gumroad and others. He discloses he co-owns his preferred platform (name garbled in the transcript), which handles hosting, payments, delivery, support and analytics. His stat: 571,000 customers but only about 10,000 sellers, a supply and demand imbalance.
- The page needs a clear headline speaking to the customer's pain or desire, plus a VSL (video sales letter) explaining what the product does, who it helps, what is inside and why to act now.
- He names Ghost Writer OS as a tool with an agent that writes landing page copy.

chunks.heading: Step 3: Create the product with an MVP
chunks.text:
- Start with an ebook as a "gateway product": cheap and easy to make, quick to proof of concept, and good for building trust. Once it sells, turn it into a course or something more intricate.
- Workflow: have Synthesize AI generate the ebook copy by synthesizing existing information on the topic, then brand it in Canva by searching "A4 ebook templates" and pasting in the content.
- Ship the imperfect V1. His own first version was not the best either.

chunks.heading: Step 4a: Traffic method one, influencer arbitrage
chunks.text:
- Partner with micro influencers (20-50K followers, sweet spot 30-40K) who have loyal audiences but little monetization. This is how he expects the first 1-3 sales.
- **Finding them:** search a niche keyword on Instagram (e.g. "productivity" for a Notion product), then use the suggested accounts feature, which groups similar small accounts. Also use niche hashtags and check who they follow.
- **Volume:** find 200-300 influencers a day and message at least 150 daily. Reach out mornings and evenings, since influencers work in the afternoon. Follow up 2-3 times a day (morning, afternoon, evening) for a maximum of 3 days, then move on.
- **Qualify with SocialBlade:**
  - At least 3% engagement rate.
  - 10K+ views on recent reels, with real views near or above follower count.
  - Story views matching follower size, plus consistent posting.
  - Audience 17+, preferably older.
- **Red flags:** purchased followers, declining followers over 30 days, low engagement despite high follower count, constant gambling or get-rich-quick promotion.
- **Questions to ask once they reply:** active story views, average audience age, top location, gender breakdown, story views for the last 7 days, link clicks from stories in the last 30 days. Cross-check against SocialBlade.
- **Viability calculator:** story views x engagement rate x conservative conversion rate x price. His example: 35,000 views x 0.23 = about 8,050 people; x 4% = about 322 sales; x $85 = about $27,370. (The transcript's figures are garbled, so treat the arithmetic as illustrative.)
- **Outreach scripts:** "Hey, Sophia, I have a partnership proposal for you. What's the best way to discuss it with you?" or "Hey, John, I'm looking to collaborate with you on a commission-based promotion. Are you open to hear more about it?" Send by DM or reply to their story, which triggers a notification.
- **Deal structure:** commission-only, typically 30-60% of each sale. With no cost of goods, you pay nothing upfront and take little risk. Create an affiliate link for each influencer on the selling platform. He says he avoids encouraging big risks for beginners.
- **Three-story sequence:**
  1. Survey/warm-up: curiosity without naming the product, e.g. "I found a way to make $1,000 a month with your solution" plus a poll asking if they want it shown.
  2. Method and results: reference the winning poll, show proof or screenshots, briefly explain the method.
  3. Call to action with urgency: "first come, first serve" plus the link.
- He cites the Brazilian creator Natan as having made millions with this sequence.

chunks.heading: Step 4b: Traffic method two, paid ads (after the first sales)
chunks.text:
- Reinvest profits from influencer sales. Pursue ads only once there is proof of concept.
- **Google search ads:** target people already searching for a solution (e.g. "notion templates for productivity"). Find keywords with Google Trends or Ubersuggest. Set the daily budget equal to the product price (a $30 product starts at $30/day). Use AI for headlines and remove irrelevant search terms that do not convert (e.g. "notion sound effects").
- **Facebook ads:** people are scrolling, not searching, so the ad must grab attention. Create five image ads and five video ads (the partnered micro influencer can make video content). Optimize for sales with daily budget equal to the product price, run 7 days, then make variations of winners and pause the worst performers.
- He says tools like Ghost Writer can generate the ad copy and headlines.

chunks.heading: Step 4c: Traffic method three, organic content
chunks.text:
- He calls organic content the best way to sell at scale ("the unlimited money glitch") and his own competitive advantage. He says he made well over seven figures from a single YouTube video, though the results came years after posting.
- It compounds slowly and has a steep learning curve, so he places it third. Get quick wins first.
- **Start faceless.** This keeps flexibility to test topics or sell multiple products without being tied to one niche, and to pivot freely. His example is the faceless channel Business Basics.
- **Rule:** make content intentional and tied to the problem the product solves. For a Notion product, show how organized you are, demo templates and show before and after productivity.
- **Funnel:** attract, provide value, build interest, convert with a CTA. Start with short-form (YouTube Shorts, Instagram, TikTok) by modeling viral content from other creators in your niche, then add a CTA such as "click the link in my bio."
- He has seen success with Pinterest too. Master one platform first, chosen by where your ideal customers spend time, then expand.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Iman lays out a four-step path to $10k/month coaching: find a narrow unique value zone, build a high-ticket offer around problem, specific result and a named mechanism, acquire clients via outreach, referrals and organic content, then deliver with a structured call format. He stresses specialization as the source of pricing power and coaching as a way to learn your market.

chunks.heading: Choosing a unique value zone (UVZ)
chunks.text:
Iman says "niche" is not specific enough. He splits a market into three layers:
- Layer 1 is the market (health and fitness).
- Layer 2 is the niche (weight loss for women).
- Layer 3 is the unique value zone, where "all of the magic happens": weight loss for postpartum moms.

A UVZ is a specific, in-demand problem that few people solve, where customers urgently need help and pay well. Coaching moves a person from point A (current pain) to point B (desired outcome), and the outcome doesn't have to be money. It can be screen time, a marriage, or video game trick shots.

- He claims you can become credible in a UVZ in 3 to 4 weeks of obsessive focus on one mechanism. You don't need 7 years of expertise.
- To find yours, he asks four questions. Have you learned a valuable lesson, overcome a challenge, built a system or habit that works, or done effortlessly what others struggle with?
- Examples: turning a 40% no-show rate into 80% attendance, fixing your health, or being very good at Excel. He says the highest-earning UVZ he knows of belonged to a guy who coaches people from beginner to advanced in Excel.
- His line: "There's a market for everything."

chunks.heading: Why specialists charge more
chunks.text:
- Iman's analogy compares UK pubs with Japanese omakase restaurants. A pub serves burgers, curry, Italian and Mexican, so it struggles to charge more than about 10 to 15 pounds a dish. An omakase restaurant masters one cuisine and charges thousands for a set menu.
- Specialization creates perceived value. Clients aren't buying generic advice. They're buying one specific problem solved, and they trust a process from someone dedicated to that transformation.
- Summary: "Specialists command premium rates, generalists compete on price."
- His own path: he charged $50 to $100 an hour in 2017, when he was running his agency and sharing it on YouTube. If a call ran to 3 hours he didn't care, because early on you are building a name. Now he charges $18,000 an hour, after roughly 10 years in digital marketing and 7 to 8 years specifically advising info product businesses.
- He says that price won't happen on day one or in year one. His claimed credentials: eight figures in profit in low, mid and high ticket, and over $100 million in career earnings, 70 to 80% of it profit.
- Even with companies earning multiple eight figures, he still coaches, about 15 hours a month. He says that is $250,000 a month in net profit, over $3 million a year.

chunks.heading: Building the high-ticket coaching offer
chunks.text:
He says an offer needs three parts:
- **Core problem.** A painful, expensive or frustrating problem. The client should feel "seen, heard, understood."
- **Specific result.** Measurable, with a timeframe. "People do not buy coaching. Coaching is the vehicle." They buy outcomes.
- **Unique solution (unique mechanism).** Your methodology, which gives hope that this time will be different. The simplest start is to name what you already do. Different clients will love or hate different mechanisms, and that's fine, because the ones who love it latch on.

Naming examples:
- "20-minute method" for busy parents losing weight without complicated diets.
- "Three chord system" for beginners playing their favorite songs in 2 weeks.
- "Three touch nurture system" that takes no-shows from 40% to 80% attendance in 14 days.

Offer statement template: "I help [audience with core problem] achieve [specific measurable result] through my [unique solution] without [common pain or obstacle] in [time frame]." Example: "I help busy parents who struggle to lose weight achieve sustainable fat loss of 10 to 15 lbs through my 20-minute method without complicated diets in just 6 weeks."

chunks.heading: Offer outline and pricing math
chunks.text:
Iman lists what to define in the offer:
- **Overview:** program name, objective, target audience, key problems solved.
- **Structure:** step-by-step action plan, objective and actions per phase, what each call covers, timeline.
- **Delivery:** one-on-one or group, session frequency and duration, total program length, platforms and tools.
- **Support:** between-session support, follow-up after the program, channel (WhatsApp, email, Slack), response times, community access.
- **Resources:** worksheets, templates, SOPs, resource library, call recordings.
- **Expected results:** specific outcomes, realistic timeframes (for example 90 days), client transformations and past results.

Math for $10,000 a month:
- 10 clients at $1,000.
- 5 clients at $2,000.
- 2 clients at $5,000.

Why you can charge premium prices even when starting out:
- Specialization creates perceived value.
- Clients pay for transformation, not information.
- High-ticket clients are more committed and get better results.
- The "10x value rule": when clients can see 10x the value, the decision is easy.

ROI isn't always dollars. For the executive who can't sleep, the person with panic attacks, or someone whose marriage is failing, he says "you can't place a numerical value on the stuff." He gives a personal example: he'd probably pay $500 for four weekly calls to get better at FIFA.

chunks.heading: Getting coaching clients
chunks.text:
He lists four ways: cold outreach, paid ads, referrals and content.
- **Cold outreach:** pick the channel by where your ideal client spends time.
  - Executives are on LinkedIn.
  - Moms are in Facebook groups.
  - Gamers and tech people are on Discord.
  - Local auto detailers are on Google Maps.
  - Phone is wrong for his own demographic: "If I don't have the number saved I ain't picking up."
  - DMs or email work better for people like him.
- **Paid ads:** he ran an agency for 6 years, 4 of them serving coaching and info course businesses, and still advises against ads early. You haven't validated the market, the offer or your messaging. His rule: stay away from paid ads until you've passed at least $10,000 a month through organic methods.
- **Referrals:** the most powerful source once you get results.
  - Over-deliver and create "wow moments."
  - Ask happy clients directly.
  - Consider an incentive: a discount, a free month, a bonus session, or cash back.
- **Content:** his personal favorite. Build a "micro personal brand" with content aimed at your UVZ. "Audience quality is far more important than audience size." The goal is not to go viral or be Mr Beast. The goal is inbound leads to message and convert.

chunks.heading: Being a strong coach
chunks.text:
- Take the "doctor approach": diagnose before prescribing. On every check-in, ask where they are, where they want to go, and what's stopping them. Clients silently ask "Can this person solve my problem? Do I feel supported? Is this worth the investment?"
- Coaching is a fast way to learn a market. After 10 clients you spot patterns. In his 15 hours a month he keeps hearing about three terms, and one is always the market's biggest desire. He uses these in offers, messaging, marketing and sales, and addresses fears and pain points before they come up.
- Call setup:
  - Dress to match your clients. His are 25 to 40, so a t-shirt is fine, but not a slob and not a three-piece suit.
  - Audio matters more than an expensive mic. He uses roughly $30 earbuds.
  - Keep the background simple (his is a black wall).
  - Light your face.
- Call structure, from the framework his team used when they offered six one-on-one coaching calls to students over about 18 months (he says 15 to 20 thousand students were coached):
  1. Intro: build rapport. Ask for a 1 to 10 progress rating and one win from the week.
  2. Transition: change tone and move to business, for example "Is it cool if we jump straight into week 3?"
  3. Set the agenda: explain how the call will go, which builds authority.
  4. Coach: the longest part, working through the action plan.
  5. Actionables and wrap-up: confirm tasks before the next call and that they know where to find everything. Always check in after calls.
- Difficult clients:
  - Late or missing: book calls ahead and set rescheduling rules up front.
  - Slow progress: identify the cause openly.
  - Resistant to change: come from understanding but be clear that better results require changing their state.
  - Need hand-holding: check in more often and make sure they have resources.
  - "There's no one-size-fits-all approach."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Iman walks through the full Facebook ads setup (page, business manager, pixel, domain) and how his agency structures campaigns: separate testing and prospecting budgets, broad targeting, and creatives as the main lever. He also covers the three metrics behind ROAS and how to size budgets and kill losers fast.

chunks.heading: Why Iman advertises on Facebook and what it does for a business
chunks.text:
- Iman cites Facebook at 1.93 billion daily active users and $28 billion in yearly ad revenue, with roughly $1 cost per click and an 11.54 cent CPM.
- He runs two businesses that use ads. His agency, IIG Media (started at 16, run for five and a half years), makes about $1.2-1.5 million a year in profit. Its CMO runs it and Iman works only 4-5 hours a week on it.
- He says he hasn't touched a client ad account in about two years. The agency gets new clients through referrals and by advertising for itself, then advertises for its clients.
- His education company helps agency owners, and about 95% of its business is organic. It still runs some ads for new customers.
- Four benefits he lists:
  - **Testing:** results in as little as a day, to validate whether the market wants an offer.
  - **Targeting:** Facebook has the most user data of any ad network.
  - **CPC:** you pay only per click. Clicks can cost as little as one cent, though typical averages are 30 cents to $2 depending on market and country.
  - **Predictability:** once the funnel and offer are dialed in, you can put in $1 and consistently get $2, $3, $5 or even $10 out.
- Goals he lists: sell more, generate leads, distribute content, drive app installs.

chunks.heading: Account setup: page, Business Manager, ad account, payment
chunks.text:
Iman's rule is to give Facebook as much real business information as possible, because accounts get disabled easily.

- **Page:**
  - Use real brand info.
  - Post at least 20 posts before running ads. Post 3 times a day for the first 7 days, then once a day, and keep the page active.
- **Business Manager:**
  - Use a work email, not Gmail.
  - Complete business verification as soon as it's offered. It proves the business is registered and helps avoid bans.
- **Ad account:**
  - Business Manager holds the ad accounts, pages, pixels and payment methods.
  - The time zone must match the currency (US time zones with USD), or ads won't deliver and you'll need a new account.
  - You start with one ad account. After Facebook first charges your card, the limit rises to three per Business Manager. He recommends creating all three immediately as backups.
- **Payment:**
  - He advises against PayPal, saying it seems to raise the odds of shutdowns.
  - Repeatedly declined cards also cause shutdowns. For those clients, use direct debit from the bank account so there are never declines.
  - Never put your own card on a client's account. The client adds their own card, so billing goes straight from Facebook and the business name matches the card.
- **Shutdowns:** he says that across his team and clients, hundreds of ad accounts (possibly 1,000) have been shut down. In e-commerce and education, it is "almost more rare to have your ad account not shut down than it is to have it shut down", so he says not to stress about it.

chunks.heading: Domain verification and the pixel
chunks.text:
- Domain verification has been required to run ads since the iOS 14 update. Methods: DNS, HTML file, or meta tag. His agency most often uses DNS: copy the code from Business Manager, add a TXT record at the domain registrar (host "@"), then click verify. If stuck, search "how to add txt dns record on [registrar]".
- The pixel is code placed on every page that tracks clicks, conversions (purchases, leads, add to cart, initiate checkout) and revenue. Create it in Events Manager.
- Two install options:
  - Paste the code into the header of all pages.
  - Use the Conversions API (server-side tracking).
- Wordpress, ClickFunnels, Leadpages, Shopify, WooCommerce and Webflow have native integrations where you paste the pixel ID. He tells people to search "how to install facebook pixel on [builder]".

chunks.heading: Campaign structure and budget split
chunks.text:
- There are three layers:
  - **Campaign:** the objective (conversions, engagement, lead gen, video views, traffic). He mostly optimizes for conversions.
  - **Ad set:** targeting, bids, placements, schedule and budget.
  - **Ad:** the copy, headline, image or video, and destination URL.
- He usually builds one campaign per offer, with separate testing and prospecting campaigns:
  - Testing campaigns: one for audiences, one for creatives, one for landing pages.
  - Winners are promoted into a prospecting campaign that holds the best creatives, audiences and landing pages.
- Budget split: 70-80% prospecting and 20-30% testing.
- Testing campaigns use ad set level budgets, so each ad set gets enough spend for a statistically significant call. Prospecting campaigns use campaign budget optimization, because they are more consistent and need less upkeep.

chunks.heading: Targeting: go broad
chunks.text:
- Think about the majority of your customers (age, gender, interests) and use demographic targeting.
- For interest targeting, test one interest at a time so there are fewer variables.
- One of the agency's historically best audiences across all industries is broad targeting, meaning no segmentation. Facebook's machine learning has so much data that it tends to beat micromanaged targeting, and more pixel data makes broad work better.
- Always pick large audiences. Small ones cause delivery problems, high frequency and CPMs that skyrocket. Profitable ads need low CPMs.

chunks.heading: Creatives are the biggest lever
chunks.text:
- If you take one thing from the video: "80% of your focus should be on developing better creatives and testing more variations of them."
- A great creative can work with bad targeting, structure and bidding. Perfect targeting, structure and bidding can't save bad creatives.
- Formats:
  - **Single image:** simple, but it has made his clients "multi multi multi eight figures".
  - **Video:** his best performing format, with no length limit. It needs a strong hook, a dynamic video to keep people watching, and a strong call to action at the end.
  - **Carousel:** good for showing multiple products or services. It usually gets a higher CPM, so test whether it's worth it.
  - **Collections:** an on-platform instant experience that takes more screen space and tends to get higher click-through rates.
- Three keys to a high performing ad:
  1. It stops the scroll, with a visual that triggers a reaction.
  2. It earns the click, mainly through curiosity, without being clickbaity (which gets ads rejected).
  3. It doesn't look like an ad. It should look like a post from a friend, because people have "banner blindness".

chunks.heading: Ad copy that avoids disabled accounts
chunks.text:
- Don't focus on benefits or promises about the end result, as typical copywriting courses teach. Claims put your account at risk of being disabled.
- What works for him: talk about product features, and tell a story or use a metaphor or analogy.
- Avoid:
  - results-oriented claims
  - health claims
  - personal attributes
  - sensational words such as "fantastic", "wonderful", "secret" and "unbelievable"

chunks.heading: Budget, ROAS and optimization
chunks.text:
- ROAS is driven by three metrics:
  - **Cost per click:** a function of CPM and click-through rate. Facebook penalizes ads it considers bad with high CPMs and rewards high engagement with low CPMs.
  - **Conversion rate:** his rule of thumb is above 2% for e-commerce and above 1% for education. Invest in conversion rate optimization.
  - **Average order value:** raise it with post-purchase upsells and by experimenting with pricing.
- Testing budget: never go below 0.5x the product price per ad set, which would equal a 2x ROAS if you get a purchase. Ideally test everything at 1x the product price or more. Example: testing a $2,000 product with $20 a day for 3 days is only $60, which would be a 33x ROAS if it sold, which is unrealistic.
- Prospecting budget has no rule: set it as high as possible as long as it brings in sales profitably.
- Optimizing:
  - Account for the customer journey length (7 days, instant, or 30+ days). If customers take about 3 days to convert, don't judge yesterday's results.
  - After an ad set spends its full testing budget, keep it if it hits your target KPIs and kill it if not. Kill clear losers fast, because they drag down overall account performance.
  - Never judge ROAS alone. Look at CPC, conversion rate and AOV side by side, find the one hurting most, and fix that bottleneck.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Iman breaks down five AI side hustles with pricing, retainer math and pros and cons, then scores each with his CLEAR framework (competition, longevity, effort, autonomy, recurring). AI digital products rank first because income decouples from hours. Voice agents rank second because a steep learning curve thins competition and clients stay sticky.

chunks.heading: Iman's framework for choosing an AI side hustle
chunks.text:
- Iman says the real problem is too many options, not a lack of them. People save 20 "perfect" ideas, start none, and fall behind those who "just picked one."
- He covers five AI side hustles he calls proven, all using specialized AI tools so a beginner needs no experience.
- To avoid analysis paralysis he ranks them with a scoring method (see the CLEAR section below).
- Order of the final ranking, best first: AI digital products, AI voice agents, AI websites, AI short-form clipping, AI UGC.
- His closing advice: "I don't care what AI side hustle you start, just as long as you start a side hustle."

chunks.heading: AI UGC (user-generated content) ads
chunks.text:
- **Why it works:** Brands run UGC-style videos as ads. Content that looks shot on an iPhone now often beats high-production ads. Unpaid UGC depends on virality, and the only way to offset luck is volume across platforms.
- **The gap:** Brands need a constant stream of new creatives each month because the videos have short life cycles. Making them manually is time-consuming.
- **Workflow:**
  1. Write the script.
  2. Upload or create an AI face.
  3. Upload product pictures.
  4. The software outputs a video of a person talking to camera and holding the product.
- Iman names Pictory as an example tool. He says you can spin up 20 variations in an hour, in any language.
- **Pricing:** A single AI UGC creative is $50 to a couple hundred dollars. The real money is monthly retainers for a batch of videos. Example: 5 retainers at $2,000/month is $10,000/month.
- **Pros:**
  - Near-zero startup cost.
  - Low skill barrier.
  - Demand repeats because brands need new creatives forever.
  - High margins.
- **Cons:**
  - Everyone is starting, so sales skills matter.
  - AI videos can look off and audiences are better at spotting them.
  - Some brands avoid AI UGC entirely.
  - It is a service, so income scales with your work and has a natural ceiling.
- **CLEAR score: 12/25.** Competition 1, Longevity 1, Effort 5, Autonomy 2, Recurring 3.

chunks.heading: AI websites for local businesses
chunks.text:
- **The gap:** Plumbers, dentists, gyms and renovators often run on a Facebook page and a phone number. They have been pitched $5,000, 2-month builds in technical language they don't understand.
- **How it works:** Tools like Lovable and Bolt build a site from a plain description and a few uploaded images, so there is no code. Iman notes "you're not the person solving this problem... AI is."
- **Pricing:** It is a one-off project. Example: $999 for the build plus a $99/month maintenance and hosting fee. A beginner can charge $1,000+.
- **Upsell path:** Once the site impresses the client, sell SEO or paid traffic. His example is a cheap $999 site followed by $1,999/month for SEO/ads. This takes more skill and often a team, so he suggests starting with websites only and adding services later.
- **Pros:**
  - Higher ticket than UGC.
  - Minimal upfront investment.
  - Obvious demand that needs no education.
  - You can show prospects a demo of the finished site.
- **Cons:**
  - Competition, since the tools are free for everyone and DIY builders exist.
  - One-and-done pricing means "you never stop selling."
  - Hard to reach full autonomy.
- **CLEAR score: 15/25.** Competition 2, Longevity 5, Effort 4, Autonomy 2, Recurring 2.

chunks.heading: AI short-form clipping
chunks.text:
- **The gap:** Podcasters, YouTubers and coaches sit on hours of long-form content. Cutting an episode into 20 vertical clips takes hours, so they don't do it.
- **How it works:** AI tools such as Opus Clip scan long content, find the best moments, cut the clips and burn in captions. Your job is quality checking and delivery. Hours of editing becomes "the same time it takes to grab a coffee."
- **Pricing:** Monthly retainers of $1,000 to $2,000 per client. Example: 5 clients at $1,500 is $7,500/month.
- **Pros:**
  - Recurring by design.
  - Lowest skill barrier of the five (you only need to tell good from bad).
  - Almost no costs beyond the software.
  - Growing demand.
- **Cons:**
  - Crowded, which leads to price competition ("a race to the bottom").
  - Small ticket size, so you need volume.
  - You are "essentially a factory": more clients means more clips and more hours, and income stops when production stops.
  - Creators may eventually do the clipping themselves.
- **CLEAR score: 14/25.** Competition 2, Longevity 2, Effort 4, Autonomy 2, Recurring 4.

chunks.heading: AI voice agents
chunks.text:
- **The problem:** Local businesses (dentists, clinics, law firms, home services) live on phone calls. A missed call goes to the next business, and a customer is worth hundreds or thousands. Owners rarely notice because they never see the missed calls.
- **The pitch:** Walk in and tell them exactly how much they are losing, then offer to stop it. The agent answers on the first ring 24/7, sounds human, holds the conversation and books into the calendar.
- **Setup (Vapi is his suggested starting tool):**
  1. Train the agent on its job: what it says, what it asks, what it does with the answers.
  2. Give it calendars, knowledge bases and extra instructions.
  3. Set up call forwarding from the business's number.
- **Pricing:** Setup fee of $1,000 to $3,000, then $800 to $1,500/month management. Example: 5 clients at $1,000/month is $5,000/month plus a setup fee per new client.
- **Leverage:** Once the agent answers the phones, canceling means missing calls again, so clients feel the loss immediately and don't cancel.
- **Pros:**
  - Highest ticket of the service models.
  - ROI is obvious in the pitch.
  - Sticky clients.
  - Runs without you day to day.
- **Cons:**
  - Steepest learning curve and the most effort of the service models.
  - Glitches, updates and changes still come back to you.
  - Growth still means another client and another agent.
- **Why it still ranks high:** The difficulty filters people out. "Fewer people push through the barrier," which is why it pays the most.
- **CLEAR score: 16/25.** Competition 4, Longevity 3, Effort 2, Autonomy 4, Recurring 3.

chunks.heading: AI digital products
chunks.text:
- **Core idea:** Every service above ties money to your showing up. A digital product (ebook, program, template, paid community or tool) is built once and sells the same way to each buyer. Iman calls it leveraged or front-loaded income rather than "passive income," which he says is BS.
- **What AI changed:** AI can research a topic, structure it and produce a full draft faster than a human. You no longer need to be an expert or have a production team or custom platform. You need to point the AI at a problem.
- **Distribution options:**
  - Sell to your own audience.
  - List on a digital product marketplace.
  - One of his favorites: build it for someone else's audience and take a cut of every purchase.
- **The math:** Price at $500 and 20 sales/month gives $10,000. Price at $1,000 and 10 sales gives $10,000, which is less than one sale per day. The 10th sale costs the same as the 200th.
- **Pros:**
  - No marginal cost per sale.
  - No ceiling tied to your hours.
  - Almost no costs beyond tools.
  - No client to manage or deliver to.
  - You step into demand that already exists.
- **Cons:**
  - A winner isn't guaranteed first time. He compares it to "a slot machine with unlimited plays."
  - It doesn't sell itself, so you need a distribution channel working.
- **CLEAR score: 20/25.** Competition 4, Longevity 4, Effort 4, Autonomy 5, Recurring 3. It is the only option where stopping work doesn't automatically stop the money.
- Iman's team built two tools for this, Synthesize AI and Ghostwriter OS, and he says he has seen it work firsthand.

chunks.heading: The CLEAR method for scoring a side hustle
chunks.text:
- Iman scores each side hustle out of 5 on five criteria, for a perfect 25.
  - **Competition:** how crowded is it? A high score means the lane is open; a low score means "knife fighting a thousand other people on day one."
  - **Longevity:** will it still pay in 5 years, or is it a trend gone in months?
  - **Effort:** how much effort to acquire the skills needed to succeed?
  - **Autonomy:** does the business run without you, or does income stop when you stop showing up?
  - **Recurring:** does it keep paying, or do you wake up at zero every month hunting for the next payment?
- **Final scores:**

| Side hustle | Score |
|---|---|
| AI digital products | 20 |
| AI voice agents | 16 |
| AI websites | 15 |
| AI clipping | 14 |
| AI UGC | 12 |

- His takeaway: every service model ties income to effort, and digital products is the only one where that link can be broken.
- He notes the biggest online entrepreneurs mostly run digital product businesses, and "everything starts as a side hustle." Which hustle works best also depends on the market.
- His advice for beginners on the service models: start with one simple offer (for example websites) and add services like SEO or ads later.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Iman Gadzhi lays out a stripped-down path to a solo $10K/month business: pick a simple business model, niche down hard, productize with digital products, use AI as leverage, build an audience organically, ship imperfect work, and don't scale before product-market fit.

chunks.heading: Pick a simple model and validate before building big
chunks.text:
- Iman says most beginners fail by picking business models that are "way too advanced" and trying to build the next Amazon or manage a team of 20 before earning a first dollar online.
- His analogy: don't run a marathon before you've run a 5K. Validate the idea in a small way first, because "ideas are dime a dozen."
- His target is a $10,000/month one-person business: no employees, no overhead, no complex systems, just a laptop and the right strategy.
- He has run service, software, digital product and physical product businesses for over 10 years. His most profitable ventures are consistently the simplest: him plus a proven system.
- Leverage that used to be out of reach (AI, software, platforms) is now available to individuals. He cites predictions of a billion-dollar company with one employee.
- He frames making money online as "problem solving and using leverage." Most people fail because they don't take enough action or quit too early.

chunks.heading: Productize: build once, sell forever
chunks.text:
- Digital products (courses, ebooks, templates, even a Shopify theme) are anything bought online, delivered online and built once.
- His comparison: 40 hours on one custom website for a $3,000 client, versus 40 hours on a course sold hundreds of times at $300. The result is $3,000 plus headaches versus $30,000 plus freedom. This is "working in your business versus working on your business."
- He says to build assets, not just income. Digital products work 24/7: "They never have a bad day. They never ask for a raise." You front-load the work, then sell for months or years.
- Personal proof: programs he created once became multiple six-figure-a-month income streams years later.
- Service work is still a valid start. It's how he began almost 10 years ago, and it needs no money, so you can fail for 6-12 months without going bankrupt. But with services "every dollar requires another hour of your time," and you're "essentially just buying yourself a job."
- Models change, so match the business model to the current market and your situation.

chunks.heading: Niche down hard and make the offer specific
chunks.text:
- Going broad to reach a larger addressable market backfires because "your marketing message gets diluted."
- Example: don't be a fitness coach. Be the guy who helps busy dads in their 30s lose their beer belly in 90 days "without giving up weekend beers." The last clause adds specificity and attracts one demographic.
- He calls the offer his "unique value zone" (UVZ). "Specificity wins every single time." The goal is for the viewer to think, "this person is talking directly to me."
- He applies it himself. His beginner-focused channel speaks to people in his earlier position. His other business channel speaks differently, to potential advisory clients doing $500K/year at the low end, about $5M on average, with a top client at $120M last year.
- "The riches are in the niches, but the real fortune lies in the subniches."

chunks.heading: One funnel, one offer, one outcome
chunks.text:
- $10K/month is "about simplicity, not complexity": one funnel, one core offer, one clear outcome. Find one thing that works and double down until revenue is consistent, then expand.
- Common mistake: five products, three funnels, ten audiences.
- He has seen people make multiple six figures with one landing page and one product, while others try 47 things and wonder why nothing works.
- He expanded to many businesses only after 10+ years, and says he started small too.
- Example: Armono, a customer of his Monetize program, was new to digital products. He sold one product on a digital product platform to one specific group (improving their marketing) and made over $100K in 30 days.
- Iman co-owns that platform (he says he "wrote a very large check" earlier in 2025). He also owns Consulting.com, which he says did $75M in revenue and which advises info, knowledge and coaching businesses.
- Claimed platform stat: the average creator makes $7,382/month. Monetize members range from $10/day to $200 and $2,500/month. His advisory clients reach $10M/month.
- Summary: "Simplicity scales, complexity fails."

chunks.heading: Use AI as leverage; solve problems, not passions
chunks.text:
- In 2025, not using AI to replace work that would normally need employees puts you behind. "It's not human versus AI. It's human versus human that knows how to use AI."
- He says he could build a $10K/month business with only AI tools. He needs three things: knowing which tools fit which job (like using the right blade for sashimi versus a tree), knowing how to use them, and having access.
- "The only difference between you and multi-billionaires is they have more leverage than you."
- On what to sell: "No one gives a about your passion. People care about their problems." Monetize what people need solved, not what you love.
- Look for where the audience is "bleeding": frustrations, pain points, urgent problems. "The market does not pay for what you want to teach. It pays for what it needs to learn."

chunks.heading: Distribution: build an audience first, ads later
chunks.text:
- Don't blow money on ads early. Pick one platform (YouTube, Twitter, Instagram or LinkedIn), stick to it, give massive value and build trust.
- Add paid traffic only once you have an engaged audience and a proven offer.
- Using ads to fix a broken offer, or to build an audience from scratch, is "an expensive mistake."
- Organic converts better because people already know, like and trust you.

chunks.heading: Ship imperfect work, stay consistent, protect early customers
chunks.text:
- You don't need to be a genius. You need consistency and a willingness to ship imperfect work. Most people quit at 3 months and jump between ideas.
- "Your first course, your first landing page, your first sales video" will be bad. Successful people test repeatedly through that stage.
- "I would much rather have an ugly offer that's live and generating revenue than a perfect one that never sees the light of day." Done is better than perfect, and "perfect is the enemy of profitable."
- "Consistency beats intelligence every single day of the week." He says he was never the smartest kid in class, just good at taking action and learning from mistakes.
- Treat first customers "like royalty." They give testimonials, case studies, referrals and feedback. He still has early clients (he names Oura Ring, Genflow, Camden Rose) in his network referring people.

chunks.heading: Don't scale before product-market fit
chunks.text:
- A common killer: people at $5K/month hiring teams and building complex operations. His analogy is getting the car to start after hours, then turning it off and pushing it yourself.
- Order of operations: perfect the offer, dial in systems, make sure unit economics work, then scale.
- "Scaling a broken business will just break it faster and cost you more money."
- His summary checklist: pick one model, niche down hard, build once and sell forever, stay consistent, ship fast, solve real problems.
- Sticking with it past 90 days already puts you ahead of about 90% of people, in his view.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Iman pitches a beginner business model: partner with micro creators (10k-100k followers) who have audiences but no products, win them with a free "monetization game plan", build the product with AI, and launch via a 14-day Instagram story sequence for a revenue share. He also gives a six-metric framework for judging how beginner-friendly a business model is. The video is a long funnel for his paid consulting program, so treat the income claims with caution.

chunks.heading: Why Iman says growth marketing is the most beginner-friendly online business
chunks.text:
- Iman argues most beginners fail (he says "over 90%") because they pick models that are viable but hard, like "playing a new video game on the hardest difficulty."
- He scores business models on six metrics: unit gain per transaction, startup capital, speed to first dollar, skill requirements, fulfillment complexity, and scalability.
- His ideal beginner model:
  - At least $2,000 per project, so a handful of sales reaches $10k/month.
  - Startup capital close to $0.
  - First dollar in 14 to 30 days.
  - Basics learnable in a week, low fulfillment complexity, and growth without more hours.
- His verdict: partnering with creators to build and launch digital products for them fits every criterion, and AI now does the specialized work.

chunks.heading: How he rates the common beginner models
chunks.text:
- **High-ticket sales:** Good unit gain, near-zero startup cost. Needs 2 to 6 months to first dollar and "one to two years" of practice to get consistent. Scalability is poor because every sale needs a call, so it trades time for money.
- **Drop shipping:** $20 to $50 per sale, so $10k/month needs 200 to 500 sales. Needs $1,000 to $5,000 to test products and run ads. At his agency, they tested "20 plus products before finding one that works." Skills needed: ads, product research, support, logistics. Margins thin as ad costs rise.
- **Affiliate marketing:** $50 to $250 per sale. Needs $1,000 to $5,000 for ads or audience building. Two to four months to first dollar. Thin margins: 60 to 90% of revenue goes back into ads, so $10k revenue might leave $1k to $4k.
- **Trading:** Unit gain is undefined (win $200, lose $300). Needs $5,000 to $10,000 capital. He can "count on one hand" the people he knows who are consistently profitable long term. He calls it gambling with money you need.

chunks.heading: The creator gold rush: why the market gap exists
chunks.text:
- Iman cites the creator economy at over $250 billion, projected at $500 billion by 2027, with over 50 million creators.
- Most creators have an audience and trust but no digital product (course, template, guide, community).
- His claim: everyone with an audience, even those who say trading or drop shipping, ultimately earns through digital products sold to that audience.
- Small creators spend 6 to 8 hours a day on content and lack time or tools to build products. That is the gap.
- Whop (he is a co-owner) data: users took 4 years to earn the first billion, 6 months for the second, and are on pace for the third in 4.5 months.
- He says the next 12 to 24 months are the best window to start.

chunks.heading: The model: partner with micro creators for a revenue share
chunks.text:
- The "growth marketer" partners with a creator, builds the digital product with AI, and keeps a percentage of profits.
- Target micro creators: 10,000 to 100,000 followers on a very specific niche (fitness coaches, language teachers, photographers, gardening). He cites Linktree data of 41 million such creators.
- He says only about 1% already monetize with a digital product.
- Examples he cites:
  - A creator with 17,000 followers led to six figures.
  - A sober living homes creator with 39,000 followers produced $57,000+.
  - A student got $6,000 setup fee plus a 70/30 split in week one.
- Math he gives: a creator making $30,000/month from 5,000 followers at a 30% split pays $9,000/month with no extra work, recurring while the creator keeps promoting.
- Targets: 1 to 2 new partnerships a month at about $5,000/month each, adding $5k to $10k in monthly recurring revenue each month.
- Suggested split when starting: 70% to the creator, 30% to you, to make it a "no-brainer." Later it can move to 60/40, 50/50, or favor you.

chunks.heading: Step 1, Find: win creators with a monetization game plan
chunks.text:
- Mistake: generic outreach like "Hey, want to work together?" He notes you would ignore it yourself.
- Instead, give value first: a custom monetization game plan so the creator realizes they are "sitting on a gold mine" and you "have the map."
- The plan contains:
  - An audit of their profile showing which content performs and what the audience wants to buy.
  - Money left on the table and projected revenue.
  - Tailored product ideas with pricing based on audience size and niche.
  - A launch strategy and the exact 14-day process to sell.
  - Validation carousels the creator can post to test demand.
- Workflow he demonstrates: paste the creator's Instagram handle into Ghostwriter (his AI tool); it transcribes and analyzes their content in minutes, then generates the plan.
- Outreach message is short and offers value up front. Then a call to settle which product idea and the revenue split.
- He cites one student who signed a second creator 2 days after the first at a 30% share, and another who got $3,000 upfront plus 20% from a one-hour conversation.

chunks.heading: Step 2, Build: create the product with specialized AI
chunks.text:
- Tool shown: Synthesis AI. Flow:
  - Feed in the Ghostwriter audit export of the creator.
  - Choose the expert path (product built around the creator's personal brand, face and voice).
  - AI generates hundreds of ideas and surfaces the top 20, each with a score (the demo ranged from 27 to 34).
  - Pick the highest-scoring unique value zone, then a format (coaching offer, ebook, or video course).
  - AI generates the transformation map, offer USP and name, a five-week action plan, 15 worksheets, and a program outline with module content.
