- He says this used to take him "4 to 6 months day and night" when building programs 7 to 8 years ago.
- He says he built a product with it in about 90 minutes that more than 13,000 people bought, earning over $370,000.

chunks.heading: Step 3, Launch: the 14-day Instagram story sequence
chunks.text:
- Creators already post stories daily, so audiences are trained to watch them. The creator does the selling; the growth marketer supplies the scripts and support.
- Three phases:
  - Days 1 to 3, warm-up: curiosity, gathering intelligence, investment, identification, community.
  - Days 4 to 9, value delivery: authority, trust, reciprocity, social proof, story.
  - Days 10 to 14, open cart: the product is released.
- Workflow: export the product charter from Synthesis, paste into a Google Doc (shared "anyone with the link"), create the product in Ghostwriter, then generate each day's story copy (with hook variations, CTA variations, visual suggestions) and send to the creator.
- Typical result he cites for a creator with 50,000 to 100,000 followers: 100 to 250 sales at $100 to $200, so $10k to $50k revenue and $3k to $15k for a 30% cut.
- Creators can reopen the offer monthly. He says doing 1 to 2 launches a month with different creators takes people from $5k to $30k/month.
- His own claim: 10 story sequences written with Ghostwriter produced $1.4 million, about $140,000 per sequence.

chunks.heading: Why he says to get tools and guidance (and his offer)
chunks.text:
- Two reasons people stall: generic AI tools instead of specialized ones ("butter knife instead of a chisel"), and nobody to ask when stuck.
- He promotes Uplevel Consulting at consulting.com: application-based, with Synthesis AI, Ghostwriter OS, a dedicated consultant for 6 months, four weekly calls, a quarterly 8-hour mastermind, and a playbook.
- Disclosure he states: he is co-owner of Whop and owner of consulting.com (enterprise pricing starts at $25,000), so he profits when students succeed. He also says he cannot guarantee results.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Iman shares 17 lessons from the wealthy people he knows. They cover buying assets with windfalls, doing the practical thing over the sexy one, discipline over motivation, small circles, radical responsibility, and compounding years of private work. Most of it is mindset and wealth habits rather than tactics.

chunks.heading: Iman's framing and where his observations come from
chunks.text:
- Iman presents "17 success secrets of the top one percent" as lessons he has personally observed. He made tens of millions of dollars in his 20s and made his first million in cash at 18.
- He says he has spent time with very wealthy people, including self-made owners of large companies and multi-billionaires. He stresses that what he shares applies to the top 0.001% in any industry, and that his own results are "respectable" but "nowhere near" theirs.
- He says the ideas are conceptual life lessons that need applying, and he points viewers to his most popular video, which compares business models with an equation and formula, for concrete steps.

chunks.heading: Wealth: buy assets, buy A1 assets early, build bank relationships
chunks.text:
- **Buy assets with lump sums.** After a big payout (a company sale, a huge month, a big contract), the top earners put the money into assets. In your first 10-20 years of career you are "a massive liability to yourself" because you may spend it, hit a rough patch or have a midlife crisis.
- **Favor hard-to-sell assets.** He suggests physical gold, houses and, in recent years for himself, equity in businesses. Stocks and crypto can take a share of the portfolio, but they can be sold with one click, so they don't protect you from yourself.
- **Hold A1 assets for decades.** His wealthiest friends bought them early and held them for 10-20 years: property in London, New York, Paris and LA, license plates, hotels. Returns are not the most exciting, but "you're never going to lose money" and the assets last generations.
- **Strong assets unlock leverage.** His example is a $20M jet: put $4M down and the bank lends the rest. With A1 assets in your portfolio, banks "will have absolutely zero issue giving you money."
- **Build bank relationships early.**
  - Banks are useful for creatively financing a business acquisition or buying equity in a new business.
  - As income grows you move from normal banking to premium banking to private banks.
  - He started reading finance books at 14 to understand banking.
  - He holds no mortgages and owes no bank money, but knows he could access $10M within a week and that wires of a few million won't cause trouble. Normal banks treat even clean, long-track-record clients like suspected criminals.
- **Win, then keep winning.** "If you sleep on a win you're going to wake up with a loss." He made his first million cash at 18, and says many people in that spot buy the Lambo, get the apartment and become "king of the castle." He argues it is much harder to keep and multiply money than to get it. Celebrate wins, but don't keep revisiting the past.

chunks.heading: Pick practical businesses over sexy ones
chunks.text:
- Iman says the most successful people he has met did not get rich through an activewear brand or a complicated product needing $73M of investment.
- They made money in boring, traditional ways: B2B services, building software and licensing it to big corporations, import and export, logistics, timber.
- They don't chase a billion-dollar unicorn. They find market inefficiencies or do something "even three percent better" and take more market share.
- His conclusion: "there's money literally all around you and it doesn't need to be as sexy as you think it does."

chunks.heading: Timing and sequencing: do things in the right order
chunks.text:
- He criticizes the social media advice "don't do what someone says, do what they do." Someone 10 years into an industry saying "if I was starting out I would do this" can't be copied by a beginner from square one.
- "It's not always about doing the right thing, it's about doing it in the right order."
- What you can do grows with time. In about 30 years, with a good career, he says you could call someone and have $5M in the bank the same evening on goodwill and reputation. You could sell $100k, $1M or $5M of a product or service before creating it, because loyal customers trust the quality.
- Some businesses cost about $4M to start, break even in year one and become $40M-a-year companies within five years. You can't start those without the $4M.
- Practical rule: if you're a real estate agent, don't study what an agent does in their 15th year. Study what they did when they started. Pick the right opportunity for your current point in your career.

chunks.heading: Discipline, routine and the long road to mastery
chunks.text:
- **Discipline beats motivation.** Motivation is like runner's high in a marathon: it comes for a small part of the race. You don't quit when it fades, you "lock in" and do it whether you feel like it or not. Motivation is "fleeting," so rely on discipline.
- **Morning routine over wake-up time.** Some multi-billionaire friends wake at 10am (time zones) and some at 6am (physical offices). You don't need 4-5am. What matters is a set routine and not starting the day with a high-sugar breakfast, phone scrolling and YouTube.
  - His own: wake at 8am, wash his face, get direct sunlight, stretch and warm up for 30 minutes, train about an hour and a half, eat breakfast, start work.
  - When travelling and training less, he may just have a coffee and start working.
  - He woke at 5:30 in London, then 6:30 with a personal trainer at 7am. Now in Dubai, with 150 employees mostly in the US and UK, he wakes at 8 or 8:30.
- **Private victories lead to public victories.** The bigger the public win, the more unseen private wins behind it. A Gucci or Balenciaga hoodie takes few; a $60M jet or a boxing title takes years of sacrifice, discipline and doing what you don't want to do.
- **Mastery looks effortless after about 10 years.** After a decade or more on one thing it looks elegant and easy. Early clunkiness and being bad at it is part of the process, so it shouldn't scare beginners. He advises picking something you respect and dedicating yourself to it even on zero-motivation days.

chunks.heading: Communication, opinions and who you let in
chunks.text:
- **Talk less.** Don't spill secrets. In negotiations "you should never ever be the first one to say the price." Fewer words mean fewer mistakes under stress and more attention when you do speak. The most successful people he knows listen, analyze the room and want other perspectives, not just to win.
- **Opinion vs. say.** "Everyone deserves an opinion, not everyone deserves a say."
  - He is happy to say "I don't really have an opinion on that" about topics he hasn't researched.
  - This covers parents, friends and sometimes people in your business. He takes everyone's opinion in his business, but not everyone gets a say.
  - Weigh advice from people who have done what you want to do (extremely successful people) more heavily. Always separate opinion from good advice.
- **Keep your circle small.** You can have many acquaintances and business associates, but few people can keep pace with your evolution, and "loose lips sink ships."
  - Private business should stay private.
  - His rule: never tell anyone outside the trusted inner circle anything you wouldn't want others to know. Assume it will spread, and mentally prepare for that.

chunks.heading: Mindset and values: responsibility, old vs. new money, small improvements
chunks.text:
- **Radical responsibility.** Failed marriage, failed business, a knee injury that stopped tennis for six months: "it's your fault." He says that is the only way to analyze the inputs that led to the outcome. Blaming externals won't get you far.
- **Work like new money, act like old money.** He wanted old-money dress, financial literacy and values from an early age (he is 23 and says he is not perfect and talks about money more openly than old-money circles would like). New money has hunger and drive. Old money has wisdom. Combine them to make a lot of money and avoid losing it.
- **You won't change the world, but you can make it slightly better.**
  - His example: if Apple didn't exist he'd be happy with Samsung, so it didn't change the world.
  - Japanese sushi chefs spend 40-60 years on apprenticeship and perfecting rice, knife work and cuts. That doesn't change anyone's life but makes the world slightly better.
  - He calls "I'm going to change the world" grandiose and self-absorbed. Do your thing as well as you can, "I don't care if I'm a waiter I want to be the best waiter out there."
  - "If we all do that, that's how we change the world."

chunks.heading: Choosing your partner
chunks.text:
- Iman calls the woman you choose "the most important decision" a man makes outside of work. He speaks specifically to ambitious men.
- Dating around and a playboy era are fine and a distraction, but the destination should be an incredible partner. Some multi-billionaires he respects have had only one partner all their life.
- An ambitious man needs home to be a safe, loving, nurturing space while he "conquers" for his future family. Many ambitious men pick partners who are too turbulent or don't understand his ambition.
- Don't choose on looks alone. "Looks fade and so does attraction," even for 10 out of 10s, and the man at home gets bored. Grand ambitions mean turbulent times, so you need a good person beside you.
- He says high-level men don't respect a partner chosen as a trophy for dinner parties. A real partner has social intelligence and represents herself and her man well.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Iman Gadzhi argues success is mostly timing: market timing plus matching the business to your career stage. Beginners should skip the "million-dollar business" trap, start a simple minimum viable business to reach $1,000, and move fast through optimization cycles. He also pitches his Digital Launchpad course.

chunks.heading: Timing is roughly 80% of success, and there are two kinds
chunks.text:
- Iman argues "80% of success is timing", on top of hard work, which is required but not the deciding factor. If it were, every hardworking person would be a millionaire.
- Timing is controllable. If you've worked hard and gotten nowhere, he says the missing piece is timing, not effort.
- He says the people who win make a few right decisions that outweigh all their wrong ones. Those big decisions share one factor: timing.
- Market timing is the external environment: getting into the right industry early (real estate, stocks, crypto, now online businesses).
- Career timing is where you currently are on the spectrum. Wrong decisions "don't matter in the long run" if you match career timing to market timing when choosing what business to start.

chunks.heading: Match the business to your stage, one step at a time
chunks.text:
- Under $1,000/month trying to build a $10M/year business has odds "slim to none": you lack capital, experience and a team.
- The reverse also fails. At $10M, starting a $100K/year business will probably work but never reach the scale you want.
- "The business you should start to get to $10 million is not the same business to get to a million", and not the same as for the first $100,000 or first $10,000.
- Ladder: $0 aim for $1,000; $1,000 aim for $10,000; $10,000 aim for $100,000. "Do not try to skip steps or you will fail."
- He made his first $1,000 online in 2014. He cites starting his marketing agency at 16 and a software company a few years later as moments where market timing met career timing.
- Don't copy what a favorite entrepreneur is starting now, since it may be a $10M or $100M business.

chunks.heading: Don't follow your passion; pick what produces practical results
chunks.text:
- He calls "do what you love and you'll never work a day" bad advice: "do what you love and you'll stop loving what you do."
- Passion careers often pay barely enough for bills. Add the parts of any job that suck, and over time you resent the thing you loved.
- The only question: "does it generate practical real life results?" Successful people chose something practical, not their passion.
- Example: he didn't start his agency because running Facebook ads was his passion. It's "a very boring type of business" from the outside. It was a practical way to make money for himself and his mother.
- Passion followed success: "as a man you fall in love with the process of becoming successful and the vehicle that takes you there."

chunks.heading: Build a negative vision of your future instead of setting goals
chunks.text:
- Exercise, which he calls "the opposite of setting goals":
  1. Write down what you don't want (a miserable job, constant money struggle, asking others for what you want).
  2. Write down where you'll be in 5 years if you keep your current path. If unsure, observe where the masses' mindless choices lead.
  3. Write a page describing that outcome in detail, then ask if you want to be there.
- Takeaway: you either act now to change the trajectory or end up there.
- He ties success to "extreme responsibility" over your situation and actions. Successful people take responsibility; unsuccessful ones let others decide their path.

chunks.heading: Speed of implementation: go through more iteration cycles
chunks.text:
- Early on, things go wrong, and speed is the best weapon. Improvement comes from trying something new and seeing the result; either outcome teaches you.
- Someone testing 20 new things in a period beats someone testing 5 "every single time", even if all 5 worked, because of the iteration count.
- Opportunity cost: starting in 1 month vs 3 means the faster person earns during the extra 2 months and runs many more improvement cycles, so you can't catch up.
- Example: after taking over Twitter, Elon looked at how often updates shipped, fired non-contributors (Iman says over 80% of the company), and pushed updates 10 times more often.
- "You either do it fast or you fail." Cutting your learning curve pays dividends.

chunks.heading: You don't need a massive business; start a minimum viable business
chunks.text:
- He uses a pendulum idea: public opinion swings between extremes (his example is crypto going from scorned to embraced and back), and when it's skewed far one way, move the opposite way.
- Starting a business went from risky to trendy to a given that you "must" build a million-dollar company. He says this belief "has created a generation of failing individuals."
- A minimum viable business is simple, easy to learn, needs no money or hires, can be done solo, and makes your first $1,000 almost inevitably.
- Example: ask neighborhood businesses to improve their Google listing photos, shot on your phone, for $50 to $100. Pitch: people search for them but give up because the pictures look bad, so better photos can double online visitors.
- His favorites at the time: viral organic e-commerce using free traffic, appointment setting, and AI copywriting, because they pay the most for the least input.

chunks.heading: Struggle is a requirement for success
chunks.text:
- Everyone struggles (family not supporting you, money, breakups). The reaction decides whether it makes or breaks you.
- Some use struggle as an excuse to stop believing in themselves; others use it as fuel and work twice as hard.
- "There's not a single successful person that hasn't suffered." Struggle builds the stress tolerance and endurance success needs.
- He says working with tens of thousands of students showed him this pattern.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Iman Gadzhi talks to his younger self about money mistakes: inaction and comfort cost more than any purchase, cash flow beats revenue, and early income should be reinvested in yourself and tools. He also covers lifestyle creep, geographic arbitrage, buying used, and why passive income is not passive.

chunks.heading: Opportunity cost is the biggest expense
chunks.text:
- Iman made his first million at 18 but only started investing meaningfully at 20, and only felt his investing thesis was solid around 23.
- He says the businesses never started and the side hustles procrastinated on are the biggest expenses in a person's life: "that inaction is the biggest expense you're ever going to have in your life."
- Watches were his early investment: roughly $5-6 million spent, with the portfolio up well over 50%. He bought new and direct from the brands.
- He regrets leaving cash in zero-interest bank accounts for years. Cash is fine, but it should earn something: a high-interest savings or fixed deposit (about 4-5% in his recent experience) even if he only parks it for a week or a month.

chunks.heading: Cash flow first, and invest in tools and yourself
chunks.text:
- His rule: "Revenue is vanity, profit is sanity, and cash flow is reality."
- His eyewear brand does millions a year in sales, but sales are not what the business keeps. Advertising and staff costs take a share.
- He started with an online marketing agency, which had minimal costs. He used geographical arbitrage: charging European and US clients while hiring remote staff in Brazil, Colombia and South Africa.
- He holds large stakes in VC-backed companies that lose millions a month. That is a deliberate enterprise-value play, not something to copy at the start. Early on, "focus on being practical first and just getting your first few wins."
- Business tools are an investment, not a cost: software, AI workflows, and similar tools. They let his businesses do with 1% of the input what competitors need 10x or 100x as long to do. Even solo operators should stack competitive advantages, since tools are "pretty much always ROI positive."
- Until a team is roughly 20 people, he says the founder is still the bottleneck. A solo operator is the company's entire output.
- So the first $2,000, $5,000, $10,000 or $20,000 should go back into skills and abilities, not stock picking. Stock investing comes later, when free cash flow is more than you know what to do with.
- A company that doesn't invest in R&D, talent, consultants, software and equipment goes backwards. He says to treat yourself the same way.

chunks.heading: Getting in early on AI
chunks.text:
- He wrote a check in November 2024 for an AI company (named "LRA" in the transcript). He is the largest shareholder besides the co-founders. It was accepted into Y Combinator and is about to close an unpriced round at a $40 million valuation.
- His view: "being involved early in AI truly is like being involved early in the internet days," and an opportunity like this may not come again for a decade or two.
- He says he was too young to capitalize on the internet or crypto early, and tells viewers not to miss this one.
- He is not telling people to build multiple AI software companies. He says to give AI attention.

chunks.heading: Spending, depreciation and the "how much will I lose" test
chunks.text:
- Buy used cars and let someone else take the depreciation. He buys cash but still counts depreciation mentally.
- Example: a 765LT that the prior owner bought for about $700,000 two years earlier, which he bought with low mileage for about $300,000. Losing around $200,000 a year would ruin the enjoyment for him.
- Wealthy people don't ask "how much does it cost?" They ask "how much will I lose?" He measures this as a percentage, amortized over the holding period (for example 5 years), because the first year is often the heaviest hit.
- His Ferrari was bought at a summer discount in Dubai from a motivated seller, and he expects to lose nothing on resale. He argues this is more responsible than a new Tesla, Cadillac or Jeep losing about 30%.
- A million-dollar asset that is still worth a million is better than a $200,000 asset that sells for $130,000. The same logic applies to watches and property.
- Credit cards, used responsibly, are a tool. Pay them off on time and raise limits slowly. He pays for his mother's Maldives trips with points, about 70% of the time, including business and first class flights. Good credit history leads to better lending terms, equity release against property, and Lombard-style loans against a stock portfolio. He warns they can be destructive for people who are financially irresponsible, and this is not financial advice.

chunks.heading: Lifestyle creep, comfort and geographic arbitrage
chunks.text:
- Comfort is "the biggest wealth killer." Peers who ran level with him five years ago stopped early: "they hit a fast 5 km" but never wanted to finish the marathon. Staying successful is "substantially harder than getting success in the first place."
- Lifestyle creep bankrupts more entrepreneurs than failed businesses, especially younger ones. He made tens of millions before buying his first car, a Range Rover in 2023.
- He now spends about 10% of what he pays himself through salaries and distributions. Earlier in his career his target was to save and invest 70% and live on 30%. When income doubled he did not double expenses.
- Geographic arbitrage: earn in USD, GBP or EUR from Western customers and live where costs are lower. In 2021 he rented a seven-bedroom house in Cape Town for about $10,000 a month, a house he says would cost $20-40 million in Dubai.
- His eyewear company is based outside the US but sells mostly to US customers. His own bases are Dubai and London. Time zones made Bali hard when managing agency clients and team in 2018-2019, so he cautions about that.

chunks.heading: Mentors, creating, and outdated advice
chunks.text:
- Mentors shorten the path to success. Some arrive naturally and some you pay for, and he has done both. A mentor drilled the buy-used-cars rule into him. Mentors pour more into you once you have shown results and will implement what they teach.
- "Stop consuming, start creating. Consumers stay broke." An economy is a value exchange: choose to be paid for value rather than only paying for it. Examples are a digital product the market wants (AI can help build it) or creating content rather than only consuming it.
- Parents' financial advice is likely about 30 years outdated: keep money in the bank, buy a home, go to college. Property and the S&P 500 are still safe, timeless choices.
- On hiring: in hundreds of hires over 10 years he has never asked for a CV. By the time a candidate reaches him their competence is established, so he looks at culture fit.

chunks.heading: Passive income and the real way to get rich
chunks.text:
- Passive income isn't passive. It takes active setup and often management. Work can be frontloaded so something runs passively for 6, 12 or maybe 18 months, but "things in life always face entropy" and conditions change.
- Even stocks take mental bandwidth. The closest thing to passive is bonds, which he bought heavily in Q4 2023 when rates were high, though they can still cause worry about a US debt default.
- "You don't get rich by saving money. You get rich by raising your ceiling." Early income caps ($100 a month, then $1,000, $5,000, $10,000) are mental limits.
- The only things stopping you are your mental ceiling and time. Remove the ceiling, invest in your output, and let time work.
- Evidence of the long process: he uploaded his first video about a week before turning 16, struggled for two years before that, and keeps his old videos up to document the full 10-year journey.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Iman covers the emotional rollercoaster, constant client churn, and the fact that you can't hide from people when running an agency. He argues for three-month minimums, treating retention as the biggest profit lever, and doing sales yourself, drawing on four years of agency experience.

chunks.heading: The three "dark sides" of running an agency
chunks.text:
Iman frames these as the realities that keep agency owners up at night. He draws on four years in the agency game: a creative agency, then social media plus advertising, then an advertising-only agency. He has handled clients from $300 a month retainers to over $20,000 in a single month of billables (base plus performance fee).

- The emotional rollercoaster of outreach, first wins, and losing clients.
- Churn is unavoidable, even when results are great.
- You are in the business of people, so you cannot hide behind a screen.

chunks.heading: Riding the emotional rollercoaster
chunks.text:
- He describes the swing from zero replies to outreach, to setting a first meeting, to signing a first client (the first client's impact is "undescribable" whatever the fee), to the despair of losing one or not delivering results.
- The swings don't stop. "It just becomes a little bit more steady."
- Expect about 95% of clients to get great results only after two to three years. Early on, calibration takes time: not every business can be helped, and "some business owners can't even help themselves."
- With experience, he learns which promises and expectations to set. Some clients he knows he can add $20k to $500k a month of revenue. Others might get five extra leads a month (a realtor) or a $4-5k a month return on ad spend, which can still be big for that client.
- Example of the swings: in March 2019 he lost three clients in 48 hours, all of whom brought marketing in-house, including a five-figure-a-month base-fee retainer. They had been getting incredible results. That cost him about £25,000 to £30,000 in bottom-line profit with agency expenses unchanged, because two were "whales."
- Pattern he sees: "when it rains it pours." He signs clients in clusters (five in one week recently) and loses them in clusters too.
- His mindset fix: "this too shall pass." Treat wins and losses as seasons, stop labeling things good or bad, and accept that you need dualities (night and day) or things go stale and you never grow.
- Agency owners tend to feel enslaved by the highs and lows for the first 18 months. After that he sees maturity and resolve to weather the storm.

chunks.heading: Three-month minimums and living with churn
chunks.text:
- Every client should be signed on a three-month minimum. He made this a rule from the start of 2018. Before that, clients had no minimum and could leave after month one, the most stressful month.
- Why it works: the first month is often 7 to 10 days of onboarding and getting ads live, so a client judging results at day 20 is premature. You may also need to teach them how to nurture and convert leads, or build that system. The minimum gives time for results and stops clients acting on emotion.
- He also says you must be able to stomach clients leaving. Clients can leave even with incredible results because they decide to build an in-house culture.
- When clients bring work in-house they reason that for the same fee they could employ four performance marketers full-time. He says they often come back about six months later and you start nearly fresh.
- He won't judge them: in his own education company everything is in-house with no contractors, and he doesn't want service providers there.
- Most clients leave at the three-month mark. After roughly four months they usually stay 9 to 12 months. His longest was about 16 months, just under a year and a half.

chunks.heading: Retention is the biggest lever
chunks.text:
- His 2020 realization: "retention is probably the most important thing when it comes to an agency." It's much easier to keep a client than sign a new one.
- Average retention: he calculated his at about 6.8 months. He says he has never met an agency owner with average retention over 12 to 14 months. The average includes three-month-minimum leavers, so a 12-month average means some clients stay 18 to 24 months.
- Benchmarks as he sees them: 7 months is very healthy; 9 to 12 months means "you're a boss."
- His 2020 goal: lift average retention to 10 to 11 months. His math: that is about 50% more profit with no new clients, e.g. going from £400,000 a year to £600,000.
- He even cut one already-happy client's fee by £500 a month (about one-eighth of that retainer, still on his lowest retainer) when they did a six-month extension, as an experiment in incentivizing longer commitments. He was brainstorming lower monthly retainers in exchange for longer terms to hit a 9 to 11 month average.
- Levers he names: deliver better results, and incentivize longer-term contracts.

chunks.heading: Why you should not outsource sales
chunks.text:
- He argues you can outsource nearly everything in an agency (ideally eventually building a full-time team and company culture rather than contractors) except sales. "Just because you can doesn't mean you should."
- His math: to sign 10 new clients a month at a 20% close rate you need 50 calls a month, about two calls a day. That's two hours of an eight-hour day driving revenue. He would not outsource unless doing around 100 sales calls.
- Revenue requires speaking to other business owners, who are often sophisticated buyers. It stretches you: you reach out, prospect, and get no's.
- Example: in 2017, at 17, he was grilled for 20 minutes by one of three co-founders ("you don't have a marketing degree, you're 17"). He snapped into the zone and handled the objections. That founder later became a good friend.
- His reframe: it's only a conversation between two business owners about what you can do for their business, a small price for how life-changing an agency can be.

chunks.heading: Systems, but not at the expense of relationships
chunks.text:
- His goal is to build a machine. In 2019 he took that too far: he never joined client check-in calls and removed himself from everything except sales. About 80% of his ads ran as cold traffic on Facebook to a case study funnel.
- The lesson: "you're still dealing with humans." Late 2019 and 2020 focused on client delight and retention.
- His team delivered results that made clients "obscene amounts of money," but he personally didn't commit enough to rapport or show he cared beyond results.
- He doesn't believe in truly passive income. Systems help, but the owner still guides and shifts things.

chunks.heading: Agency economics versus other models
chunks.text:
- Agencies aren't a "sexy" business model, but he says he's yet to see something that gives a better lifestyle for you and your family.
- He owns an e-commerce company and an education company, and compares margins. Revenue is far removed from what lands in your pocket.
- Education companies: friends and competitors have told him it's harder than expected with thinner margins than anyone mentioned. A real education company (not a course business with one big month) is "a blood sucking leech."
- He pairs this with encouragement for agency owners: it takes courage, and the right community, mentorship and guidance make it easier.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Iman Gadzhi argues productivity comes from guarding attention and removing decisions, not from elaborate routines. He covers treating YouTube and books as entertainment, planning tomorrow tonight, uniform clothes and meals, deleting TikTok, muting Instagram, and a short three-step morning routine.

chunks.heading: Attention is the real asset: protect it from feeds
chunks.text:
- Iman treats YouTube as entertainment, not education: "in life you get ahead by applying not learning." He says the same of his own videos and most books ("15 pages of gold and then 300 pages of fluff").
- Real education is intentional: you know the specific problem in your business or career, then immerse yourself in that exact topic. Watching a podcast "because it might be useful" is a trap.
- Tactic: install a tool like Unhook. Turn on hide home feed, hide the video sidebar recommendations, and hide comments. Leave only the subscription box.
- He admits this costs him views ("shooting myself in the foot") but wants viewers to get ahead.
- He says content value shifts by stage: useful when beginning, less applicable at intermediate level, and relevant again at an exceptional level when you view it from the perspective of someone who has made it.

chunks.heading: Delete TikTok and mute people on Instagram
chunks.text:
- Unless short-form is directly tied to how you make money (e.g. an affiliate marketer or short-form editor, or one of the roughly 1 in 50 who gets leads from TikTok), delete TikTok. Otherwise it only robs attention.
- His own team grew his TikTok to about 1.5-2 million followers before he had ever downloaded the app. He downloaded it only three or four months before the video, when short-form (TikTok, Reels, Shorts) was getting about 200 million views a month, so he could understand the platform for work.
- The upside of one good clip is outweighed by the "mental spiral" of the other junk.
- On Instagram, he accepts it matters as a "social CV" (dating, career), but he has about 90% of accounts muted. He only follows close friends and c-suite or top managers of his companies (CEOs, CMOs).
- Rule: you need the same focus and protection around your attention that he applies.

chunks.heading: Plan the next day the night before
chunks.text:
- Iman calls this the most important productivity hack. Setting intention the night before makes your brain work on it overnight, so you start the day with real intention.
- Keep it simple: write down three to five tasks (three main things works too) the evening before.
- Today he checks his calendar for the next day's calls, meetings and duties, with an assistant helping, then writes the 3-5 things to accomplish.
- From 2016 to roughly 2019-2020, when he drove the business himself without today's leadership team (business partners and CEOs across his companies), he planned his day hour by hour.
- He suggests trying it that same night.

chunks.heading: Remove daily decisions: uniform, laid-out clothes, meal prep
chunks.text:
- **Dress the part.** Dress for the context. Especially when young, overdress, because people already try to discredit young founders and a hoodie and graphic tee does not help. For meetings he wears smart casual or a suit; on a casual Zoom or YouTube recording a suit would look odd.
- **Home uniform.** On days of calls at home he wears the same thing: the same few jeans or trousers, the same shoes, and the same brand of t-shirt in different colors. This removes thinking about it.
- **Shoes indoors.** He wears shoes in the house because it signals "serious work" mode; flip-flops or sweatpants belong to off time. Avoid sloppy clothing and take yourself seriously.
- **Lay out clothes the night before.** The worst morning problem is decision fatigue about what to wear. It takes two minutes at night and makes mornings seamless, especially if you work out in the morning or struggle to wake up.
- **Meal prep weekly.** Prep the same breakfast, lunch and dinner for the whole week. To avoid boredom, change the meals week to week but keep them identical day to day. Early on he did this (and intermittent fasting, so no breakfast, for a few years).
- **Food is fuel.** Unless on holiday, retired or rich, food is not leisure. Restaurants and holidays are for enjoyment. His daily food: lots of meat, fish, healthy fats and lots of avocado. He now has a full-time chef at nearly every home, which he looked forward to once he made serious money.

chunks.heading: A simple three-step morning routine
chunks.text:
- Most morning routines are "absolute BS." Iman used to run a 10-step routine that took four hours, so he is not judging, only reporting what works.
- Wake up at whatever time suits you; 5am doesn't matter. Exception: if you have school or a job, get early working or exercise hours in.
- Why his timing shifts: he dropped out of school at 17 because he already had an employee and "crazy money," and had to support his single mom. He woke early while in school, disliking it. He has woken at 5, 6, 7:30 and now 8:30, because he spends most of the year in Dubai and his team is in America and Europe, with leadership calls often 5:30 to 9 pm.
- Rule: three steps, no 10 or 12 steps, nothing that takes four hours. From waking to being at your desk working should take no more than an hour to an hour and a half.
- Past routine in London (about three years before): wake 6:30, journal over coffee, personal trainer arrives, walk two minutes to the gym.
- Current routine: cold plunge in the home gym, shower and get ready, then coffee at the desk and 30 minutes of "me time" writing ideas, vision for his companies, and reviewing corporate structure, investments and which holding companies and trusts they sit in.
- He trains at 4 pm now; earlier on, first thing in the morning was the only practical time.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Iman reflects on 2025: why he now prefers owning 5-20% of big companies over building his own, why who you build with matters more than the mission, and why he keeps some businesses as pure passion projects. He also explains why a chip on your shoulder is still useful after success.

chunks.heading: Ownership over building: why Iman buys 5-20% stakes instead of building unicorns
chunks.text:
- By 2025 Iman concluded that "for this stage of life" he does not want to build a billion-dollar company. He prefers owning large pieces of billion-dollar companies.
- His target is roughly 5 to 20% of a company. Above 20%, he says he doesn't want to be involved in "the changing of a CRM or really the minutia." He wants to be impactful where he can be impactful.
- Big Day vs. Cadence: at the end of 2023 he started Big Day, a sparkling electrolyte drink (his version had a bit of caffeine). The founders of Represent (George and Ross) then pitched him to come in as a third partner on Cadence. The choice was 70% of his own venture or about 33% of another one.
- Big Day and Cadence were neck and neck in revenue for the first 9 months, and Ross even wanted to merge them. In 2025 Cadence moved to a different level. Big Day didn't get the "labor of love" it needed because he and his business partner both had too many other ventures.
- He cites Watt (his term: "the biggest case of that") as the clearest example of the stake strategy working.
- Oura Ring lesson: at 18 he charged Oura Ring 7,800 pounds a month, which equated to $10,000 a month, his first five-figure retainer. The then-CEO Harpreet offered either the retainer or the equivalent in stock, and Iman took the retainer.
  - He worked with them for 9 months. He calculates that Oura is now worth $11 billion, and that the equity offered in 2018 would be worth about $19 million today, the equivalent of about $2 million a month.
  - His takeaway: "no one teaches you the value of ownership."
- Caveats he adds:
  - Early on you have to think short-term; when you're "drowning" you take the cash, and that's reasonable.
  - 20% of nothing is still nothing. You have to identify good companies where even 1 to 5% becomes huge in the long run.
- He says there are many ways to reach your destination. You have to pick the path that fits who you are: owning a big stake in a unicorn lets him go fishing and hunting on a random Tuesday, which running one would not.

chunks.heading: Keep your passion project separate from how you make money (the HEELS example)
chunks.text:
- Iman says he has always been good at keeping passion apart from how he makes money. This doesn't mean you shouldn't enjoy your work; he loves his.
- HEELS (formerly GAGGI): GAGGI started with clothes in 2019 and moved into glasses in 2020, so he has made glasses for about 6 years. It began as a labor of love, built because he wanted a specific type of blue light blocker. His admitted bad habit: when something he wants doesn't exist, he makes it himself, "which of course is generally not the best way to run a business."
- In 2025 he brought on business partners with a strategy that "100% works if executed", but he didn't want to execute it, and it didn't work out directionally.
- Advice he got from a founder whose e-commerce company did just over a billion dollars in 2025 (he refers to him as Hudson, owner of Comfort):
  - Raise the price to $60-$70.
  - Run buy two, get one free.
  - Activate TikTok Shop affiliates.
  - Iman says this is "100% right" and still chose not to do it.
- His reasoning: even at $30-40 million a year in revenue with 20% net margins, it wouldn't change much for him. Getting there would mean doing a lot of direct-response marketing he doesn't want to do.
- HEELS currently does "low multiple seven figures" in revenue. His plan:
  - Run it for 10 years.
  - Even if revenue reaches $20-30 million organically, he doesn't want to take money out; he wants to reinvest everything in the business and brand.
  - He doesn't want it to lose money, but he'd keep funding it even if it did, because he loves it.
- Examples of financially senseless things he does on purpose: expensive packaging, one-off products, candles he isn't sure he'll sell, and money clips. He told his COO Liz that in 2025, unless they were losing money or in a "code red," she shouldn't talk to him about projections or hitting numbers.
- His analogy: like artists choosing between a mass-market role and a niche indie film, "there's certain things in life that should be left just as passion."
- Brand evidence he cites: celebrity athletes and artists (including a Latin American artist with about 37-40 million followers) wear the product without being sent it, and wealthy friends who wore other luxury eyewear now wear only his. He compares the positioning to Chrome Hearts in the '90s: "anything it touches may not make sense from a commercial perspective but you just know it's going to be the best."

chunks.heading: "It's not what you do, it's who you do it with"
chunks.text:
- His big 2025 reflection: success is less about the mission and more about the people. The mission doesn't need to be world-changing.
- Example mission: a cooking knife company whose purpose is "we want to make sure that anytime you cook, you have a smile on your face." His advice is to pick even a small problem, attach meaning to it, respect it, and do it with incredible people.
- He doesn't know what he'll be doing in 10 years, but says that if he does it with people he loves, "you can keep playing this game forever."
- What you remember is the inside jokes, the hard days and the small random moments (such as driving to sort out a license for a new office), not the expensive purchases or the milestones.
- Team principles he endorses:
  - Everyone plays their role, respects each other's role, and there is no ego.
  - Acknowledge what others can do that you can't, and work as a team.
  - "Life's too short to work with people you don't love and respect."
- He says clients ask why he doesn't start his own agency; he'd rather be part of a bigger company that aligns with his values and culture, working with high performers.
- He values real-world experience (his mother worked as a receptionist at an NHS hospital and at Harrods) and says watching how people treated her is why he stays kind and respectful to everyone.

chunks.heading: Keeping a chip on your shoulder as a motivator
chunks.text:
- Ten years into entrepreneurship and content, he says he feels "the most unaccomplished I've ever felt" and went to Scotland to reassess and decide next steps.
- 2025 was a "generational year" for him, with two massive moves: a stake in WSO and acquiring consulting.com. Specifics of the deals, he says, aren't all disclosed publicly.
- He first thought it was bad to still feel like an underdog, then concluded it's good and worth keeping: "you still need to keep some of that dark motivation."
- He cites Michael Jordan, who reportedly found or invented slights even 20 years into his career to stay motivated.
- He says it's easy to get comfortable after success and that the hunger of earlier years made it easier to get up in the morning. New challenges and targets bring that hunger back.
- He believes his achievements get less credit than the same moves would from others. Examples he gives: buying consulting.com and giving what people paid $80 million for to all customers going back to 2018, and the structure of his WSO stake. He says he has the data room and intimate details of the businesses in the space, and WSO is his favorite company in it.

chunks.heading: Why people dislike you: "hate with emotion, justify with logic"
chunks.text:
- Iman's 2025 realization: people dislike others emotionally and then invent logical justifications. His examples are the Kendrick vs. Drake beef (accusations that stuck without being proven) and a dinner at his home.
- At that dinner, an extremely wealthy person called a business owner "a scammer" with no real basis. Iman, a customer of that business, had found it the best experience of its kind in the world. His read: the person just didn't like him but couldn't say so, because disliking someone for no reason reflects poorly on you, so you need a "logical" reason.
- His takeaway: you can't be everyone's cup of tea, and you don't need to keep disproving every claim. He says his approach is to stay gracious and humble, and notes he pays for everyone at the table, even friends wealthier than him.
- He says envy is a driver: "they never want to see you doing better than them," and winning consistently annoys people.

chunks.heading: Perspective lines worth keeping
chunks.text:
- "What you're living through right now is what you look back at and you're like, these are the good old times." He includes the bad stretches, e.g. a late-2024 crisis in which he had to "take the biggest L we ever had and turn it into a W" and felt like an episode of Succession.
- Don't be so fixated on the dream life that you can't enjoy the simple version you're in now; "still strive and achieve and try to push for more."
- Competitive drive for him is intrinsic ("it's for me"), not a way of earning love or approval.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Iman argues you should replace result goals with measurable daily-action goals, then pick one monetizable skill using four filters (ease of learning, perceived value, barrier to entry, personality fit). He shows how to turn copywriting, cart-recovery sales or viral TikTok e-commerce into a concrete action count, and notes that most people fail because they lack a proper execution plan. The video ends in a pitch for his courses.

chunks.heading: Action-based goals beat result-based goals
chunks.text:
Iman argues that you should stop setting result-oriented goals such as "get to $10,000 a month" or "get in shape". His reasons:

- Result goals put the outcome on a pedestal, which tells your brain you don't deserve it.
- They give you no objective way to judge whether today's work is moving you forward, so you fall back on feelings. That is why people feel busy but never arrive.
- Set a destination without a map and you end up consuming hours of content and trying countless methods.

His fix is to set goals as actions repeated consistently. Fitness example: instead of "put on 10 lb of muscle", set "complete 220 weightlifting sessions this year and have 250 days eating over 3,000 calories". The result becomes a byproduct. If you miss, you know exactly where and by how much you failed. He says most people fail because they don't do what they already know they should, not because they lack information.

chunks.heading: How to pick a money-making skill: four parameters
chunks.text:
Iman says there is no one-size-fits-all answer, so he scores each skill on four parameters:

- **Ease of learning:** pick something you can learn the basics of fast. Highest-paying means nothing if it takes years (his example: learning Mandarin).
- **Perceived value:** how much clients will pay. Formatting computers is easy but pays low; a tax adviser who saves companies eight figures can justify a seven-figure fee.
- **Barrier of entry:** tools or upfront investment. Beginners should avoid high barriers "like the plague".
- **Personality fit:** the most overlooked. A skill that fights your personality will fail even if it scores well elsewhere (coding for someone who hates screens, sales for someone who hates socializing). Play to strengths, not weaknesses.

He adds that if you already have a skill, such as blockchain development or coding, you can ignore ease of learning and barrier of entry. A high barrier then works in your favor by thinning the competition.

chunks.heading: His skill scorecard: why copywriting, sales and e-commerce win
chunks.text:
Iman rates seven "top income skills" for 2024:

- **UX design:** medium difficulty to learn. Perceived value has dropped because Wix, Squarespace and Webflow let businesses do it themselves. Low barrier. Suits creative introverts.
- **Copywriting:** basics are easy via proven structures that remove about 90% of the guesswork. Very high perceived value because it directly generates sales and clients can track the return. Low barrier (computer and internet). He sees the best copywriters as analytical, logical thinkers. Write at "a fifth grader level" and use Grammarly.
- **Coding:** hard to learn, high value, medium barrier. Suits analytical introverts.
- **Sales:** easy in its simplest form, cart recovery (see below). High value, since you can attribute revenue directly. Barrier is a smartphone and internet. Works for extroverts and introverts, but poorly for people who need creative work and dislike repetition.
- **SEO:** easy, but value has fallen from tool-driven supply. Much of it can be done with AI. Boring for analytical or creative people. He recommends copywriting instead if you are above-average capable.
- **E-commerce:** building a Shopify store is easy; getting traffic was the hard part, but viral TikTok product videos changed that about 18 months before this video. High value, low barrier (phone and TikTok account).
- **Blockchain:** high value but extremely hard to learn, with few resources. Not for beginners.

His conclusion: copywriting, sales and e-commerce have the best balance. Pick one by gut feel, "no need to overthink it", because any of them can work.

chunks.heading: Action-based goals for each skill (copywriting, cart recovery, viral TikTok)
chunks.text:
Iman defines success per skill as a volume of actions:

**Copywriting ("learn as you earn"):**
- Pick 10 to 20 brands you'd love to work with and write emails, ads or landing pages for them as if they were clients ("mock clients"), using one copywriting framework.
- Send the best pieces with a note like: "I love the work that you guys do, I've recently started taking on a few copywriting projects and to practice I decided to write you a few emails for your brand... feel free to send them to your email list or use them on your ads."
- Some will respond, and you then offer to write for them on a retainer.
- Goal: write 1,000 pieces of copy in 6 months, about 5 a day. He says sending that volume to 500 to 1,000 businesses and getting no client is "virtually impossible".

**Sales (cart abandonment recovery):**
- Find online sellers (stores, coaches with a course or high-ticket program). Offer to message everyone who started checkout but didn't buy, answer questions and nudge them to finish.
- Work for free upfront and take a commission on recovered sales. Zero risk for the seller, since you only get paid on sales they'd otherwise have lost.
- He says this can lift an online business's revenue by 30 to 50%.
- Goal: send 10,000 cart abandonment messages by year end, about 55 a day (he notes the average 20-something sends about 128 messages a day).
- Math: a 5% recovery rate (which he calls "terrible") at a 20% commission is about $10,000.

**E-commerce (reposting viral product videos):**
- Download product videos that already have millions of views from other TikTok accounts and repost them without editing. Find the right viral videos and products.
- Goal: 20 videos a day for 6 months, about 3,600 videos.
- Conservative math: 1% pop off (36 videos) at 100,000 views each is 3.6 million views. At 0.1% buying, that is 3,600 orders. At $50 per order, about $180,000 revenue, and at a 30% margin about $54,000 profit.

chunks.heading: Why you need an execution plan, and what he recommends
chunks.text:
Iman says 90% of people fail at step five, the plan, because they improvise it from a few YouTube videos. His fitness analogy: 220 gym sessions needs a trainer's protocol (exercises, order, reps, sets, weights, deload periods) and 3,000 calories a day needs a nutritionist's meal plan. In business, the equivalent is a plan for how you will write 1,000 pieces of copy, send 10,000 messages or post 3,600 videos.

Two options: build it yourself (valid if you can't afford anything else, but a higher failure risk) or have a professional build it. Hiring a top copywriter or store owner for a personalized plan is too expensive for most, so Iman says he paid for three experts to record step-by-step courses:

- Copywriting: Penta Profit program from his CMO Louis Berger (emails, ads and sales copy using AI and fill-in-the-blank structures).
- Sales: Six Figure Sales Rep program from his former sales manager Paul Daly (appointment setter or online sales rep).
- E-commerce: a program from Jordan Welch showing how to build a Shopify store from scratch and get the first $1,000 in sales organically.

He says each cost him six or multiple six figures in upfront speaking fees to produce.

chunks.heading: How he packages and sells the entry offer
chunks.text:
Iman's funnel structure in this video:

- He builds urgency through "lost opportunities": a free event (Time's Up), seven free master classes cut from his $1,195 program, and a limited enrollment for his Agency Accelerator. He claims 16-year-olds reached $22,000 a week from the free event.
- He targets people who wanted Agency Accelerator but lacked the money, with a goal of making their first $1,000.
- Each course sells separately for $1,500. Digital Launchpad bundles all of them plus other courses (trading, men's fashion, digital nomad) for $270 a year, or $37 a month (monthly gets fewer perks and no 40% discount).
- Annual subscribers lock in Agency Accelerator at $995 versus the $1,995 full price, and what they spend on Digital Launchpad counts as credit toward it. Enrollment for Agency Accelerator was closed at the time.
- He positions the low-priced tier as a way to earn the first $1,000 and then upgrade, and says it is not meant to make people millionaires or $10K a month.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Iman argues focus comes from starving distraction: block feeds on your computer, strip your phone, optimize your workspace, then run a time-boxed "monk mode" with a few non-negotiables plus your own variables. He favors a flexible protocol over rigid challenges like 75 Hard and starts beginners at 21 days.

chunks.heading: Monk Mode as a protocol: five variables, 21-day first cycle, and why Iman rejects rigid programs
chunks.text:
Iman has run intense focus periods since age 14 (about seven years at recording) and named them "monk mode" in 2020. His first formal version came at the start of 2020, during six weeks in Cape Town: no caffeine, no alcohol, keto/carnivore, no more than 60 minutes of screen time a day, and 45 minutes of daily exercise (even on Saturdays, his usual day off; a brisk walk counted). Version 2 added an hour a day of meditation, which he calls "extremely extremely hard."

His definition: a period of immersion you commit to, with intense focus and even isolation, and he sees "immense power" in simply stating that you are in such a phase.

- Constants across all his cycles: no alcohol, no caffeine, limited screen time, sticking to the diet (strict keto).
- Variables he adds or removes per cycle: once-a-day prayer (he is not religious but spiritual and believes in God), meditation, exercise.
- Lengths vary: some cycles 60 days, others a strict 21-day burst, after which he eases off slightly without abandoning his routines.

chunks.heading: The five-variable monk mode template
chunks.text:
Monk mode is exactly five variables: three non-negotiables plus two of your own. Iman warns that ten daily rules becomes too much.

**Non-negotiables**
- Meditation: at least 10 minutes every day, any kind (he has done up to an hour).
- Exercise: 30 minutes every day (gym, yoga, run, basketball, brisk walk). The goal is an elevated heart rate. On days you fear overtraining, take a long walk.
- No alcohol or weed: "not even a beer." He rejects the "I can still smoke a joint at night and be fine" argument.

**Example variables to pick from**
- No caffeine (his personal favorite)
- Stick to a diet (he does keto)
- Pray once a day
- X hours of a specific outreach per day (e.g. 2 hours of outreach "no matter what the day is", or 10 Looms a day)
- Screen time under a set limit
- Delete Instagram from phone and computer

chunks.heading: Tracking, timeframe and why not 75 Hard
chunks.text:
- Write the protocol on a whiteboard or set it as desktop wallpaper so you see it daily.
- Log your streak at the end of each day.
- First cycle: 21 days, since it will be "a shock to the system." Take about a week off, then try 30 days and work up. Jumping straight to 60 days may be too much.
- He criticizes programs like 75 Hard as too rigid and too long for entrepreneurs. Example: training twice a day is not beneficial for entrepreneurs, whereas he trains 45 minutes about five times a week anyway. A protocol should let you add what matters to your business.
- Action step: write out your protocol (three set plus two variables), post it in the community, and reply to your own post after the 21 days.

chunks.heading: Computer setup: starve distraction
chunks.text:
Iman's thesis after four years of testing (he says he spent over $200,000 on health optimization and about $150,000 on desks, computers, keyboards, mics and office setups): "less is more." Focus is largely starving distraction; the analogy is horses wearing blinders. He adds that adding new productivity apps often just adds clutter. His desktop stack, which he says everyone should use, even someone aiming for a first five-figure year:

- **Facebook News Feed Eradicator** (Chrome extension): use Facebook on desktop with no feed or ads. "Zero value" in checking what others are up to.
- **Unhook** (remove YouTube recommendations): blocks home and sidebar recommendations. He keeps comments on, because he sometimes reads them.
- **Focus for Mac** with hard lock mode: choose sites to block and a timeframe, then it locks. It can allow specific sites (e.g. Business Manager for running client ads) while blocking others. Turn it off for prospecting or outreach; turn it on for studying, building your website, onboarding, hiring and systems work.
- **Brain.fm** for work music, which he has used for three-plus years and says is the only audio he works to. Spotify is blocked via Focus because notifications, new releases and playlist hunting hook you, and he calls working to rap "the worst idea ever." Brain.fm has research backing it.
- **Clean desktop:** one "triage" folder with subfolders, Mac Stacks turned on, and never more than six items on the desktop. His view: messy desktops usually come with messy minds.

chunks.heading: Phone and YouTube rules
chunks.text:
- Minimalism: if you do not use an app daily, remove it, and remove anything that could distract.
- Add the Screen Time widget to the home screen. Many people are at about 8 hours a day while "building an agency." Use app limits to taper (e.g. from 1.5 hours on Instagram to 1 hour, then 30 minutes).
- For agency owners, the phone and social media are likely "the single biggest detractor" to success. Delete Instagram and Facebook from the phone; both work well for prospecting on desktop (Facebook even has a dedicated app).
- Iman runs two phones: one with four apps that nobody has the number for, used from waking (about 6:30) until about 1 pm, and a full one turned on at 1 pm. He gets a cortisol rush just from notifications arriving. A cheap used phone (about $150-200) or an iPod would do. His claim: turning your phone on in the morning costs about 50% of your focus. Cheaper alternative: keep the phone off or on airplane mode for the first hour, then push it later. He suggests gamifying how low you can get your screen time.
- In his office the phone, iPad and other devices stay downstairs. He distrusts people with six monitors, an iPad, an Apple Watch and constant pings: one good 5K screen is all he needs.
- YouTube: delete it from phone and tablet, and unsubscribe from all but about 10 channels (he has about 15). Use it at a desk, intentionally, with Notion or Google Drive open for notes and a watch-later list.
- His argument: "99% of the stuff you're watching is dumbed down" and made for someone else's benefit. About 70% of his own content exists to drive lead flow for GradiAgency.com (the transcript says "gradiency.com"). The real gems tend to be low-view interviews with software founders or high-level entrepreneurs.
- Students already have the paid material to rewatch (main course, bonus courses, Q&A recordings, student interviews).

chunks.heading: Spending on your environment: justified expenses
chunks.text:
- Rule: when money first comes in, spend it on making work easier and more pleasant before status items. Most of it is a business expense (check with your accountant), unlike cars, drinks or luxury clothes.
- Gate: roughly after your first $5,000 month for the big desk and chair items; for headphones, after your first or second client, to create a positive feedback loop (sign a client, buy something that makes you excited to work, sign more).
- Why he skips a supercar despite being able to afford many: insurance, depreciation per mile, and he does not go anywhere to drive it, so it would be an unused liability that distracts from the business. Watches have no mile counter and hold value. He was holding over $1 million in a safety deposit box while in London for three months.
- Clothes: he buys expensive but unbranded pieces (a Bottega or Lauren black t-shirt around $400), so there is no need to wear them out to justify the purchase. Test every purchase by how it changes your daily routine, not just its price.

chunks.heading: Desk, computer and gear list
chunks.text:
- **Desk:** Fully stand-up desk, hardwood. His first laminate desk showed fingerprints, so he switched. The highest-end model was about $1,000 in the US, and his current one about £1,100 (the transcript says "1100 pounds"). Treat it as a 10-year purchase. Footrest mat that mimics a forest floor.
- **Chair:** Herman Miller Aeron, about $1,500, with a 10-year warranty; he has had it three years. It is "the Rolls Royce of chairs."
- **Computer:** a fully specced MacBook Pro, replaced yearly because he sees "no higher ROI." He gives the old one to a team member or friend. This is not a recommendation for beginners.
- **Monitor:** an LG 5K with integrated 1080p webcam, single-cable setup, built-in speakers (no external ones). He says he spent upwards of $7-8K trying other monitors.
- **Audio:** Shure SM7B through a Focusrite Scarlett interface (admits it is overkill; he previously used a Blue Yeti), Bose QuietComfort 2 headphones (second-best he has found; AirPods Max are about $600, similar sound quality but overkill). He says over-ear headphones noticeably deepen focus 30 minutes into a Brain.fm session.
- **Other:** yellow paper (a habit from hearing a famous author used it), a Montblanc pen, incense burning on every floor (about $10-15 for 50 sticks plus a $20 holder on Amazon; he accepts the health trade-off), and tidy cable management. He says it does not need to be perfect and a couple of visible cables is fine.
- Mindset: he treats his desk as "my temple," so small expenses that improve it are insignificant relative to a four-year-old agency.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Iman lists seven habits he credits for reaching $10M liquid by 21: weekly reading, high-income skills, an abundance mindset, daily meditation, high-value skills, character over tactics, and early investing. He says to build the business first, then let investments compound.

chunks.heading: Reading as a non-negotiable early habit
chunks.text:
- Iman credits reading as the single biggest contributor to his success. From 2014 to 2017 he read a book every week.
- He says "there is no medium that's as powerful on earth as books" and that medium doesn't matter (print, audio, borrowed, library), though audiobooks "go in through one ear and straight out the other" for him.
- Cheap sourcing: in 2016 he bought used books at Brixton Bookmongers in London for 2-3 pounds instead of about 15 pounds new at Waterstones. If you can't afford that, borrow from a friend or use a library.
- Zen beginner's mind: early on he had no ego about executing. A book said meditate, so he meditated. A book said journal, so he journaled. He executed "blindfully" and says that strategy is powerful if you pick the right books.
- Today his ego makes him more selective, picking only what resonates. He says that is partly good but also a drag.
- Reading is non-negotiable when starting a business or career. Later, in a phase of pure doing, he reads less because he already knows what to execute.

chunks.heading: Acquire high income skills, even without a plan for them
chunks.text:
- His first business, flipping Instagram accounts (about nine months, started with a page he ran at 14 in 2014 that someone offered to buy), taught him copywriting and social media growth.
- He learned videography/photo in 2016, which landed his first social media marketing client.
- Those three skills (copywriting, social growth, photo/video) combined into a creative agency. For 18 months the agency was exclusively creative; he pivoted to an advertising agency in early 2018. At 17 he was pulling in 25,000 a month.
- Advice: learn a high income skill even if you can't see how it pays off. You can't predict how it will help seven years later.
- Reading fed copywriting too: he kept a Evernote "lexicon library" of new words.
- One skill he wishes he had learned: coding.

chunks.heading: Abundance mindset: don't brake while accelerating
chunks.text:
- He says many people have "your foot on the gas but also your foot on the brake," usually unconsciously.
- Media and school teach that wealthy people are evil or sacrificed ethics. His experience with self-made entrepreneurs is different: they see money as "a transfer of value," and a business must provide value to the market.
- People who work hard without results often haven't done the internal work; they don't believe they're worthy of wealth or that abundance exists.
- He recommends going beyond shallow books like The Secret and reading heavier ones such as Reality Transurfing, which he read at 15 and found life-changing.

chunks.heading: Meditate daily for emotional control
chunks.text:
- He believes half of building wealth is "emotional homeostasis": managing emotions through thick and thin.
- Example: crypto and stock markets are a transfer of emotion; the winner has the best long-term view and the best emotional control.
- Meditation is observing your thoughts and realizing "your thoughts are not you." It exposes triggers behind habits such as eating and spending.
- His example question: when you have a good month in your business and find a way to spend all of it, why do you do that?
- He has meditated for seven years and says it helped surface unconscious behavior.

chunks.heading: Stack high value skills after high income skills
chunks.text:
- High income skills (copywriting, sales, content creation, programming) are easy to quantify and get paid for directly. High value skills matter just as much but aren't paid directly.
- Sequence: build high income skills first, because you need revenue; then collect high value skills for long-term benefit.
- Example 1, talent: he credits about 70% of his business success to his team. He is very good at finding, convincing, attracting and retaining talent, using mission, compensation and performance bonuses. Danny is CMO of the agency, Kieran runs the education company, and the software company is the only one with a business partner. He says no one can manage multiple businesses without senior people running day-to-day operations.
- Example 2, accounting and cash flow: even with an expensive bookkeeper and accountant, he reads his own P&L and understands run rate.
- His agency is the cash flow business funding his lifestyle and investments. His other businesses carry millions in R&D costs that won't turn to revenue for years, so he tracks how long he can fund R&D before recouping.
- For his e-commerce eyewear brand Gadgey, restocking the G1 blue light blockers takes three months, and developing and stocking a new model takes five months, so cash flow planning is critical.

chunks.heading: Focus on who you must become, not on tactics
chunks.text:
- Over five years he has asked "who do I need to become" to make the money he wants, rather than which tactic to implement. Tactics "come naturally" when character is right; he says character is about 80% of the equation.
- He admits ego made decisions worse from roughly 2017 to early 2020, with a chip on his shoulder from a bad high school experience and dropping out. He says he only dialed his ego in over the last year to year and a half.
- His traits to work on for going from 10 million to 25 million after tax by age 25: punctuality (he's "notoriously late" and slow to reply outside Slack; lateness "is breaking a promise to yourself"), humility, and gratitude (things feel stale or numb).

chunks.heading: Invest early, but build the business first
chunks.text:
- He says to start investing as soon as possible, even 50 a month, because it compounds. He thinks starting at 18 instead of 20 would have added roughly 5 to 20 million dollars by 21.
- The jump from a few million at 20 to about 10 million liquid at 21 (investments plus cash reserves, not net worth) came from investing.
- Passive income view: investing is "the only true passive income." Affiliate income decays; he saw one software affiliate payout of 15,000 a month fall to about 8,000 in a year.
- Investing keeps lifestyle in check: his lifestyle barely changed when the agency went from 30,000 to 100,000 a month.
- He now puts 50% to 70% of monthly income into investments. His budget is what the portfolio earns monthly. His next goal is a 25 million portfolio by 25, which he says would let him spend four to six times as much as now.
- Target setting: at 16, after reading Money: Master the Game, his number was 2 million for a comfortable life; he has reached about five times that. Pick your own number, for example 1 million.
- Order of operations: until you reach 10,000 a month, don't expect investing to get you there; just dollar cost average small amounts into any asset class. "Your business is going to make you rich but your investments will make you wealthy long-term." Growing a business from 10k to 30k a month is far easier than growing a portfolio the same way, which could take a decade.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Iman Gadzhi explains why beginners should pick digital products or services where failure is cheap, how to build a personal brand around a specific business goal, and why intensity must give way to patience and rigid routines give way to new interests. He also shares his case for WAP's content rewards as an advertising channel.

chunks.heading: Two seasons: intensity first, then loosening up
chunks.text:
- Iman compares early success to getting a plane off the ground: takeoff burns a lot of fuel, then cruising "just kind of sips fuel."
- At 16-18 he was rigidly locked in ("almost a little autistic"), with everything diligent and regimented. He says that served him up to a point.
- He then plateaued. Relaxing his schedule and adding hobbies and interests is what let him make more money again and reach the next level.
- He says the most successful people he knows eat what they want, have no 15-step morning routine and aren't "super optimized." Each has their own quirks.
- He says his videos aimed at his 16-17-year-old self make him look more monk-mode than he is now.
- On urgency: short term (today) you need agitation and urgency. Over a 1, 3 or 5 year horizon you must be patient. "The only thing stopping you from reaching your goals is time." You can shrink that time but it still has to play out.
- More success means more sacrifice and responsibility. He compares it to training: 3x a week is good, 2-3 sessions a day does more harm than good. He says people understand this for training but not for money.
- He says most advice is bad advice for any one person. Pick what applies to you rather than copying someone's whole life.

chunks.heading: Focus, dopamine and where a founder's time goes
chunks.text:
- He treats a dopamine detox like fasting. It resets your baseline (caffeine, TikTok, games) so ordinary work feels rewarding again.
- Fried dopamine receptors mean you "can't sit down for even an hour and focus on one task," which makes building a career very hard.
- He says he isn't a focused person now. Deep focus was a skill he had to build for a season, when he "was basically the whole business."
- He once dismissed Gary Vee as "just doing meetings and on calls" and now owes him an apology, because that is nearly all he does. His real work is meetings, calls and decisions, sometimes thought through on a walk. He almost never sits down to build.
- Rule: use deep-work intensity while you are the business, then shift to leverage and decisions.

chunks.heading: Best businesses for beginners: digital products and services
chunks.text:
- His filter is risk: choose businesses where failing for 6-12 months costs about $50-100/month in software, not $30k in physical stock or ad spend.
- He says physical product models like FBA, brand building and dropshipping can work, but they make him anxious for beginners.
- His own physical-product risk: a packaging issue at one brand cost about $80k in packaging and delayed release by 6 weeks. He can absorb that because he has other cash flow. A beginner cannot.
- He sends million-dollar wires for stock at his own brands. Customs once held stock for 3 months, even during Covid.
- Digital product examples from WAP, where the average user makes $9,000/month: a creator earning $8,000/month selling Fortnite maps, and another earning $71,000/month teaching Pokemon card trading.
- He says one $30 Excel course has made $150 million. Buyers don't check credentials, they check price and reviews.
- Other digital products he lists: Shopify themes, niche communities.
- At 12-13 he traded FIFA Ultimate Team coins and sold them to kids at school.
- Services path: his first agency client was in 2016 at about $300/month, doing photo and video for local businesses, later moving into advertising. He calls services "a foot through the door," not an instant multimillionaire path.

chunks.heading: Content rewards and clipping as distribution
chunks.text:
- He says his team has run an internal clipping department for 2.5 years. At its peak he spent about $250,000/month on short-form clipping.
- Beginner version: pay about $30-100 for an editing course, then clip for companies or on a platform like WAP.
- He says content rewards let brands pay fans and creators instead of platforms. Spend goes to clippers rather than Facebook or Google, at roughly 5-10% of the CPM of Facebook ads.
- Example: $5k into content rewards instead of paying a platform for ads.
- Bounty example: pay $100/week for the thumbnail he picks. He has three full-time in-house thumbnail designers, which he says is overkill for most people.
- He says large advertisers have told WAP they want to put $10M/month of ad budget into content rewards by year end. The bottleneck is clippers, not buyers.
- He argues distribution is moving toward many accounts posting the same content with links back to the main channel or funnel. Follower and subscriber counts matter less than giving the algorithm more chances.
- He frames WAP as bigger than Shopify-style tools because it combines payments, checkout, delivery of digital products and advertising in one platform. He became a co-owner for a very large sum, and says he turned down offers from every other company in the space. He picked it partly for positioning, not wanting to be "on the wrong side of history."
- He compares digital products today to e-commerce between 2012 and 2022.

chunks.heading: Personal brand: be intentional about the business backend
chunks.text:
- His top mistake is not being intentional. He says views don't equal success; they only matter if they feed the game you actually play on the back end.
- For his first 2.5 years he didn't monetize his personal brand at all. It was a vlog diary. Agency clients then came from it, including his first big client Affle (now Gemflow), who found him via a YouTube video.
- Today he says the brand's biggest payoffs are hiring, deal flow and the terms he gets when investing.
- Example mismatch: broad "millionaire mindset tips" content cannot sell high-ticket B2B services to enterprise clients.
- He recommends starting with a high-ticket, niche audience. Niche advice attracts a niche market, and broad content turns away high-level viewers.
- That's why he runs multiple channels. His main channel is for beginners, a business channel covers backend topics like thumbnail rehash SOPs and cart abandonment flows, and vlogs reach wealthy viewers who only watch vlogs. He says this is specific to his goals and not for everyone.
