- Case study: Harry Stebbings' 20VC podcast has about 200k subscribers and, per Iman, raised $500M from the podcast. He cites it as proof that a niche show can be hugely valuable.
- He runs a B2B licensing program (AFL) that refuses beginners. He says broad content would be pointless if AFL were all he sold.
- Example: one AFL member makes a few hundred thousand dollars a month from a podcast, with done-for-you and coaching offers on the back end. Iman suggests a separate business-of-podcasting channel for that, rather than promoting it on the main show.
- His own monetizable broad assets: an eyewear brand, a consumables brand and a roughly $30/month mobile app.

chunks.heading: Spending, investing and money lessons
chunks.text:
- Spend early money on whatever makes you more excited to work: a good chair, MacBook, desk, headphones, sleep wearables (Oura Ring, Whoop, Eight Sleep), a better gym, a cleaner, laundry service or meal prep.
- He says that at 5K-10K months, a clean space is invaluable.
- His first 6-figure purchase was a trip to Paris for his mom, which he promised at 17 and says cost a couple thousand dollars. Another promise was a dream house with a Range Rover out front, which he did at 23. He says making promises to loved ones is a strong anchor, because "people will do more for their loved ones than they will for themselves."
- His dumbest purchase: three Bored Apes in early 2022 at about $400k each (about $1.2M), an ego purchase. He sold two for $200k each and kept one.
- He put $1M into Bitcoin in November 2022 (he calls this a treacherous year). He says his net worth swung between about $5M and $15M. He says it is now over $100M, and notes illiquid assets (multi-million-dollar domains) make it hard to value.
- In the past year he has focused on investing in companies, as "a tiny little fish" in a world of sharks. He says he relies on good advisers.
- Example of why he stays humble on terms: a $60M napkin advertising company wanted him to invest, and he said he doesn't add enough value to ask for discounted equity.
- On lifestyle: spend on whatever has meaning for you, and don't shame others' spending. He says that even wealthy friends' spending sometimes shocks him until he scales it to their wealth.
- On mentors vs books: books are best for most people, but further along "mentors are more valuable."

chunks.heading: Finding meaning in the work, and giving
chunks.text:
- He says money isn't an object for him, so he'd do what he's doing now. He sees WAP as reforming education and says he had "reforming the education system" in his Instagram bio in 2017.
- His eyewear brand is priced around $95-120, aimed at people who otherwise choose $30 frames or $250 Ray-Bans. He sold 4% to a strategic partner in May; the partner has done $1B in eyewear. He says the brand will do eight figures this year.
- His credit goes to his partner (Alex Hawkes) for product and WAP's engineers for building. He says his own contribution is steering: deciding where to focus.
- On mission statements: they need to be rooted in reality. His imagined knife brand's mission, "never cook again without a smile on your face," is not fully attainable but still credible. Overreaching missions demotivate teams.
- He says he can find meaning in any industry if he works with people he loves and improves the product.
- His reason for operating at scale: being "the container" that creates opportunity for others. He kept one employee for 8 years (since 2017) by setting up win-win-win deals.
- He says "the more you give, the more you get" but only with boundaries; pushovers don't serve anyone.
- His best advice: "this too shall pass," in highs and lows alike.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Iman explains how his approach changed from 7/10 to full throttle: only enter businesses where he holds an edge, use his personal brand to feed them, and hire operators over thinkers. He also lays out why low-risk service businesses sold to other businesses are the best beginner path.

chunks.heading: Why he turned the dial up three years ago
chunks.text:
- At the time of the first podcast, Iman was a few years past his first million, earning a couple million a year with eight employees, "living seven out of 10" of his capability.
- He says he can't name a mindset shift or environment change (he rejects the idea that Dubai drove it): "one day I just woke up" and wanted to take things bigger. He framed it as an experiment: "what would this look like if I was to just turn up the dial on everything."
- He admits his life was "substantially better" at 7/10, because that level gets roughly 70 to 80% of life's benefits without the stress and complexity.
- His current mission is to build for the people around him ("Entourage season"). He gets his fulfillment from what the team gets to experience, not from material things.
- He says fulfillment comes from doing hard things, which is why he feels more at peace now despite having far more to run.

chunks.heading: Habits change by stage: don't copy what he does now
chunks.text:
- Early on (2016 to 2019) he was obsessive: back from the gym at a set time, at his desk at a set time, no breaks. He says a beginner has to be that detail-oriented because "you are the business operator as opposed to being the business owner."
- Back then, one McDonald's lunch meant brain fog and roughly 50% less output, and since he was the whole company, the company's output fell 50%.
- With 100 employees, if he takes a day off or eats badly, net company output drops about 1%. His wealthiest friends eat clean but will have the dessert or take the day off.
- He pushes back on "don't do as I do" criticism: he is buying a roughly $750,000 physical business in Dubai, and says a beginner "shouldn't" do that, nor copy his habits, 10 years in.
- Owners who micromanage stay "80% of the company's output" because they never put leaders in place.

chunks.heading: Personal brand and synergistic businesses
chunks.text:
- The biggest change since the last podcast: he now believes "anyone should build a personal brand," because it correlates with whatever their business does.
- Earlier, the content team was one or two people and he saw it as the "least profitable" department. Taking it seriously grew the YouTube channel from about 170,000 subscribers (Aug 2021) to about 5 million, with roughly 250k about two years before the recording.
- He says his team posts about 300 million views a month on its own accounts, systemized across every platform, with no affiliate program.
- He builds businesses synergistically: he only enters one if he has a competitive advantage and can funnel his audience into it. On his e-learning platform, the real money is on the back end, since he owns or invests in most of the software he promotes.
- He says he is "a business person that creates content," spending two to three hours a month on content, and runs his businesses day to day. He dumbs himself down online and avoids talking about 95% of the real behind-the-scenes business.

chunks.heading: Hiring, operators and playbooks
chunks.text:
- His other big learning curve was running a real company (legal, HR, accounting, finance, department leads), with no business school or prior employer.
- He learned who is an operator and who is a thinker. A visionary CEO paired with a visionary founder "just simply doesn't work," so he sometimes needs a COO-type who actually operates.
- Playbooks don't always transfer: a competitor to his software company Floy had raised $475 million and can acquire customers at a loss, while he has raised nothing. A CEO from a $3.2B company wouldn't know how to run his self-funded company.
- Masterclass, he notes, is valued around $2.7B on about $94M in revenue and is not profitable, so he can't follow its playbook.

chunks.heading: Competitive advantage, uncorrelated assets and what a business is worth
chunks.text:
- Rule: he only invests where he has a competitive advantage, but he is now also buying uncorrelated assets. The Dubai business he is buying should do roughly $1.5M a year once turned around, and he gets 50%.
- Reason: in a recession his stocks and property fall, while some businesses (cigarettes, fast food) barely move, whereas Ferrari makes less. Collector handbags (Birkins, Kellys, vintage pieces) are another uncorrelated asset he has held for years.
- GGI, his eyewear brand, does a few million dollars a year with zero advertising, but he says it is "worth absolutely [ __ ] all" because it has his name on it. He brought on a partner who sold an eyewear business for a few hundred million and is renaming it to a five-letter name to sell it.
- He says a business is worth what someone will pay, not a multiple: "I could say my e-learning company is worth $400 million... no one's going to pay that." Name risk is why Gucci is worth more than Tom Ford on identical fundamentals.
- Risk philosophy: five years ago he'd take a guaranteed few million a year over a 20% shot at $250M. Now he can take risks with "basically no risk" because he has leverage and cash flow. He says it is the reason he stresses: "get rich guaranteed" first, don't copy his risks as a beginner.
- His software company started in 2020 only worked because his business partner was an agency client already running a software in another industry; they repositioned it into AgencyFlow, later rebranded Floy.

chunks.heading: Digital Launchpad: positioning, pricing and delivery
chunks.text:
- Digital Launchpad is a $37/month subscription (yearly is 40% off, about 74 cents a day, $270 a year) with a new 10 to 20 hour program launching every month, around 200 hours at launch, and about 15 coaching calls a week.
- Production: shot on Red Raptors in a roughly $100,000 setup. He says competitors could do loom and a webcam but he wants Netflix-grade quality at that price. It also has an app, allowed on the App Store.
- Teachers include Mike Thurston, Jordan Welch and a boxing YouTuber with 2 million subscribers, plus tailor, detox and relationship content, so it covers health, wealth and relationships.
- Promise: "we're here to help you make your first $1,000 online," not "become a millionaire." At $270 a year, a buyer has about 3.5 years to fail and still break even.
- His goal is to reform the education system, so he is trending toward cheaper products, not a $30,000 program. He says Masterclass is about $180 a year and doesn't teach hard practical skills.
- Why big names join: financial incentives, a few who own software that he features and who got big growth from it (one sold his company for a life-changing sum), the pull of being around his team, and his reputation as a long-term player. He says he has the pull now to call anyone, which he couldn't do three years ago.
- He only features the best solutions in a category, and brings in outside experts where he isn't the best: 75% of Agency Accelerator is taught by others, and outreach is taught by the owner of lemlist (he says it processed $118M of deals in a month).

chunks.heading: Why service businesses, and how the arbitrage works
chunks.text:
- He prefers service businesses for beginners because you can fail for 8 to 18 months for about $30 to $50 a month in software, whereas e-commerce or Amazon FBA risks serious debt or dead stock. He cites his own dead stock from 2021 in one company.
- His own first client came by accident in August 2016, and his second came seven months later; he didn't quit because trying cost only about $30 a month.
- Sell to businesses, not consumers: "$1,000 to you and $1,000 charged to your business are two different things." In the UK a business can reclaim 20% VAT and reduce its tax bill, while a person would need to earn about £2,000 pre-tax. Even a small coffee shop has about $40,000 a month in expenses.
- Pick services beyond Facebook and Google ads. As an example, three weeks learning Zapier and backend automation could sell at $5,000 a project, and he says you can get up to scratch on many skills in about 14 days.
- Agencies (and creative agencies) beat solo services like personal training or videography because you can take a day off and delivery continues with contractors.
- Arbitrage model: the client pays upfront, the contractor (e.g. Facebook ads in South Africa, Zapier in Brazil, email in Slovakia) is paid after delivery, so you get positive cash flow, like insurance float or dropshipping. He says you still need to know something about the service.
- Limits: any service in any niche can reach about $10,000 a month, but not every niche reaches $100,000 a month. He says getting the first client is hard but no harder than anything else.

chunks.heading: Investing: know your investor type
chunks.text:
- His biggest regret: he only started investing in 2020. He put $1M into Bitcoin around Nov/Dec 2020, held up to $8M in a hot wallet, and sold in late 2021. He says it was luck and calls most crypto gains luck.
- His style changed: he now buys bonds yielding 5 to 6% (Saudi, Apple, US government; not banks, which he says produce nothing), and does automatic weekly dollar-cost averaging into stocks every Tuesday, avoiding Monday and Friday volatility, even though he thinks the market is overvalued.
- In property, he moved from buying a property every month to about twice a year, preferring bigger assets and fewer tenants, and requires a year of rent upfront, accepting a lower price and fewer tenants. He has a family office and CFO handling investments, accounting, tax and offshore planning.
- Advice: find your risk tolerance and use competitive advantages in investing too (e.g. a family in property for 30 years should get into property). He says the best early investment is yourself, including a boring accounting or finance qualification, because as the business is you, your capability sets the business's ceiling.
- On first $10,000: have a plan for the money, or you end up blowing it.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Iman recounts building a social media agency from a £300/month soccer club client to six figures a month. He covers the fake audit cold outreach, the Expedia-style contractor model, why results-based services beat content retainers, and the founder discipline that kept him scaling.

chunks.heading: Origin story and the "why" behind the business
chunks.text:
- Iman was born in a small Russian village and moved to London at age 3 with his mother and stepfather. He went to expensive private schools while home life deteriorated.
- By 14 his stepdad had cut off his mom entirely (though still paying school fees). Iman describes it as "a Rolls Royce but no money to pay for petrol."
- At 14 he decided "either I step up and do something or we are [screwed]." He read a book a week from 14 to 17, buying used books at Brixton for about 3 pounds instead of 14.
- At 16-17 he drifted into nightclubs and drugs. A New Year's morning where his mother realized she was losing him made him commit to business seriously. At that point he had one client paying 300 pounds a month.
- He says his motivation was desperation first, then inspiration. The "why" of supporting his mom got him to 10-15K a month but could not carry him further.
- He stalled at roughly 50-80K a month for about six or seven months (February to September of the prior year) because he had no new reason to push. He moved on once his why became reforming the education system through the best online programs.
- When he turned 18 his stepdad filed for divorce and demanded they leave within seven days. Because of the business, he could cover a divorce legal bill he describes as costing "a couple hundred grand."
- He says he would not have grown as fast without the pain of his mother's situation, and calls it a matter of motivation, not ability.

chunks.heading: How he got the first clients (before the agency took off)
chunks.text:
- Early money came from flipping Instagram accounts (2014): grow niche accounts, then sell them or use them to sell shout-outs.
- Then he did personal training (about 30 pounds an hour to friends' wealthy parents), studying the certification books he bought from trainers on Instagram.
- At 16 he bought a camera (a Canon) to move into content and videography, a higher-leverage skill.
- Client 1 was his semi-pro football club. He told the coach their social media was terrible; the owner asked "how much?" before he could say yes. Package: 75 pounds a week (300 a month) for 4 YouTube videos, 30 Facebook posts and 30 Instagram posts, all shot and edited by him on Saturdays.
- He valued the recurring retainer. Predictable cash flow stops emotionally charged short-term decisions.
- Client 2 was a fitness company, Athlete, found by cold-emailing gyms and fitness businesses with a video, then a shoot, then a management retainer. He packaged it in tiers and quoted 1,900 pounds a month (about $2,500). He got the yes while sitting in class and left.

chunks.heading: Dropping out and the 45-day jump to about $15K a month
chunks.text:
- A mentor, Bob, got him a video shoot with a Bang & Olufsen owner in Holland (about 800 pounds plus paid travel). On the flight he decided he wanted freedom and to feel like "a respected business owner."
- He set a rule: if he could secure his overhead plus rent (about 2,500 pounds a month, so roughly 10K in contracts, deposits or lump sums) within two months, he would drop out of school.
- He signed Athlete, Zebra Fuel (about $3,500), Furo Systems and a personal trainer within about two and a half weeks, then went to the local council to make the case for leaving school.
- In roughly 45 days he went from about $2,500 to about $15,000 a month.

chunks.heading: Cold outreach: the "fake audit" strategy and other prospecting tactics
chunks.text:
- The first clients all came from Instagram DMs and cold email. His hook was a short video story: "give me 5 seconds and I'll show you 3 ways you're leaving 10K a month on the table," followed by an offer of a coffee and a free 15-20 minute consultation.
- "Leaving money on the table" is a phrase that resonates with owners. He also tells them "your social media isn't congruent to the size of your business."
- Fake audit strategy: sending 100 personalized videos a day was too slow. Instead he took a screenshot of the prospect's homepage, added a play button in Canva, and put it in a template email saying he had made a free audit of three ways they were leaving money on the table.
- The link did not play. About 10 of 100 replied "your video wouldn't play," which showed they were interested; only then did he spend time on a real 15-20 minute audit.
- Subject lines: he never capitalized the first letter, because promotional email capitalizes everything, so lowercase looks different.
- He now uses Loom for audits, because it uploads in seconds and shows whether the prospect opened it.
- Target the CMO or founder, never the social media manager or paid traffic person, because an agency threatens their job. A CMO only cares that marketing makes money.
- Finding the decision maker: LinkedIn for company size and roles, then Facebook, then the person's previous employer's email format, since people often keep old emails.
- He says there is no single best outreach method. It depends on niche and country (cold calling is banned by a registry in Holland). He gave examples: dentists are hard to reach by phone because the owner is often practicing.
- Force versus power: early on you must use force (cold outreach, calls, networking). Later you get power (inbound and referrals) through a niche authority built via value posts in Facebook groups and LinkedIn.
- Case study funnel: he sends cold traffic to a one-hour case study page built in ClickFunnels with a pixel. Even people who bounce get retargeted aggressively for 30 to 60 days until they book a discovery call.

chunks.heading: Handling objections and positioning against big agencies
chunks.text:
- Against full-service agencies he positions as a boutique that specializes in one thing. A large agency splits 100% of its effort across ten services.
- He tells clients the extra 7,500 a month a big agency charges is paying for rent, an espresso machine and payroll, not expertise, while he uses contractors.
- A one-day internship at an agency doing about half a million a month in retainers showed him their inefficiencies and that their campaigns were optimized for brand awareness and reach, not revenue.

chunks.heading: The pivot from social media retainers to results-based Facebook ads, and the Expedia model
chunks.text:
- Retainers based on content stopped working around month three or four, when funded clients asked for ROI. He concluded he had to sell on tangible results.
- First attempt: he added Facebook ads to existing clients for only 500 pounds extra a month. He lost his first 4 or 5 clients, who dropped everything, not just the ads. His agency "got smashed to pieces" in late 2017.
- Lesson: you cannot learn Facebook ads in 30 days, nor email marketing or SEO. Claims that you can start at zero and sell and deliver 3K ad retainers within 30 days are false.
- He bought every Facebook ads course and coach, and says none of it worked. He compares it to learning to ride a bike by reading.
- The Expedia insight: Expedia made about 11 billion in revenue as a glorified affiliate connecting customers to services, like Uber owning no cars. He realized he was "a glorified contractor."
- He hired a Colombian contractor (Danny) at about $600 per month per client and resold the service at $2,000, then $3,000, then $5,000 and eventually a $10K a month retainer. Danny also served as his coach, so he learned by shadowing: for instance, why a retargeting campaign uses a conversion objective rather than reach.
- He had to teach Danny copywriting. Danny now works for him full time.
- Work on the business, not in it. He built systems (onboarding, scheduling) and tested them, rather than running around "like headless chickens."

chunks.heading: Systems, hiring and team building
chunks.text:
- Scheduling system: Acuity Scheduling (he says Calendly works similarly) with a universal Zoom link in the confirmation email, so prospects get an iCal or Google invite. Clients get a Slack channel and email, never his phone number.
- Where to hire: Facebook groups, not Upwork or Fiverr. Upwork people often work for the hourly rate. He found Danny in a Facebook Ads group because he kept asking and answering questions with no agenda.
- A good team member takes initiative. Danny joins sales calls, vets the client, and checks their pixel data without being told.
- You don't need to deliver the service yourself. He gives the example of his girlfriend's LinkedIn agency, where she trains the team and oversees delivery.

chunks.heading: Facebook ads and client retention tips
chunks.text:
- Tip 1: Sign "easy clients" with existing pixel data. A new client like Mattress.com (mattre.com), with podcast features on Tim Ferriss, Kevin Rose and Joe Rogan, lets him backdate six months of traffic and retarget initiate-checkout and add-payment-info visitors for fast sales. The same logic applies to a large Instagram, Facebook or YouTube audience. Warm audiences beat cold.
- Tip 2: Study copywriting. Copy and creative matter most; for info products and e-commerce long-form copy works. Avoid stock-photo-looking images, because if people see an ad they scroll past.
- Tip 3: The 90-day emotional journey. Clients are happy in the first weeks, then around days 20 to 40 they get anxious and make emotional decisions. He now sells a three-month minimum then month to month, so they cannot cancel at the dip. Earlier he ran month by month and "stacked the odds against" himself.
- Billing: every client is on auto-invoice with a card on file via Stripe, accepting the 2% fee. "Every invoice is a reframe," and he does not want clients re-deciding monthly.
- He ran about $2-3K a day on ads for himself and clients and says agencies waste money chasing awareness.
- Niche research matters. In real estate, seller leads beat buyer leads because sellers often buy too and the agent gets double commission. For cars, a larger purchase means you can target a radius of about 100 miles, versus about 3 miles for a gym.
- Dental offer idea: free teeth cleaning as the front-end offer, then the dentist mentions stained teeth from coffee or wine to upsell whitening or crowns in the thousands.

chunks.heading: Focus, routine and mindset
chunks.text:
- "You don't have business problems, you have personal problems manifesting in your business." His stall at 50-80K was due partly to waking at 5:30 only 70% of the time: "how you do one thing is how you do everything."
- Most of what he teaches is not outreach tactics: block distractions, wake at the same time daily, and do one to two focused hours a day. In his view that gets you about 80% of the way to six figures a year.
- Tools he uses: the Alarmy app (he must scan a barcode in the kitchen to stop the alarm), Facebook News Feed Eradicator, a YouTube blocker for comments and recommendations, and Focus, which blocks email, Spotify and sites. He keeps a second phone for work that is on only eight hours a day.
- He warns that social media lets you get the validation of work without doing it, so he limits exposure to it "like a drug dealer who doesn't use his own product."
- Mentor Sam Ovens helped him from about 100K a month through focus, efficiency and routine, though he says Sam's marketing and sales material was not revolutionary.
- His vision: reform the education system with the best online learning platform, including a custom portal (about $500K to build) integrating Oura ring, QuickBooks and course content so students can see how sleep and finances affect their business.
- With about 1,500 students he saw that some get no results while others make 10K a month in weeks. He credits systems, routine and mindset, plus whether they actually take action.
- His closing advice: work on the business not in it, focus on income-producing activities, and "wherever you go, there you are": success does not remove personal problems.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Iman Gadzhi explains how his team runs quarterly challenges with 1.2M registrants. He covers speaking to the four audience tiers, using short-form purely for reach to cut ad costs, building offers around objections, and baking in refunds. He also stresses profitability over revenue and building on existing competitive advantages.

chunks.heading: Who Iman serves: four markets, two at a time
chunks.text:
- Iman splits audiences into four markets: beginner, mid-market, advanced, and mass market. He says people often miss the fourth one.
- Beginners have "solved out all the kinks in their inner dialogue." Show them a process and they will follow it.
- Mass market is different. The process is not their problem. Mindset and limiting beliefs are, so a guaranteed process does not move them.
- Mass market language must be dumbed down. Words like "sell," "selling online" and "funnel" scare them, and his team stops filming when those words slip out.
- Mid-market hates his style. He gives consultant.com as the example: take a 2-minute idea and stretch it into 2 hours.
- Advanced people "look at the results, not how the words someone uses."
- You can hold two markets at most. For his brand that is mass market plus advanced. Moving toward one market moves you away from another.
- His rule: "You shouldn't be for everyone." Some segment will always dislike you, and that is fine.
- Mass-market content takes constant effort to stay dumb. He says dumbing it down is "so much harder than you would think" for logical people like him and his CMO Luis.
- He admits the team narrowed its content over the past 18 months, partly from ego, and now plans to go wide again.
- His barometer for the main channel: if the team would happily watch the video, it is the wrong video. Make it for "me 10 years ago," not for the team.

chunks.heading: Organic plus ads: short form as reach, not conversion
chunks.text:
- His view: "I don't think in today's day and age it's organic versus ads. I think it's both."
- Short form runs about 70 owned accounts. At peak the team posted around 15,000 pieces a month, now fewer. Monthly views run 150M to 300M.
- Short form has no CTAs and no links. It exists for reach and face familiarity.
- The payoff is lower ad costs. A big organic month is followed by cheaper advertising the next month.
- True cold traffic only appears past about $2.5M of monthly ad spend. Before that, most people seeing the ads have already seen his face.
- He tried funneling short form to leads (including ManyChat flows) and found little. One month with 240M views produced roughly 5,000 to 10,000 leads. Years ago it was around 50,000. TikTok and Instagram throttle CTA-based content.
- He no longer tries to funnel it. The return comes from lower CPMs.
- The department was renamed from short form (clipping) to the narrative team, because the goal is to set the message and manage PR, not maximize views.
- He avoided outside clippers and built in-house. His reason: view-incentivized clippers hurt the brand, and "not all publicity is good publicity."
- He is never the first mover. He studies what the first mover did and avoids their mistakes.
- Source of content: internal "car podcast" and similar. About 6 minutes of chatting yields roughly 8 clips, which can reach 100M to 500M views over their life. He dislikes public podcasts and does internal ones instead.
- Interactive, lifestyle content beats a plain podcast format. He regrets not pre-scripting more scenarios and questions, such as the clip where he was asked about his bank balance, which went around half a billion views.
- Practical habit: doom-scroll TikTok 10 to 20 minutes a day to find hooks that work, then reuse them in ads.
- Acting classes or a public speaking coach help on camera.

chunks.heading: Running a 1.2M-registrant challenge
chunks.text:
- The last live event got about 1.2M registrants: roughly 200,000 organic and 1,000,000 paid.
- Lead capture spend was a little under $2.5M over 3 weeks.
- The event also produced 42,000 VIPs in 3 weeks.
- Prep runs 8 to 10 weeks out. Concepts to be taught at the event are seeded into videos beforehand as warm-ups.
- The Notion task list starts at about 500 tasks per event and ends around 700 to 800. Every department is involved, with hundreds of creatives.
- His own face is the bottleneck on creatives. He says output could reach about 20,000 creatives a month without that limit, versus 600 to 700 before an event.
- Before this, offers were evergreen with 2 to 3 events a year, including pre-recorded 4-part launches that he knew converted worse but did "because it was sick." His advice: it is fine to do some things in your business just because you like them.
- Then they moved to 5-day live challenges, roughly 3 to 4 per year.
- They only sell about three weeks a year. He says this lowers revenue but also lowers regulatory exposure, since live sales are less exposed than evergreen.
- Context he stresses: this works for his objectives and does not automatically transfer to yours.

chunks.heading: Offer design: guardrails, licensing and objection-first
chunks.text:
- His first step: list the objections, then reverse-engineer the offer. Give people "what they want," deliver it, then give them "what they need."
- Parts of the offer are not revealed publicly until someone is a client, because they would scare buyers.
- He treats "course" as dead: "You're not in the business of information, you're in the business of transformation." Stay undogmatic about the format.
- Tier structure at consultant.com:
  - Mass market: software, with preset guardrails so customers "can't mess it up."
  - Mid-tier: services, such as a dedicated consultant.
  - High end (Quantum): strategy, because those clients already have teams and software.
- He licenses instead of building. Example: a Brazilian company with about 50 marketing agents (Instagram story sequences, VSSLs, YouTube and more) that Luis was already using.
- Illustrative deal shape (he says the numbers are not exact): about 20,000 seats a year, a $1.5M to $2M annual check, and a roughly 90% wholesale discount. The software is white-labeled under his name and placed inside the offer stack, not resold separately.
- Leverage comes from buying volume, so he can demand aggressive discounts.
- He tells others they license too little and build too much.
- Standalone software is a trap: "my recommendation is don't ever try to sell as a standalone thing, just put it in your offer." He ran his own software to six figures of recurring revenue but only his own audience wanted it. He ended up buying out his partner and bundling it.
- The 80% failure fact: most buyers of any effortful product do not succeed. His analogy is DJ decks, where most buyers never become professional DJs. Build your numbers on that, not on the idealized picture.
- Refunds are priced in as a "get tax." His guarantee is truly no questions asked: 7 days on the front end, 7 days after the event for VIP tickets. Refund rate runs roughly 5% to 10%, last event around 9%.
- For late refund requests (even months later) the team can refund to avoid headaches, because that roughly 1% of angry customers is who triggers regulators. He says they have never had a verified negative customer review.
- He wants carrots dangled outside refund windows to reduce refunds.

chunks.heading: Sales team vs no sales team
chunks.text:
- He claims to have run large volume with no sales reps, and says the live events do this at scale. He says every sales hire adds risk and liability.
- When challenged on dialers for a low-ticket funnel (an audience member's $350 CPA free-course funnel into a $52/month tool), he says that setup often gets shut down within 6 to 12 months. His reasoning: platforms pay out upfront for beginner signups, cancel rates are high, and eventually the finance team pulls the plug.
- His advice there: run it for all it is worth, but do not close your high-ticket offer, because reopening it is hard.
- He says full compliance is impossible. Study the biggest known risk items, remove the worst ones, and do not tiptoe around everything.
- Avoid phone sales on hungry low-ticket offers where reps upsell the next thing.
- For compliance he cites the FTC suit over Element's hydration claim and says to know what others have been penalized for.

chunks.heading: Investing, partnerships and competitive advantage
chunks.text:
- Core filter for any opportunity: what are our competitive advantages? He turned down a Qatari hospitality family because he has no edge in hospitality.
- Build outward from the core. Amazon began with shipping, then built AWS. He prefers an ecosystem around what works over starting from scratch in a new field because of ego.
- His stance on opportunities: he never says no, he says "not right now."
- Keep the main thing until a strong operator runs it. He credits his COO Max as the backbone of the business.
- Ask founders in other industries about the worst parts of their work. Everyone hates around 80% of what they do. He passed on starting a fund because managing other people's money and 100K investors "on my case" sounded like a nightmare.
- He prefers owning 5% to 25% of great businesses that will succeed with or without him, and does not want sweat equity.
- Investing vs partnership: investing is a cheque and a lost cheque is survivable. Partnerships need slower, deeper due diligence because you are tying your brand to theirs (he gives the example of a CEO scandal). The WAP deal took about a year and a half and talks with every company in the industry. He calls it the largest part of his net worth.
- Trust and personal chemistry matter in partnerships. He is skeptical of giving equity to affiliates; instead consider letting them buy in on favorable terms and giving titles like advisor or investor, since people want to feel special.
- Advice to someone weighing an equity offer: both sides depend on each other, and conditions exist for a reason. Ask what drives the counterparty.
- His team gets phantom equity in the businesses he invests in, which has made several of them millionaires.
- Hiring: no side hustles, stated on day one. He "anti-sells" the job, asking whether working for someone is really a step forward, to find the real driver. Everyone on his core team has a team-sport background.
- He wants clarity on what you want: "biggest creator" and "monetize the most" are different goals. Know your lifestyle burn, and when your investment portfolio covers it "all the bull's gone."
- For a creator in an off cycle, he suggests using the quieter season to build skills, hire and train. He says growth is uneven: one year of 2x to 5x, then a few of 10% to 20% while foundations are built.
- Build the brand for longevity, not short-term cash. His brand stays ambiguous on purpose, and he avoids over-committing to AI even though they use it, because audiences tire of any narrative.

chunks.heading: Content mechanics and brand longevity
chunks.text:
- Time on content is about 8 to 10 hours a month. Scripts are written by his team from his concepts, he gives feedback in a weekly writers' room (30 minutes to an hour), and an internal tool called "Scripty Man" holds everything he has said over 11 years.
- Casual videos use bullet points he riffs on. He says a restaurant does not need a new menu daily: audiences graduate and get replaced, so repetition with variation is fine.
- YouTube channels are split by awareness level: a main mass-market channel, a business channel, a beginner channel and a vlog. People usually graduate off the main channel after 6 to 12 months.
- Every personal brand hits face fatigue and a "handbrake phase" where views trend down. He says talking-head formats suffer most because viewers learn everything about you.
- Vlogs and multi-character content last longer because they show a team and friend group. He thinks creators should film their office culture.
- Formats degrade: his own editing style worked for 1.5 to 2 years then got stale. He says the message matters less than packaging and format, and the next move is more dynamic production.
- He runs three full-time thumbnail people, a department running for four years.
- On AI: he does not think AI personalities replace personal brands, since fans want a real person they might meet or hear rumors about. He says his team uses AI in many ads and it performs well.
- Information at the top end (10K per hour consulting for specialized insight) stays valuable. At lower and mid levels, sell transformation, not information. He has bet most of his net worth on this industry.
- Ecom, he says, works like info: spend most time on ads and marketing, find a problem, agitate it, present the product as the solution. He believes an event audience could sell a $50M physical product.
- Distribution is the most valuable asset now. Even a 30,000-subscriber channel can get millions a year from companies wanting access, so tell large companies what you have.

chunks.heading: Operating philosophy and pace
chunks.text:
- Passion is overrated: "find something you're passionate about and you'll never work another day" is a "cancerous idea." Everyone hates around 80% of their work and tolerates it for the 20% they love.
- Intentionality over scale. Everything the team does is calculated even if it is not talked about.
- Focus on profit, not revenue: for an info business, "revenue is futile, just a vanity metric." Ego aside, they play dumb about their numbers when it suits the goals.
- He says the 100K-per-1M-a-month example he saw at a mastermind persuaded him revenue is not the point.
- Team size: about 75 full-time with eight-figure annual payroll. Roles named: Luis (CMO of consultant.com, started as an intern at his agency six years ago), Max (COO, German, "babysitter" for the company), Alex (head of creative).
- Core principle on pace: they treat content as a real business since 2022 (grew from about 1.5M to 4M subscribers the next year), mostly work to the same plan, and took pride in the fact that no one competes at their level of owned media.
- Founder risk: "You are always the biggest risk to the business." Burnout kills companies, so he trains, detoxes and parties hard alongside work.
- On hate videos: part of the game. His test is whether people he respects call him about it. After the 2024 wave none did, and most critics later removed their videos.
- A rule he applies when listening to others' playbooks: only apply what fits your own business objectives.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Iman argues info is a roughly 3/10 difficulty business where margins, organic traffic and a personal brand beat revenue bragging and paid ads. He explains why low-ticket recurring info fails on LTV math, how to treat YouTube like an ad platform, and why your business should follow your life design.

chunks.heading: Why Iman says profit and ownership beat revenue in info
chunks.text:
- Iman calls the info space's focus on revenue "the most Preposterous ridiculous thing". He says he saw this in a Mastermind about seven years ago (2018) and left it for good, calling it a "weird cult" of people comparing revenue numbers.
- Revenue matters for software or e-commerce, where it feeds company value. In info it does not, because the founder is the service and the mechanism for getting customers, so the company is not sellable.
- His first question to any info founder is "what's your profit?" He cites the top person in the space doing $36M revenue and $1M profit.
- He would rather make $2M profit on $3M revenue than $3M on more complexity. He prefers $15M revenue with $3M profit to bloated, high-ego numbers.
- Revenue figures are often not cash collected. He gives his own example of an $800K month with about $490K collected.
- He says info is "the best business on Earth" for printing roughly $5M a year, and e-commerce friends are jealous of its margins. The mistake is applying billion-dollar-company ideas, such as "build a sellable asset", to info.
- He says he and one other person from that Mastermind each cashed out roughly $50-100M. He claims "over 100 million" total in info, with 95M+ mostly from YouTube, and says only about $2.5-3M went to Facebook ads, nearly all retargeting.

chunks.heading: Paid traffic vs organic customers
chunks.text:
- Paid-traffic customers have higher refund and dispute rates and are less forgiving. Organic customers who know, like and trust him are patient.
- Example: his custom platform has had outages of 1-2 hours over four to five years. With paid traffic that triggers "scam" alarm bells. With organic customers it does not.
- Ad spend is rented: "they were renters and eventually their landlord kicked them out". A Facebook spend of $10M/year leaves nothing behind once it stops.
- He is not against ads. His rule: "if something's working you don't touch it" (profit, not revenue), but build organic in parallel.
- For events he spends about $300-400K on retargeting. Leads cost about $2 on average, and he gets 350-500K leads per event. Leads are scored from a Typeform into A/B/C/D tiers, and D leads will not buy. He says cost per qualified A-tier lead is about $1.
- He treats his short-form accounts (300M views a month) as retargeting data for events, not as a sales channel.

chunks.heading: Why recurring low-ticket info is a trap
chunks.text:
- He launched a $37/month mobile app offer and says "don't recommend it", calling it "the stupidest model". He claims nearly eight figures of profit from low-ticket recurring, with the offer a year old and close to eight figures.
- Info and continuity clash: impact is highest in the first month, "imagine you bought a book today and in 4 months they're still charging you for it". Continuity works for software, meal delivery or supplies.
- Reason from LTV, not MRR. His $37 product has about 6 months average retention and $222 LTV, and he ships a new masterclass every month (one this month with a boxing expert with a 2M-subscriber channel, filmed on RED cameras).
- Worked example of the $100/month fantasy:
  - 1,000 members at $100/month looks like $1.2M a year.
  - At 4 months average retention, LTV is $400, so 1,000 customers is about $400K.
  - Getting 1,000 buyers at a 1% sales-page conversion needs about 100,000 clicks, which would cost far more than $400K in ads.
- He says he told a $1.4B-a-year education owner his e-learning acquisition's numbers before being told them: about 4-month retention, under 10% on the yearly plan, and not profitable.
- Dan's side agrees (a $97/month site that stopped being worth it), but Iman's point is that the same effort goes further at higher price points.
- He prefers B2B software, where products embed in a business and are hard to leave, such as inventory management for e-commerce firms with 30-100+ SKUs and $5M+ revenue, packages from €200 to $10K/month. He finds B2C software churn brutal.

chunks.heading: Reinvesting, time-for-money, and non-negotiables
chunks.text:
- On "I need to reinvest in the business": info has no real startup cost and ad returns show within 30 days. Inventory-based businesses actually reinvest, and he has wired over $1M for stock. For info he asks "what are you reinvesting in?"
- Info is "a three out of 10 difficulty business". His path was to reach $10M liquid, then choose between retiring or placing bigger bets. He took the bets into software, physical products and investing in software companies.
- On "never sell your time": Taylor Swift and F1 drivers sell their time and earn hundreds of millions. Time is fine to sell if it is valuable enough, and customers often buy the founder, so removing yourself kills the appeal.
- Example: someone at $100K/month wanted to 2.5x with a $15K offer while fully removed. Iman's answer was to give the buyers about 2.5 hours a week of one-on-one.
- Everyone gets non-negotiables. His is no sales team. He would accept a bit less money for that.
- Life design first: ask "what do you want in life?" and "what monthly passive amount would make you chill?" His own target is about $500K/month with a team he can count on two hands and 25 days a month free.
- A lifestyle version he describes: a micro-niche YouTube channel, a course, a community and some one-on-one, 15-20 hours a week, about $60-100K/month.
- He buys the domains of failed info companies that once did $25-30M a year, "just to prove a point".

chunks.heading: YouTube and content strategy
chunks.text:
- YouTube is for people who want to learn, short form is for consumers in "entertainment and consumerism" mode. He says short form is not worth it for info or services, and suits physical products.
- His short-form results: 300M views a month across his own accounts. He once had 65 full-time staff posting about 15,000 pieces a month and 150 accounts. He now has about 10 people and 70 accounts, with 3x the views. He personally spends roughly 90 minutes to 2 hours a month on it.
- A $37/month offer (Digital Launchpad) sold to the short-form audience made about $30K in month one before he took it off, because "they're non buyers" (wrong countries and mindset).
- Content team: $20K/month on a team keeps paying off, unlike ads. Editors cost about $1,000/month each, and $5K/month is enough to start. He wants the team's scripting involved for customer-facing roles but does not outsource his own ideas.
- A new YouTube channel can work in 30-90 days. He suggests sending your existing list or friends to it for retention data.
- Don't chase virality: "there's a big difference between a viewer and a lead".
- His approach is to treat YouTube like an ad platform: the thumbnail is the creative, the title is the hook, and the video concept is the targeting. Example of bad targeting: a "day in the life of a Dubai millionaire" video brings in anyone who likes Dubai, not buyers of your $20K B2B offer. A day in the life of a $5-10M infopreneur is better.
- He expanded audience in steps. He started with SMMA/agency content, took it to the top, then went to online business and later general self-help. His business content is on a separate channel (about 10K subscribers) that he never promotes, and he opens with "if you're making less than $250,000 a year, just click away".
- Production quality: high-ticket and educated audiences are put off by heavy production, so he keeps advanced content less produced. Mass-market audiences like animation.

chunks.heading: Emotional vs logical selling, and selling on YouTube
chunks.text:
- A savvy, upper-end B2B audience wants about 90% logical, value-based content. Amp up emotion only in the conversion phase (a VSL or live event). A wider mass audience needs more emotion and less tactics.
- Consumer products: eyewear buyers do not want a motivational speech. He told his team to cut a monologue from a shoot as "patronizing".
- Men buy aspirational lifestyle products, with "show, don't tell". He says his female creative director and COO want relatable content, and he pushes back for male buyers.
- Where to send viewers:
  - Cheap products can be sold directly in content. He mentions a new eyewear collection in a vlog doing $150K that day.
  - Hot, tactical videos that make viewers want the system go straight to a call. His VSL of nearly 10M views made about $20M.
  - Conceptual videos (such as hiring A players) send people to Instagram to nurture.
- He sells his higher-end offer only after screening: nothing under $250K/year revenue, no crypto/trading or OnlyFans businesses, and no businesses he doesn't think he can help. Sales go through a call, and he sends people to a 3-day event.

chunks.heading: Personal brand as the real asset, plus physical products
chunks.text:
- He claims his brand has brought him advisory shares worth over $10M, discounted equity in every company he invests in, his pick of talent worldwide, and access to hard-to-get products. He says "take away everything I have, leave me my personal brand, I'll make 100 million back within 3 years."
- You don't need to be famous. A small but strong brand in your niche is "the tip of a spear". Everyone already has a personal brand, and for most it works against them.
- Brand costs: his entire content team is about $250K a year, versus the multi-million-dollar ad budgets of rivals who ended up with nothing.
- Eyewear business (iWare/Eazi, with a partner who sold a billion dollars of eyewear, and 100 stores via Hawkers):
  - He started about four years ago; the first order was around $30K.
  - He says it has made close to $8M, all organic, with 80-95% gross margins. His partner bought 40% of the company 8 months before the interview.
  - Eyewear is a utility product with timeless shapes, so it needs no brand story (unlike clothing).
- E-commerce caveats: even at $30M revenue and 20% EBITDA ($6M), about $3M is held back for stock. Customs delays have held his products for 3-4 months during covid.
- He says he spent between $100K and $1M a month on lifestyle and felt no difference above $100-250K a month. He bought a Phantom for the seats, and for cars like the Maybach he suggests a 2-3K-mile high-trim S-Class and letting someone else take the depreciation.
- Take operators seriously: he has a technical co-founder or partner in every non-info business, and hired a new COO from Munich for Madrid.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Iman Gadzhi explains how he stacked self-education, health, social skills and wealth in order, runs 6 months of monk mode followed by months of play, and why he teaches agencies as the lowest-risk path to 10k a month. He also covers hiring and profit share, trauma, and why money alone doesn't fix insecurity.

chunks.heading: Early foundation and reading habit
chunks.text:
- Iman started building himself first: from 14 he read roughly a book a week (2014 to late 2016), buying used books at Brixton Bookmongers in London instead of 12-13 pound new copies at Waterstones, so three to five books cost what one new book did.
- Early reading: Rich Dad Poor Dad, Think and Grow Rich, The Way of the Superior Man, The Kybalion, The Five Love Languages. He read The Fountainhead (about 1,100 pages) at 15 and decided "if I can read this I can read anything."
- At 14-15 his plan was to become a real estate agent (inspired by Million Dollar Listing) and move into property. He had decided he would never go to university.
- He dropped out of private school making roughly $8-10k. He was already doing client work in class: reaching out to prospects and sending proposals, "all the things that actually don't work," as a beginner does.
- He grew up on government benefits with his mother, in private school, with the most financially challenged background among his peers. He says that drove him.

chunks.heading: Money, children and inheritance
chunks.text:
- He plans to leave his children nothing and to give wealth to causes such as schools in Nepal. His reason: he never wants them to get pride from something they have not earned.
- He would hand down something meaningful (for example a watch) only once they have "made it on their own," around 30.
- He argues money complicates life: "it's way worse to cry in a Lambo," because with no next checkmark left, the unhappiness is yours alone to face.
- He says he has felt unhappy for stretches of a couple of months even with every checkmark ticked.
- He expects to treat sons and daughters differently (he frames it as masculine vs feminine energy). A son gets no income support. A daughter pursuing a lower-paying craft with deep respect and full effort might get her income supplemented.
- He credits his Russian mother's "non-bullshit" outlook as one of his biggest superpowers.

chunks.heading: Disagreement with the "grind in your 20s" advice
chunks.text:
- He disagrees with Gary Vaynerchuk's "eat [expletive] in your 20s" line unless you are compensated for it.
- His view: the best time to build is roughly 18 to 26. But collecting experiences matters as much as collecting money, and he would not want a life with no 20s or 30s.
- Once you reach a certain stage, "hard work is about as low down as it gets on the importance factor" for moving the needle. He says mainstream business content gives good sound bites but not stage-specific, practical nuance.
- Numbers he cites: at 17 he made $30-40k a month; at 18 he was flown business class to New York for a client training and paid $20,000 for two days; that month was his first with $200,000 profit; he later made $10M in 2021.
- He says his liquid net worth could, via low-risk yield farming, return about $1.9M a year net after tax.

chunks.heading: Stacking skills in the right order
chunks.text:
- His core principle: stack skills so each remains valuable even if a specific business disappears. He asks of any skill: "if that business goes away, will it still give me dividends for decades?"
- His order of stacking: self-education and meditation first, then body (gym, nutrition), then social skills (he was going out with 21-22 year olds at 16), then wealth.
- He thinks order matters. People who stack wealth first often "go crazy" chasing women and then find their health and social skills are not in order.
- His pattern: throw himself into something in an unbalanced immersion, then back out and integrate it sustainably. Example: meditating an hour a day at 14-15, now 15 minutes in the morning and 30 before bed.
- He also names "private victories" (from The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People) as the work that sits behind visible "public victories" like expensive watches. He has it tattooed as a reminder that public wins require many times more private ones.

chunks.heading: Monk mode and seasonal work cycle
chunks.text:
- He claims 70% of success is: stop drinking, stop smoking weed (he rejects "it makes me creative"), and get nine hours of sleep. Tactics matter less than whether someone digests and implements the information.
- His year: about six months of monk mode (no alcohol, no caffeine, no sugar, 30 minutes of meditation a day), roughly three to four months of looser living, and a transition period. He says he is the hardest-working on his team for the first six months and the least hard-working for about three months.
- He notes this only works because he now has a strong team. He could not do it in 2017.
- His self-awareness point: know your own rhythm rather than fighting it. In his case he cares only about work early in the year and only about wine, travel and experiences by June to August.
- He also says place matters: he makes his most progress in Cape Town (stripped back, "love of the craft") rather than London or Dubai, where visible wealth such as 20-30 million dollar yachts keeps the "not enough" feeling alive. He would not raise children in a big city.

chunks.heading: What he builds into his education programs
chunks.text:
- His education company teaches agencies, because a service business is the best route from zero to $10k a month: you can fail for four months with no costs. By contrast, his e-commerce blue light blocker brand has had $150,000 production batches that took about nine months to turn into revenue.
- He says he could make more money teaching e-commerce but sticks to agencies because that is how he reached $20-30k a month at 17.
- Two tiers: a program for getting to $10k a month, and one for scaling agencies from about $10k to $100k a month.
- He deliberately "sneaks in" life content: the $10k program has four to five hours on mindset, meditation, detox, removing distraction and EMFs, and his monk mode protocol. The $100k program includes detox coaching, psychedelics, Epsom salt baths, steam sauna, liver cleanses and sleep biohacking.
- He has spent hundreds of thousands on biohacking gear (a Bemer, hyperbaric chambers, red light therapy) and concluded "less is more." He worked with a detox coach, Josh Mason, found via a YouTube presentation.

chunks.heading: Hiring, delegation and the semi-retirement plan
chunks.text:
- Once past a certain stage, he says the most important thing is hiring and maintaining company culture, so that for every task someone on the team can do it better than him and he is "just there to steer the ship."
- His team gets profit share once they have been in the company long enough, so they are as incentivized to grow it as he is.
- Stated goal (announced as a first public statement): reach $20M net after tax by the end of 2022, roughly double what he had then. After that, semi-retire for 10-15 years, working a maximum of 20 hours a week.
- His reasoning: $20M can yield about $2-3M a year in cash flow if invested well. He is not shutting businesses down. He plans to keep scaling them while using the other hours for skiing, tango in Buenos Aires, cooking and climbing Everest.
- He expects to marry and have kids around his late 30s to 40, and to stay in business until his deathbed because he loves building.

chunks.heading: Mental health and closing advice
chunks.text:
- In summer 2020, after a very peaceful six months in Cape Town, he had six to eight weeks of daily panic attacks, crying multiple times a day, and suicidal thoughts. The symptoms often lifted around 5 to 6 pm. He calls it a "dark night of the soul." He leaned on friends he describes as spiritual rather than wealthy.
- His advice: do the inner work as early as possible. He says most billionaires will not examine why they still feel "not enough," and he sees the same insecurity in himself about his business. For his physique he feels nothing to prove, for his business he still does.
- Practical tip: meditate, and take walks without your phone to be alone with your thoughts.
- He says he plans to eventually help with men's social and dating life and then trauma and spiritual work, before going offline.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: In a community Q&A with Eddie Maalouf, Iman frames the agency as the best vehicle for roughly $1M a year in profit and a launchpad into bigger ventures. He argues beginners should sell to service-uneducated clients, avoid info-product and growth-operator models early, and build a personal brand aimed at the right buyers.

chunks.heading: Why Iman thinks an agency is the best launchpad
chunks.text:
Iman (in conversation with Eddie Maalouf, who runs a 20 million plus a year agency) agrees that an agency is the best way to get to roughly 50-100K a month with no cash or capital.

- He says that if he started an agency today with no money, he would be at 100K a month "by the end of April guaranteed", because he knows how to get clients and service them.
- Past a few million a year in profit, he argues it gets harder: you have to hire hundreds of people, the team stops being "10 of us in a room", and it becomes an HR and sales-team headache.
- He frames an agency as a skill-building Launchpad. You learn sales, copy, ads and cash flow, then use that to go start or buy other businesses.
- He calls the 50K-a-month floor a safety net. Because no one can take the skill from you, he can take bigger swings.
- He says agency income tends to compound with age. Repeat clients and referrals build, and people prefer an agency that has been around seven years over one that has been around one. He contrasts this with e-commerce, where a brand can go stale.

chunks.heading: Agency exit multiples and the "agency as engine" model
chunks.text:
Iman describes the exit math and how he uses his agency to fund acquisitions.

- **Multiples on profit:** a small agency sells for roughly 1-2x yearly profit, so 100K profit gets about 200K cash. Bigger agencies reach about 7-10x.
- **Offer received:** they were already offered 6x on profit but declined to grow further. His example: 7 million profit at 6x is 42 million cash.
- **Exit target:** about 150 million, probably in the next 3-5 years. He would stay a couple of years because the agency is the engine for his other companies.
- **Acquisition play:** he buys companies with good products but weak marketing and uses the agency to scale them. He bought a 7-location restaurant franchise and says he tripled sales across all seven in 90 days.
- **Investments:** he put 1.2 million cash into a 10% stake in a company, aiming for a 100 million exit, which would make his stake worth at least about 10 million.
- **Cash flow:** the agency brings solid cash about 10 months a year, enough to reinvest and buy three or four companies a year.
- **Stress:** at 200 employees, "there's problems every day". He says that at 50K a month he would live the easiest life, so selling means getting "five to 10 years worth of my money all in one day".

chunks.heading: Team structure and getting out of client communication
chunks.text:
Iman describes how communication and structure evolved as the agency grew.

- **Progression:** WhatsApp group chats at the start, then Slack (easier to bookmark, no personal numbers shared). He ran early tasks from a handwritten notebook until about 60-70K a month, then moved to a CRM and project management tools.
- **Advice on infrastructure:** when small, keep it quick and intimate. Adding rules and software too early puts everyone "in a box".
- **Hire the opposite of yourself:** if you are good at sales, hire fulfillment; if you are good at fulfillment, hire sales. Hiring another salesperson just takes your best player off the court.
- **Early on, do both:** his first employee was a VA at 1,000 a month, which was hard to afford.
- **Current setup:** 8-10 direct reports (heads of email marketing, Facebook ads, Google, HR, marketing). He admits he is over-involved and talks to 30-40 people regularly.
- **The first hire to be free:** someone whose job is to talk to clients. Otherwise "you're just an employee for like 30 other businesses". At 50 clients he was talking to only one of them.

chunks.heading: Choosing a niche: follow who responds, then check size and access
chunks.text:
Iman says to pick the niche from where clients actually come in, not from research alone.

- **Start broad:** they cold emailed small businesses and saw who replied. Early niches were kids' birthday parties, chiropractors and car shops. If 100 of 10,000 emails respond and most are chiropractors, learn chiropractors.
- **Why:** he says people go deep on a niche they then cannot close, because there are too few of them or they are unreachable.
- **Birthday party venues:** closed Monday to Friday, so owners answered cold emails within minutes and got on calls. He says he rarely shares this niche because it was so good.
- **Three tests:** how big is the market, how accessible are the buyers, and do you like the work. The first two matter more.
- **Too small example:** custom car wrap shops, about 50 per state, only around 2,000 reachable, and it got hard once competitors arrived.
- **Good examples:** chiropractors and nail salons (answer the phone every time, roughly one on every corner). He says nail salons can easily reach 100K a month.
- **Expansion:** the agency now has three divisions under one roof, local, coaching and info products, and e-commerce. He recommends starting with local.

chunks.heading: Getting clients: run ads for yourself and never rely on one source
chunks.text:
- Iman says his biggest early obstacle was getting clients, and about 80% of his time went to it.
- He used cold email, Instagram DMs, cold calls and even driving a Google Maps route to walk into 14 dentists a day. One client in a day was a win, and 20 days a month meant roughly 20 clients.
- **Hedge channels:** emails may take six months to work, so do not sit idle; use several sources at once.
- **Ads turned it around:** he says it is like a basketball coach who does not play. Once he ran ads for his own agency in 2020, it took off. At the start of 2020 he had about 15 clients; in July 2020 they signed 15 clients in one day from ad-booked demos.
- **Personal brand:** "your content is really your resume". He says that in the last 18 months a personal brand became necessary for agencies.
- **Quality over reach:** he needs about "10,000 of the right people", not a million views. Build content aimed at your niche (for example, dentist marketing) and avoid surface-level content that gets likes from the wrong people.
- **Example:** a "day in the life" video does nothing for clients who want to know what works for them.

chunks.heading: Content operations behind the personal brand
chunks.text:
- He has six video and photo people plus 12 editors, serving about four YouTube channels, six Instagrams and client work.
- **Weekly rhythm:** a Monday afternoon meeting covers a 10-day content schedule across all pages. His team posts everything; he only responds to comments and DMs.
- **Approval:** the team sends a sheet with each post, thumbnail and caption, and he has final say.
- **Planning ahead:** big days need about a month. Their April Fools stunt, renaming the company from "Bad Marketing" to "good marketing" with t-shirts for staff, took that long.
- **Doubling down:** film ahead and copy what is already working for them or others.
- He suggests learning the camera basics yourself (ISO, aperture), which "you can just learn in like one day".

chunks.heading: Which agency models to avoid as a beginner, and why
chunks.text:
- **Info-product growth agencies and "growth operator" deals** (split profits with a creator): he does run an info agency, but only after 10 years, and he hires people with multiple six-figure salaries.
- **Reasons against:** you depend on the creator, organic reach runs out, then you must spend money against top marketers. The creator can also decide you are useless.
- **Rule of thumb:** wait until you have run an agency for "at least two years" before those models.
- **Service-educated vs uneducated clients:** compare knowledge out of 10. Local businesses are about 1-3, e-commerce owners about 5-7, info creators about 8-10. Target clients who know less than you about your service.
- **E-commerce warning:** a client who can afford you and knows little about their main growth driver is an alarm bell.
- **Hiring evidence:** a media buyer posting drew 2,600 applications, trimmed to 700 and then about 150, with very high quality.
- **Progression:** their agency went local first, then e-commerce, then info. He says some things can go from 5 years to 2, but not to 2 months.
- **Beyond ads:** other agency types are automations (Zapier or Make, learnable in 60-90 days), Excel, and Discord setup and security. He says his automation employees earn hundreds of thousands a year.

chunks.heading: Skills, imposter syndrome and staying organized
chunks.text:
- **Learn the full process:** he tells a student to learn copy, sales and ads together, then expand. He says a single call at 10-15K from an agency owner's experience pays far more than being only a copywriter.
- **Imposter syndrome:** you may be a 6 in Facebook ads and Zapier while the client is a 0, so you already add value.
- **Niche terminology trick:** learn key terms (for dentists: "patient", root canal, teeth whitening, Invisalign) and clients feel you know their world. He would watch a 10-minute video on the car ride in. He calls imposter syndrome "just in your head".
- **Organization:** avoid analysis paralysis. Write down the top five things each day, which adds up to 25 important tasks a week. At scale, his calendar is color-coded with every minute planned, including family dinners.
- **Tools:** he recommends GoHighLevel for running client accounts, including Google review work.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Iman walks through a five-step playbook: build an intentional personal brand, keep it micro-niche, run a content strategy, monetize with information (coaching first), then scale into group coaching and digital products. He argues audience quality beats size and that a personal brand lets bootstrapped founders attract customers instead of chasing them.

chunks.heading: Intentional personal brand: the purpose is attracting customers, not fame
chunks.text:
- Iman defines a personal brand as creating content to reach a target audience and convert it into customers. He says there is no right or wrong size: 5,000 followers or millions can both work, depending on the outcome you want.
- He says fame for its own sake is not aspirational to him. For most people the point is "being able to attract rather than chase."
- His own timeline:
  - His first YouTube upload was on Boxing Day 2015.
  - From 2016 to 2018 he only documented his agency work. He did not think of himself as a business owner until he hired his first employee in 2017, at age 17, who quit after three days.
  - He later niched down to sharing what worked in his agency.
  - In 2019 he launched his first digital product.
- He became intentional at the end of 2021. He was about to delete his social accounts while launching the software company Floy. His co-founder Pier refused, saying they would not raise tens of millions to acquire customers because Iman would acquire them. Iman says that was the first time he deliberately connected his social media to his businesses.
- He had no expectations in the early years. He started sharing his journey in 2014/2015, when being an entrepreneur was not "cool," because he had no friends at school and some online friends.

chunks.heading: Why a personal brand is the leverage to build now
chunks.text:
- Iman calls it "jet fuel" and a competitive advantage that sits above any business model. He says you should keep the job or business you have, and the brand makes it easier to attract clients, earn more and get noticed. Even an employee who brings in business becomes more valuable to a boss.
- He uses Naval Ravikant's capital, code and content framework:
  - Older billionaires made their money through capital.
  - The next wave made it through code (Musk, Zuckerberg, Sergey Brin).
  - The next generation will use content.
- Capital and code are not accessible to everyone. Content is "the first form of leverage ever that is accessible to anyone."
- For bootstrappers it is "the great equalizer," because it replaces VC-funded customer acquisition. It gives:
  - negative cost of acquisition;
  - discounted equity on acquisitions (he says he bought three software companies in about four weeks, with discounted equity);
  - easier hiring (more than 100,000 applications across his companies);
  - easier access to partners and DMs.
- He says his personal brand is worth more than all his investments combined, because he could rebuild everything else from it.
- He puts his career earnings at over $100 million, mostly in the last five years, not counting company valuations.
- A £1M physical product brand he launched on the back of his audience is profitable but "not a home run." He says the brand gives confidence that he will not lose money on a venture.
- His eyewear company makes a couple of million a year in profit. Eyewear has 80-90% gross margins, which lets him spend on paid acquisition beyond his own audience.
- Everyone already has a personal brand, because employers and clubs look you up. The choice is whether it helps or hurts you, so make it work for you even at 5,000-10,000 followers.
- Billionaires act on this. Ray Dalio's channel has 61 million views against Iman's roughly 10 million. Zuckerberg's image change and Elon Musk's purchase of Twitter are, in Iman's view, bids for influence. Iman says that once someone has money, they want influence.

chunks.heading: Micro personal brands: audience quality beats audience size
chunks.text:
- Iman argues for a micro, niche brand: higher engagement, easier monetization, a more loyal following. He says you are "one of one" and do not need to claim expertise.
- Revenue per follower (RPF) is total revenue divided by total followers. For example, 1,000 followers generating $10,000 is $10 per follower. He says more followers who are not your people is bad.
- Examples he gives:
  - Odd Muse: a UK clothing brand whose founder started creating content 2-3 years ago. With about 172,000 followers, mainly from TikTok, it reached $20M a year.
  - George Heeden's Represent: $100M+ a year. Iman says it was struggling about five years ago until founder-led content in lockdown rebuilt it.
  - A friend who went from agency to a bootstrapped software company, worth hundreds of millions per Iman. He could not spend $600 to acquire a customer, so he built a niche LinkedIn brand instead.
  - Alexandra, a Fiverr freelancer who documented buying farmland.
  - Nick, an AI entrepreneur with 11,000 subscribers, whom Iman guesses makes $500K+ a year.
  - Alexi, a 13-year-old making about $50K a month with 2,000 subscribers.
- Iman runs his own micro channel for business owners making over $250K a year. He tells smaller owners not to watch because the advice would confuse them. He deliberately does not want it to pop off. Its offer, "Eight Figure License," packages about 50 backend systems, such as a short-form department that gets about 300 million views a month on owned accounts. He excludes forex/trading and adult businesses, anyone under $250K, and anyone he does not think he can help.
- For 2022-2024 he deliberately "dumbed down" his main channel to corner the 18-25 market. He now splits audiences across a main channel, vlogs and the business channel. He does not recommend multiple channels to most people.

chunks.heading: Content strategy: authenticity, documentation and storytelling
chunks.text:
- He calls being real the "unfair advantage." He recorded his whole journey, including losing 40-50% of his agency retainers after taking his eye off the ball, and unsuccessful proposals.
- Ways to provide value:
  - document;
  - open people's eyes with a new perspective;
  - educate.
- You do not need to be an expert, only one step ahead. A level-1 person relates to a level-3, not a level-10, so being too far ahead is unrelatable.
- He cites the 7-11 rule: about 7 hours of content across 11 touchpoints. He thinks the four-platforms part does not apply to personality brands. Optimize for watch time, not views, because trust is built over time.
- His "magnetic persona" has these parts:
  - Show flaws, as a hero needs them. In 2021 he shared his experience of panic attacks and depression while still living through it.
  - State your values. During 2020 he made his own masks, then gave away the stock (about $10K cost) rather than sell it, because selling did not match his values.
  - Develop a signature style, such as film photography or red and blue lights in videos.
  - Tell stories rather than listing facts. His line: "You admire a character for trying more than their successes."
- His advice on mistakes:
  - Stop trying to please everyone.
  - Stop chasing views.
  - Do not try to be "the next Iman Gadzhi."
  - Stop waiting for the perfect time.
- He had one breakthrough video after four years. His action step is to record a 5-10 minute video daily for 7 days and not post it, just to get reps.

chunks.heading: Ideation, packaging and retention tactics
chunks.text:
- Pick the platform by where your audience is and which format feels natural to you. His team repurposes TikToks to LinkedIn with a different intro written for the business audience.
- Mix broad, superficial content (reach) with in-depth content (it shows expertise and makes money). Categories he lists are actionable, narrative, theoretical and "attractor" (sharing results). Beginners should lean toward actionable and theoretical.
- Ideation:
  - Do not copy only within your niche. Look at other niches and old 1950s-60s newspaper ads for headlines.
  - Use hobbies to make the brand magnetic.
  - Use the free tool VidIQ to find outlier videos (his example is a video at 8.9x a channel's average), then study the creative and headline.
- Search traffic: "mine field farming" targets what people already search for. His example is Miles Beckler, who averages 5-10K views and makes millions a year. Also use problem farming (a problem-oriented title versus a solution-oriented one), and brand leveraging (commenting on current events, such as More Plates More Dates at $100M a year).
- Ultimate guides capture existing demand, such as a 3D printing beginner's guide.
- Structure: a big idea, three main points, three sub-points and a clear takeaway.
- Growth topics: double down on your longest-watch-time topics. His have been millionaire habits, beginner-friendly businesses and monk mode. Audiences have not seen everything, so repeat and reframe.
- Packaging: he employs three full-time people on thumbnails and has for three years. A Veritasium title and thumbnail change got about 9 million more views.
- Retention: about 80% of the drop-off happens in the first 30 seconds. Hooks come in three types:
  - a bold claim;
  - curiosity or an open loop, which his team sometimes opens in one video and closes in the next;
  - a value promise.
- Speak to one person, answer comments and run polls and lives.

chunks.heading: Monetization: start with coaching, sell information
chunks.text:
- Keep your business if it works. If you want a clean slate, or your career is capped (like a one-to-one personal trainer), Iman says the one way to monetize in 2025 is information.
- He argues everyone already pays for information: lawyers, tutors, driving and tennis instructors, McKinsey. It is packaged as a book, course or coaching.
- Big names made much of their money from information:
  - Russell Brunson (a potato gun DVD course);
  - Alex Hormozi's Gym Launch (about $100M, charging $30-42K a year), by Iman's conservative estimate;
  - Alex Becker (about $75M).
