- He says you pick a "unique value zone," not a niche. His example: helping successful online entrepreneurs reduce screen time, not generic productivity.
- You synthesize what is already out there. AI makes researching a market's problems easier.
- He pays for information himself. He paid $250,000 for 10 calls with one person, and says it was worth it.
- Why coaching first:
  - It charges $3,000-$20,000 per client and needs three to five clients a month.
  - It works with an audience of a few hundred to a few thousand.
  - It needs no upfront production.
- A sample calculation:
  - $2,500 for five calls is $500 a call.
  - Ten calls a week is $5,000 a week, or about $20,000 a month.
- Courses charge $100-$1,000, need thousands of customers and an audience in the tens of thousands or more, and are hard to sell. He says courses are commoditized and "people want you."
- His own Digital Launchpad app costs $37 a month and offers a money-back guarantee.
- Coaching also validates the offer and shows what your market needs.
- Group coaching is harder to sell than one-to-one. Courses are at the bottom.
- On selling time, he disagrees with "never sell time." Taylor Swift sold nine months of her time. He says it is fine if you are paid adequately and it gives leverage. Beginners should not start with e-commerce, because ads, stock and debt can wipe out savings.

chunks.heading: Automate and scale
chunks.text:
- When coaching hits capacity:
  - Move to group coaching or a hybrid. For example, 3-4 hours of recorded training, then a final live hour for nuance.
  - Then turn it into a digital product.
- Trade-offs: you reach more people and get automated sales, but you lose personal connection and find premium rates harder.
- He sees one-to-one coaching as the MVP, because it shows where students get stuck, which you cannot predict.
- His five-step summary:
  1. Build an intentional personal brand.
  2. Create a micro personal brand.
  3. Implement a content strategy.
  4. Monetize.
  5. Automate and scale.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Iman explains how he picks investments and businesses only where he has a real edge, why he builds ecosystems and transformation around information, and how he positions his brand by audience stage. He judges everything by revenue, not views, and staffs worst-case thinkers alongside creatives.

chunks.heading: Where Iman's edge comes from (and how he invests)
chunks.text:
- Iman builds and invests only where he has a "competitive advantage." He puts most of his portfolio into private equity and software, where he can bring users, onboarding and product feedback.
- He treats property as "park money," because he has no edge there. He dollar-cost averages into the S&P 500 every Tuesday because he has no edge in stocks either. His line: "why would I try to engage in a sport where everyone else has a gun and I have a knife?"
- On deals, he is "super aggressive" and won't take one without "ridiculous, ridiculous terms." He negotiates discounted equity up front and structures the deals himself.
- If a private bank brings him a private equity deal, he reads that as a sign it isn't a good deal. In his words, "I'm a tiny fish compared to who you guys work with."
- He asks for better terms only where he can add real value. A shoe company wanting his money isn't a place he can add much beyond a little audience, so he doesn't push.
- One software investment returned 11x in 7 months. He is the largest shareholder after the two co-founders, and the company just closed a $40M round.
- His stated reason for choosing software: "if info businesses had value... I'd be a billionaire by now." He can't recycle info profits into info businesses, so software is the closest cousin.
- He doesn't monetize being an investor, so he feels no obligation to disclose positions. He would feel one if investing were what he taught. He rolls a portfolio product out to his own programs only when it is "the best product" and ready.

chunks.heading: Payments as the moat at WAP
chunks.text:
- At WAP (Iman is an investor, not the CEO) he says he is "optimized for" payments. He wants "the best payment infrastructure of any company out there."
- He says WAP is growing about 10% month on month in processing volume.
- Fees are a distraction. At scale, terms are custom, like a private bank quoting differently to someone moving $500M. Some WAP users process around $10M a month.
- He learned why payments matter from a European education owner doing about $1.4B a year (offline universities plus student lending). Without student lending, that owner said he'd lose "more than 99%" of the business overnight.
- Iman's takeaway: if info businesses had payment terms like traditional education, "our business will 100x overnight."
- WAP has exclusivity with most or all of the top payment providers. He is building an app store inside WAP, where a creator can pay a one-time fee (e.g. $5K) for a pre-built tool, or the builder takes a revenue share (e.g. 10% of $100/month).
- He is fine with platforms coexisting ("space for all of us") as long as payments are handled.

chunks.heading: Info products: sell transformation and ecosystems, not information
chunks.text:
- He says the value of cohesive, organized information doesn't go to zero. He compares it to a driving instructor or professor reading from a book you could buy; people pay for the experience and transformation.
- "Build ecosystems inside of info." Example: a ~$10K tool that scrapes everything on a person and generates interview questions, with a slider for rigid versus open-ended, plus tools for limiting beliefs.
- His old $1,500 agency product had six 1-on-1 coaching calls over 6 weeks, 15 group calls, and nine courses taught by outside experts. He doesn't know another info company that offered that at the price.
- He says "I can't remember last time we just sold a course." When students wanted outreach teaching, he brought in the owner of Lemlist, a multi-million-dollar software company.
- Customers are buying the experience of him, wanting his characteristics, but not to copy him. A "faceless AI personal brand" makes no sense because the mechanism of a personal brand is you.
- Choose the model by goal. A faceless channel selling $20-$100 products suits someone wanting an extra ~$1,200/month, with "absolutely no chance" of millionaire status. For someone showing their face who wants $10K/month, he would say do coaching, the easiest route.
- Delivery works as a joint brain: about 15,000 students coached 1-on-1 over the years, and the top coaches became product developers. They feed field experience into new product versions, and he approves all content.
- Ghostwriting is normal ("99%" of recent books, in his view); what matters is that the founder corrects what he doesn't believe.

chunks.heading: Brand, positioning and funnels
chunks.text:
- "The reality is you're going to piss people off no matter what you do. So, you may as well know who you're targeting."
- He follows a bell curve. Beginners think he's a genius, the moderately successful middle dislikes him, and the ultra-successful respect him. The middle "need things to sound more complicated than they are," and he won't overcomplicate. People at the top speak bluntly and use few words.
- He deliberately "dumbed down" his content because he was helping people at an earlier stage. His analogy is a running coach whose content is all about a 2:30 marathon while teaching a sub-4-hour one.
- He doesn't want to be known as an investor, so he declines suggestions to launch a fund. Public positioning should match what you sell.
- "Every hero becomes a villain," and after long enough a villain becomes a hero again, so he doesn't get emotional about hit pieces. His barometer is the revenue or main KPI of each business and the quality of his deal flow at the top.
- He says last year was his biggest growth year despite hit pieces. Views fell over two years by choice; views don't equal revenue.
- Content works as a funnel. The vlog channel feeds the eyewear business (he wanted eight figures this year and expects to miss it; next year is "definitely" eight figures), and the main channel feeds the mid-ticket offer he opens a couple of times a year (formerly a low-ticket digital launchpad).
- He expects formats to expire: "once something is named [after you], it's already not effective anymore," so be able to do any format.
- He says he'd stop making content if it had no business benefit.

chunks.heading: Team and leadership
chunks.text:
- He hires a "stresser" COO for each business, who thinks only about worst cases (what if the upload fails, the partner cuts the contract). He calls them "Max" and likes German COOs for this. Creatives are not burdened with this, to protect their flow.
- He asks his team "what am I not seeing?" and plans for the worst case.
- No one-size-fits-all leadership: know each person's stress tolerance and communication style, and adjust.
- Bite your tongue and play long-term strategy: "you don't say anything until victory."
- He is very high in stress tolerance but numb to emotions, highs included. He says the trade-off is real: stoicism removes the lows and the highs together.
- Team members get a raise every year, and he frames staying as "the biggest insurance policy." He doesn't encourage personal brands inside the company, and says those who leave with his blessing often want to come back.
- Let committed people run side quests (a team member is releasing a coffee-table book). Tell people honestly when they're better suited to being entrepreneurs.
- Spend time in other industries, ask about their headaches and their competitive advantages, and you stop envying or glorifying anyone's revenue level.
- He says many entrepreneurs "are not made to make millions a month" because they lack the stress or emotional tolerance.

chunks.heading: Tax and geography
chunks.text:
- His framework: "make your money in the US," protect it in the Middle East or Singapore (Switzerland "not so much anymore"), and spend it in Europe.
- He says his customers are mostly US-based. He spends about 75 days a year in the UK, and was planning to use non-dom status before the UK abolished it.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Iman Gadzhi walks through his path from a 95-pound-a-week social media client to a multi-company empire. He covers patience through a seven-month drought, contractor arbitrage, a 70/30 YouTube content split, and why he never sells hard. He also names the five skills he values most and admits his pricing mistake.

chunks.heading: Why Iman went from a seven-month drought to a $100K month (2016-2018)
chunks.text:
- Iman started with photo and video favors, then landed his first social media client in August 2016 at £95 per week. He quoted weekly because it "might sound cheaper" and was too scared to ask for £100.
- Seven months of work earned about £380 a month, which he says worked out to roughly 2 hours below minimum wage (30 Instagram posts, 30 Facebook posts, and managing Snapchat in person).
- Next client: Gymflow at £1,900 a month. Two or three days later he signed one at £500, then another at about £750. About 6 weeks after that he was at roughly $15-20K a month and dropped out of school at 17.
- Timeline he gives: about $5-5.5K a month, then $15K two months later. April 2018 was his first $40-50K month, and October 2018 his first $100K month.
- He says he did not quit during the drought because he never compared himself to others: "I was making 400 bucks a month, this is sick." Today's social media comparison would have made him feel shame, so he looked only at himself, stayed patient, and asked what his other option was.
- On the claim that he sells "get rich quick": "all I've done over the years is try to tell people hey it's going to be slow but what's your other option."
- When it rains it pours, in both directions. Multiple good (or bad) things tend to stack in a row.

chunks.heading: Pivoting from content to ads, and contractor arbitrage
chunks.text:
- Clients paid £2,500 a month for full social media management and content, but some also spent £1,000 a month on Red Bull ads and kept hounding him over his fee. That frustration made him learn advertising and offer ad services to existing clients as a small add-on fee.
- It backfired at first. He was bad at ads and charged little, and clients saw him as bad at everything, so he lost about 70% of his business and got dropped for both services.
- The upside: it forced him to look outward for contractors. He realized he could use "contractor arbitrage" and the global market.
- Example: he charged UK and US clients $2,500-3,500 a month, and could pay a contractor in Brazil, South Africa, Romania or Serbia about $300 per client per month. Three clients gives them $900 a month, which for a university student is life-changing.
- Honest take on his early career: part of it was luck, and he stumbled onto business models at the right time. He says it is the same with his early fitness videos: he was early to simple, to-the-point fitness content, and the same videos would not get the same traction now.

chunks.heading: How he grew YouTube: thumbnail testing, the 7030 content split, and the evergreen backlog
chunks.text:
- He took YouTube seriously from summer 2020 and went from about 400K to 3M subscribers by summer 2023. He says that growth rate was unprecedented on YouTube for self-development or fitness content.
- Thumbnails: since 2020 he has had three full-time thumbnail editors, each producing five options, so 15 options for every video, even though he uploads one video a week. He does not stage thumbnail shoots and uses whatever images exist online.
- Every day the team rehashes an old video by A/B split testing new thumbnails. He says that even if he did not upload for a year, he would still gain about 5,000 subscribers a day from the backlog (current average about 7,500 a day).
- The 7030 split: 70% of videos are to grow a new audience (he says he does not care if his existing audience watches these), and 30% are what his existing audience loves, so they do not unsubscribe. These are also the videos he enjoys making (events, investigations, vlogs).
- Result: every video gets at least 700K views in the first month, usually 1M or more.
- Failure modes he names: channels that only chase new audience bore their existing audience, and channels that only serve their existing audience never grow.
- Packaging matters most: the concept of the video, and why someone would click it in the recommended feed (what stands out or benefits them personally). He writes only 10-15 bullet points per video.
- Early on (2021) he did not care about YouTube and picked the thumbnail within minutes on upload day. He now has a chief content officer leading a content team of 40.

chunks.heading: Why he rarely sells or takes sponsorships
chunks.text:
- He takes zero sponsorships. His team still sends out a rate card of $250,000 for a 30-second ad read, and dozens of companies have wanted to pay it.
- He says too many sponsors dilute and damage your brand, and that he sells his own product only two weeks a year (twice a year). The rest of the year he has no bio links and no links in YouTube videos.
- He claims he leaves about $50M a year on the table by not promoting more, and accepts that for longevity. He says top athletes and celebrities who DM him as fans would not do so if he pushed products weekly.
- When he does sell, he tries to make it entertaining.
- On sponsors in general: he criticizes gambling, crypto and Forex promoters because the sponsor's revenue is a percentage split of what the audience loses, and "for you to make money they have to lose money."
- The only brands he would consider are premium ones like Patek Philippe, and maybe Rolls-Royce.

chunks.heading: Risk management, pricing mistakes, and the skills he says matter most
chunks.text:
- Five skills he names: sales, managing people (and emotions), paranoia, critical thinking, and finances and cash flow, including offense, defense and risk management.
- Paranoia means asking who is taking your spot, who is doing it better, and what the same thing for two more years would look like. He says: "there's no such thing as passive income" and that things decay: you can buy yourself time with hard work, but the market will take your spot.
- Crypto: he criticizes telling beginners with about $3,000 to trade crypto. Even with about $10M in crypto gains (he put about $1M into Bitcoin in November 2020 and rolled into Ethereum), he calls that luck, not skill, with no link to his business ability.
- His advice: work on businesses where 12 months of failure does no catastrophic damage. A $5K event or course that builds real skills will likely return more than $5K in a few years, unlike a trade that can go to zero.
- A mistake he owns: about six months earlier he made a pricing change at his main software company, which he calls "a horrible move." Growth stopped, and they are moving back to the old pricing.
- He says his biggest failures are people (someone you misjudge) and market assumptions (launches or pricing pivots), not ventures. He says he has never put money into a company and lost it.
- He says he is not a trained expert at some things but is very sharp with people. He knows who will stay 18 months and who will stay 18 years, though once in a while someone blindsides him.

chunks.heading: Spending, assets and a 30/70 rule
chunks.text:
- His rule for free cash flow (dividends and investment returns taken personally): spend 30%, save and invest 70%. He recently ran the numbers and found he was not spending enough.
- He judges assets by whether the money is recoverable, not by price: "someone could spend $50 million on an asset and if they are guaranteed to return back $50 million... they're not spending money they're just parking money."
- Properties: he rents some out when he is not using them, so he gets to enjoy them while making a bit of money. He prefers not publicizing which ones, since owner identity changes who rents (he would rather host a 55-year-old billionaire family than party guests).
- Jet: he has explored buying one (about $25M). A jet broker told him that with his travel patterns it will never make sense, and a full-time charter would lose about $400K a year. He still wants one, and says it only makes sense once a $1-1.5M yearly loss does not matter.
- Cars: despite tens of millions earned, his first personal car came in March of that year. He did not buy supercars when his brand was growing because it was not authentic to him. He says he had to be his real self, not manufacture a flashy image for growth.
- Money milestones he cites: first million at 18, about $10M personal net worth at 21 (after tax), and he says he takes home tens of millions a year now. His happiest period was ages 19-20, doing a couple million a year in profit, with less stress and responsibility.
- He says that once you have around $10M, you do not need more, and that friends with $300M in their 20s can be a suicide risk because they lose purpose.

chunks.heading: Social media, privacy and fame
chunks.text:
- He says he has toyed with leaving social media and is unsure how long he will stay. The reason he did not quit about 18 months before this interview: his business partner at his software company said he could drive so much business through his socials that quitting would be irresponsible.
- Most of his companies are unaffected by his social media, and some would do better if he could focus on them.
- He says it is better if people do not know your wealth or your abilities. People counting him out, apart from those who matter, is an advantage.
- He says he cannot show on social media what he now does (family office, corporate structures, investments, managing his team), because it does not help his audience. He was honest about every stage while he climbed (from £95 a week to a 40% revenue loss in one weekend), but that stopped being possible at the top.
- Boundaries: he will not take photos at his home or at a place of prayer. People have swum over to try to reach his house.
- On the risks of fame: being known for the sake of being known "is legitimately the stupidest thing anyone could ever do." He values being known for helping people.
- On content strategy (platform risk): he lost his Instagram blue tick multiple times and is shadow banned for his COVID content, and says he accepted the consequences. If a platform removed his videos, he would not complain about being deplatformed.

chunks.heading: Running an e-learning company and his view on university
chunks.text:
- His e-learning company, Educate, positions itself as "10 times the impact on your income for one 100th the price of University." He describes it as MasterClass for hard skills (agency, sales, copywriting and other high-income skills). Pricing: $125 a month, with the first year paid up front, then monthly and cancelable anytime.
- Educators include himself (agency), the top sales expert who works in his company, his CMO (copywriting), and Jordan Welch.
- His case against university: 98% of people attend to appease parents or because they do not know what else to do, and only about 2% genuinely want to be a doctor or lawyer (for those people he stays quiet). He calls it theory taught by people who have never run a business.
- What he thinks should replace it: critical thinking and real mentorship, like a Roman school of philosophy you pick to match your worldview.
- He also hosted an in-person event for fans, which he describes as scratching an itch to talk operations (like handling 10,000 support tickets a day, or sending handwritten notes to 8,000 new customers a week) that he cannot discuss on social media. He does not do one-on-one meetings or paid dinners and says he has turned down $50-100K offers.
- He funds school building in Nepal through the Parar Trust: two schools in 2019, then two to four a year. It took six months to find a charity that took a large yearly donation seriously, because small charities assumed money laundering.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Iman explains how a plan-driven content operation (three full-time thumbnail people, constant split tests, a 20-person short-form team) drove YouTube and short-form growth. He also covers setting honest expectations for business beginners, why paid customer acquisition fits software, and why he advises skills and apprenticeships over college.

chunks.heading: YouTube growth: moving from paid ads to a full organic machine
chunks.text:
- Iman's early YouTube growth was paid. In early 2018, a client wanted their channel grown with ads. He had never advertised for subscribers, so he built a small test ad to see if he could deliver the service.
- The ads brought in subscribers for roughly "half a dollar or a dollar" each in the US and European markets. He ran this personally for a while and got about 100,000 subscribers before performance trailed off.
- He admits he was "terrible at organic for years." One mistake was turning off monetization because he didn't like ads on his videos, which he calls a massive mistake for anyone trying to grow a channel.
- For years the process was minimal: record, trim the start and end, upload. He and his head of content, Tristan, would decide the thumbnail and title in a quick meeting on the day of filming.
- He nearly left social media about two years before this interview. His business partner in the software company persuaded him to stay, arguing that an audience lets a founder 10x, 20x or 30x the company in 12-24 months.
- Once he committed, the channel grew 2.6 million subscribers in 12 months and was still adding about 250,000 subscribers a month. He says this was done on a deliberate plan with set targets, not by accident, and excludes vlog-style channels from the comparison.

chunks.heading: Thumbnail split testing and content system
chunks.text:
- About 18 months before the interview, Iman built a dedicated thumbnail team of three full-time people.
- The channel uploads once a week, but the thumbnail team works daily on split tests for old videos.
- Each split test comes with five thumbnail options, so the team produces 15 options per video. The team runs about 30 thumbnail "rehashes" a month on existing videos.
- He claims this alone means he could stop uploading for a year and still get about 5,000 subscribers a day.
- Each week's video is a single piece of content. He spends only about an hour or two a week creating content himself, around six hours a month.
- He declined to share some of the other tactics on camera. His view is that in hyper-competitive spaces, some things you shouldn't give away because they are what got you where you are.

chunks.heading: Short-form distribution built in-house
chunks.text:
- The short-form department started around summer 2023 (about 18 months before the interview). It has roughly 18-20 full-time people.
- The team puts out about 6,000-7,000 pieces of content a month and gets around 250 million views a month. He expects roughly 3 billion short-form views for the year.
- He chose an internal team over an affiliate program. He watched what happened with Andrew Tate's affiliate clippers: the program helped him blow up but sometimes in ways that hurt his brand. Iman wanted to be omnipresent without his words being chopped up and spun the wrong way.
- Internal production gives control over how his message is cut and framed.

chunks.heading: Educate.io and the case against college
chunks.text:
- Educate.io is built as a "Masterclass for hard skills." He recruits people he respects to teach their own skills, for example Jordan Welch teaching e-commerce.
- He teaches only what he has actually done (agency, and a few other things). He says his own seven-figure e-commerce income comes from having an audience, not from skill, so it would be wrong to pretend he can teach it.
- He won't teach things he considers immoral to sell to beginners, such as crypto trading, stock trading, or Amazon FBA that requires thousands in upfront stock. Dropshipping and e-commerce can start with very little money, for example validating a product on TikTok.
- The motto: "10 times the impact on someone's income for 1/100th the price of a college education."
- On college pricing, he blames student loans, not universities. He says that if the government offered everyone a loan for online education, his own prices would go up too.
- Educate reportedly received 40,000 applications in one year. The company never asks for a CV or resume.
- Law and medicine still require college. For most people, the goal order is financial freedom, then time freedom, then location freedom, and a traditional job path rarely delivers time or location freedom.

chunks.heading: Advice on college, parents and risk
chunks.text:
- He told a young listener planning a computer science degree as "something to fall back on" that this is a cop out. The only real fallback is your skills: "you are the retirement fund," not a piece of paper.
- He says parents' career advice is outdated, not out of bad intent. Timeless life principles (how to carry yourself, how to keep a marriage healthy) are worth taking from parents, but "the best career vehicle" advice changes quickly. Your own children will likewise find your advice outdated in 20 years.
- He estimates that of 10-20k spent on online education over four years, about 50% is wasted, 25% teaches a thing or two, and 25% is life-changing. You usually have to buy a "basket" of things. That is still a fraction of tuition.
- He recommends working as a free intern or apprentice at the right company (not a bloated one where you get lost) and being around good people who can mentor you.
- He is not a "burn the bridges" advocate. He tells someone in their thirties with a wife and kids not to quit their job, because they have things to lose. A person with nothing to lose, like an 18-year-old, can go all in.
- He favors business models where failure doesn't ruin you. He is against telling beginners to get rich through crypto trading: you can lose your savings and have no skills afterward.
- He treats losing a few thousand dollars on a real business as acceptable, because you take lessons from it. He says "it's how you lost it" that matters.

chunks.heading: Timelines, expectations and disclaimers
chunks.text:
- He says people should treat the first year of a business as a write-off and not expect to win in year one.
- His own record is public: he has uploaded to YouTube since age 15, was open about being broke, and read a book a week by buying £3 used books at a Brixton bookshop because he couldn't afford £50 a month on new ones.
- He went about seven months between landing his first agency client and his second.
- He notes that many people now feel like failures if they aren't making $10,000 a month within seven months. He suggests telling older entrepreneurs about a business that made $3,000 a month in profit after nine months; they would see it as a success.
- He says he tries to attach disclaimers to his income claims: results like his are not normal, and a more likely outcome is $2,000-$10,000 a month after a first year of little success.
- He says making money online has "never been easier" but is not guaranteed.

chunks.heading: Business operations and time allocation
chunks.text:
- By this point Iman's days are mostly meetings: calls with the C-suite at his different companies, his family office, his internal finance team, reports, private banks and wealth management firms, legal and finance.
- He says he used to dismiss executives like Gary Vaynerchuk who had 12 back-to-back meetings as not doing "real" entrepreneurship, and now his own life looks like that.
- He spent most of October studying the bond market and was putting millions a week into bonds because yields were high.
- He says he is a worse business owner because of social media, since someone focused only on the business will beat someone splitting attention.
- He expects his social media relevance to last perhaps 3-5 more years and is comfortable leaving online life "when you're on top," while pushing his business career harder. He says online interest is short-lived while a business career can last decades.
- He takes long breaks from podcasts so he doesn't repeat himself.

chunks.heading: Personal brand, spending and gambling stance
chunks.text:
- He buys things that are authentic to him, not for signaling. He bought watches (Patek, Rolex) from 2018, before they were widely seen as investments, and built a car collection only in the current year, because before that he had no real use for cars.
- He avoids visible logos, saying he wouldn't do business with someone in head-to-toe Gucci because they "care too much what people think." Style, he says, comes from growing up in Europe, his friends, and having nothing to prove after making money young.
- He says that in London he drives a Range Rover to avoid drawing unnecessary attention, while Dubai allows flashier choices.
- He publicly criticized gambling promotion by influencers after a trip to Vegas, comparing it to promoting drinking or drugs. He says he was offered an eight-figure deal plus bonuses earlier that year for gambling promotion and turned it down.
- He points out that hungry, smart, diligent people are "very dangerous people" when money offers come. He kept his career "slow and steady" so he "didn't have to answer" when "the devil came knocking."
- He says he does not burn out because he doesn't want a quiet life, and could have retired with eight figures net years earlier.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Early interview with Iman at 18 on how poverty-driven hunger, a guarded social circle and relentless self-education built his agency and personal brand. He also explains how to sell social media marketing by anchoring on client lifetime value, niche research and emotional motives instead of flat retainers.

chunks.heading: Starting from desperation, not noble reasons
chunks.text:
- Iman began his businesses about 14 months before this 2018 interview, at age 17, out of fear for his own future. He didn't want college and said "no one else is gonna take care of me except for me."
- He started with social media marketing, built it for three to four months, then dropped out of high school with a year and a half left because he was running a business on two to three hours of sleep.
- At the time of the interview (aged 18, about nine months after dropping out) he ran social media marketing, affiliate marketing and a personal brand that sold digital products. He cites $72,000 profit in the previous month across all businesses, and moving into a $5,000-a-month dream apartment in London three months earlier.
- His family, friends and even his business mentor thought dropping out was ridiculous. He did it anyway because he believed in the idea.
- He spent large amounts on education, mentors and surrounding himself with the right people, because he wanted to get to his goal fast.

chunks.heading: Hunger as the engine
chunks.text:
- Iman grew up poor in a Russian village, then lived in London in a broken house in a rich area while attending a private school. His mother was unemployed for years and money was tight.
- Because his friends were wealthy, he knew success was possible and "success was never a doubt in my mind." He argues many people from poverty stay stuck because they don't believe it's possible.
- His hunger came from two facts: he had to take care of himself, and he had to take care of his mom.
- He says that without that struggle he'd "just be a rather kid", because humans aren't built to grow: "we're meant to survive," seeking maximum reward for minimal effort.
- If your parents give you monthly money, he suggests telling them to cut you off, or to put it toward a coach or mentor instead. Comfort kills motivation.
- Some people from wealthy families still build great things, but they have to find something within themselves to light the fire, because nothing external forces it.

chunks.heading: Your "why" evolves; start with an ugly one
chunks.text:
- He says you "need to go through a paradigm to understand it." His why moved through stages:
  1. Fear: if he didn't make it before turning 18, he'd have no place to live and might go back to being a village boy in Russia.
  2. Self: the dream apartment, the car, the best things in life.
  3. Becoming everything he could have been.
  4. Outside himself: he now feels he owes it to kids without fathers or role models, who get written off as he was.
- He calls an outward-facing why the strongest, but says don't start there because it's a paradigm you can't resonate with yet.
- Start with whatever lights a fire now, such as proving your mom or a friend wrong. Don't get stuck trying to find the perfect why before taking action.

chunks.heading: Social circle and deliberate isolation
chunks.text:
- His first answer for what drives success is social circle: you are the sum of the five people you spend the most time with. He doesn't take advice from people who lack the result (he gives the example of a fitness coach without the body, and an economics teacher giving financial advice).
- If your friends drink or take drugs on weekends, so will you. He says he got pulled into London high society and a drug habit about a year and a half before the interview.
- Test for a bad circle: when friends talk about "what life would be like if this happened," rather than solutions and how they'll do things, "get them out now" or slowly fade them out. They may still be good people, but they won't move you forward.
- Aged 15, he brought Tupperware chicken and rice to school because he couldn't afford food off campus, read two-pound used books from a Brixton bookshop, and meditated for 30 minutes in a bathroom stall.
- He spent Sundays in a used bookstore for four to five hours reading philosophy, relationships, social circle and sales books.
- He still kept a social circle, but spent little time with it. He says every current success traces back to an action from three years earlier.
- He claims you have to be lonely first, and then once success hits, everyone wants to meet you. He stays "lonely" on purpose, turning down parties and clubbing invitations.

chunks.heading: Self-education over excuses
chunks.text:
- Self-education was everything to him. If you say you can't afford a course, he says go to a used bookstore or go online, because the internet is free.
- He admits that not being able to afford a course or a event (he names 10x Growth Con) is a disadvantage.
- He'd still bet on someone making 100 cold calls a day with a stutter over someone with a light cold who makes none: action beats perfect conditions.

chunks.heading: Selling social media marketing like a business owner
chunks.text:
- He rejects the common advice of charging $1,000 to $5,000 a month to manage ads. If someone pitched him $2,000 to run retargeting without explaining the process or ROI, he'd laugh and find it disrespectful.
- He wants to deal business owner to business owner, not as a worker or "slave" to the client. To be treated like one, speak and act like one.
- Sell on lifetime value (LTV):
  1. Work out the LTV of a customer in the client's industry. For a dental clinic, he says typical values run from five to fifteen thousand dollars, and for a premium London clinic (Knightsbridge Dental Care, which he closed) about £32,000, roughly $40,000.
  2. Against a $40,000 customer, a $2,000 package that brings even one customer a month makes sense.
  3. Selling on short-term returns fails. For example, 100 teeth-cleaning leads with 30 upsold at $97 gives about $3,000 and just breaks even on a $2,000 fee plus $1,000 ad spend, so it looks like a weak ROI.
  4. Selling on LTV takes pressure off the marketer, because a customer stays on average four years and refers on average 0.2 people.
- The owner of that clinic didn't know her own LTV ("what's LTV?"), which positions him as the consultant.

chunks.heading: Flip the buyer-seller dynamic with niche research
chunks.text:
- Always flip the buyer-seller dynamic quickly. Know the client's industry better than the owner does.
- Start with two to three hours of niche research: for restaurants, dentists or gyms, find the best converting ads and the industry's LTV.
- Example: for gyms the best converting ads are a free week, or three sessions (or three weeks) for thirty dollars. He says he knows those "like the back of my hand."
- Once you hold the data, you have the authority.

chunks.heading: Sell on emotion, then justify with logic
chunks.text:
- People buy on emotion and justify with logic, and he says most marketers skip the emotional part.
- Simple method: ask the current monthly revenue (say $50,000), the target a year out (say $100,000), and treat the gap as the stake. Then ask the motive behind the target and keep prying beyond the surface answer.
- Real motives he found:
  - A garage owner who inherited his business from his father only wanted to make his dad proud, so he cared only about profit and not brand awareness.
  - A client who was bullied as a kid and wanted the coolest brand for validation, so he said he didn't care about ROI and just wanted brand awareness.
- Understand the person you're selling to, not just the business.

chunks.heading: What success changes
chunks.text:
- Money doesn't change him much; he gets acclimated to the apartment and travel. For him the reward is what it does for others: his mom, friends who used to buy him lunch, and charity (he once gave a subscriber a new iPhone to start a business).
- He says getting to six figures is the biggest life change, and going to seven figures changes little for happiness.
- He believes "there's no nobility in poverty" and that you owe it to your mom, wife or sister to earn.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Long personal interview covering Iman's childhood, mental health and relationships. The business-relevant parts: top-level performance carries a permanent stress tax, test a new path part-time before going all in, and how he stacked an agency, an e-learning company and software.

chunks.heading: Iman's view on chaos, responsibility and the cost of operating at the top
chunks.text:
- Iman says his year is a "season of chaos" that he chose: each year he takes on more responsibility. He rejects calling it anxiety: "when you feel bad but you know exactly why and it's a decision that comes from you... you made your bed and now you need to lay in it."
- He says his best quality of life was about 3-4 years ago, when his business was one-tenth the size, with 5-6 employees and high profit.
- He doesn't believe in the "conscious entrepreneur" idea of doing an hour of work and enjoying the wealth. Anyone performing at the very top has a "minefield" of a mind. Peace comes after selling the company, which follows decades of stress and responsibility.
- He sees himself as the "captain of the ship" (his team calls him Captain; he dislikes "boss"), responsible for the direction of about 150 employees.
- Everything has a tax, and social media hides the price. He documented 8 years on YouTube, starting at 15, including his first loss, his first hire and his first employee quitting after 3 days. He feels a duty to tell people what the life actually costs.
- He argues that someone who could stop and keeps going does so because of something innate. He wouldn't stop either ("what else would I do"), though he cites US bonds at 5-5.5% as the safe option that would let him never work again.
- He doesn't judge people who move to Southeast Asia and live on $5,000 a month instead of scaling. The test is living in alignment with who you are, which can take time to figure out.

chunks.heading: Seasons of life, trade-offs and how he defines success
chunks.text:
- Success to him means "living in accordance to the season of your life." He compares his current season to a bodybuilder who only trains chest: one area gets almost all the focus.
- He admits this costs him personally: he forgets birthdays, doesn't call his mom daily, and his lifestyle isn't compatible with being the best partner or son right now. He expects a later season focused on family and says he will "shed [his] skin."
- He bought his mom a $4M dream house and sees a tax in that too: few sons do that and also call daily. They have a weekly mother-son time. He says her love language isn't lavish gifts (their worst arguments usually follow the most lavish gifts).
- Asked about his mom wanting him present over the house, he answers that she'd be asking him to give up who he wants to be, and she knows he is living true to his current life situation.
- He says he constantly asks "am I doing enough?" and the answer is never yes. He calls it an infinite game and that is the fun of it.
- He treats self-awareness as the core skill: know whether you are wired to pursue the top (like a footballer who could coast as the 100th best but chases number one) or want a quieter life, and live accordingly.

chunks.heading: Dropping out, Plan A and when to go all in
chunks.text:
- He told his mom at 13-14 he would not go to college (no money, no student debt). He dropped out of school at 17 when he was making about $15,000 a month and supporting his mom. He started "massaging the idea" at 16.
- He distinguishes skipping university from dropping out of school. He believes everyone should finish school unless in a situation like his, and he has strong objections to colleges and universities.
- He didn't drop out when he signed his first client. He dropped out after making substantial money and proving to himself he wanted it.
- His framework for going all in: ask "what do I have to lose?" If you live in your mom's basement, go 100% all in. If you are 36 with a family, dropping everything would be irresponsible without a conversation with your partner about the risk of a rocky couple of years.
- He thinks you can start a business or the next career step with two hours a day first and prove it to yourself. Someone earning $80K at 25-26 has a good income and may be giving something up by leaving.
- Early on you need only Plan A (with nothing to lose, failing returns you to where you were). Later you need plans A through D, because markets change.
- On passive income: you are buying yourself time. Six months of work may front-load two years of success, but it decays and "someone's going to come in," so you need ways to pivot.

chunks.heading: How he built his money: agency, e-learning, software and the funnel model
chunks.text:
- He ran his agency for 6 years. He calls agencies one of the easiest businesses in which to make about $1M a year in profit, maybe $2M, but not $10M a year.
- Near the end of the agency he launched an e-learning company (Grow Agency, late 2019/early 2020) for agency owners, leveraging his public documentation of his results (clients like oring, being flown first class to New York to consult).
- That led to his first software company, Agency Flow. He partnered with a client whose husband had spent years building influencer-marketing software; Iman had the audience of agency owners, so they retooled it for agencies.
- He cites the ClickFunnels model: reportedly zero to a billion-dollar valuation in five years, self-funded, because they got paid to acquire customers (e.g. a $12 book that pays for the acquisition) and then sold the software on the back end. Iman says he did the same: the e-learning business gets paid on the front end, and the back-end solution customers use is Agency Flow.
- Grow Agency was rebranded to Educate. It's a Masterclass-style platform with different Educators. It costs $125 a month, with the first year paid upfront, and includes a student success concierge. He is adding soft skills (e.g. a tailoring program) alongside business models.
- The "more genius aspect": every online business model needs software. For the software his students use, he owns a large equity stake in it, or has 50/50 partnerships, or recommends the best tool (e.g. Shopify for e-commerce), and says if he brings a platform all those customers, "we should be compensated for it."
- He says an agency is the only business model he'd comfortably teach a beginner. His eyewear brand shows how hard e-commerce is: 11 months into the year he hadn't taken a penny of profit out, because each time money comes in he goes back to the manufacturer to negotiate unit costs down (e.g. 8%, 3%, 15%) depending on order size.
- He doesn't talk about much of what he owns (properties, businesses) because it's too unrelatable to serve his audience.

chunks.heading: Colleges, loans and pricing: why prices rise when someone else pays
chunks.text:
- His objection to universities is the student-loan mechanism. He says if the government offered a 100% loan for online education, he'd raise his prices, and every company in the space would too. He says if loans were available for tennis classes, prices would be 10x within three years.
- Colleges raised prices because loans are available to anyone, the "government's paying for it", while student outcomes keep declining. He applies the same logic to medical insurance (x-rays priced off insurance, not the patient's pocket) and the housing bubble (no-money-down loans handed out to anyone).
- He says 40 years ago everyone should have gone to college because there was a clear correlation between education and earnings; he says that correlation no longer holds in the US or Europe.
- He argues the education system was designed to produce obedient factory workers (the Prussian model), and that critical thinking matters most in life.
- He still builds education: he has built schools in Nepal for four years, for thousands of children, because a good education in that part of the world does work. Education has to fit your opportunities and where you are.
- On social media and podcasts, he says to treat his content as entertainment, not study time. He tells people to delete YouTube, and that watching podcasts isn't a substitute for doing something with your life.

chunks.heading: Money as a tool and benchmark, and how he handles comparison
chunks.text:
- He treats money as a tool for making people's lives better and a benchmark of impact and personal growth. He compares it to a marathon runner proudly reporting a faster time. He says he could only honestly say "tool for better" once he was abundant, and that saying it three years earlier would have been "talking off my ass."
- Money can also reflect timing or smart investments, not impact, but making more money is still a cultivated skill and a barometer of growth.
- He intends to "die with zero" and not leave money to his children, because he knows how depressing money's downsides are even when you've earned it yourself, and worse if you never went through the trials.
- Social media warning: it can steer you off a good track. Someone making $400K a year at 26 with a wife and child would have been a king 30 years ago and now feels like a failure online. He urges people to ask whether things (dressing like him, moving to Dubai, starting a business after seeing one person do it) are true to them, and to figure out what is right for their own season.
- He notes even he gets swayed: seeing someone start a business, he thinks he should spin one off, then realizes "this thought isn't even mine."

chunks.heading: Security, fame and how he treats the people who follow him
chunks.text:
- He says people have security for three reasons: they've upset someone, they carry valuables, or they're widely known. He says he fits the third: his head of security lives with him, people try to reach his house about five times a day (some have tried to swim to it, or rented villas), and he lives in a gated community with 24-hour security.
- He explains the obsession: his life is documented on YouTube for 6+ years, so people feel changed by him, and many just want to say thank you.
- His rule is to always stop for a photo and ask the person's name, because "they've given me their time and attention." Two places he won't tolerate it are his house and a place of worship.
- Security also keeps interactions good: his head of security blends in and politely says Iman wants to get back to his run, so Iman isn't the one saying no.
- He treats security as an insurance policy, especially in places like London, Cape Town and New York, which he calls dangerous, versus Dubai, which he calls very respectful. He says he has worked too hard to let his mom face unnecessary disrespect.
- He rejects the "arrogant" label: he says the arrogant thing would be to claim his life is perfect, and he has publicly shared losses (e.g. losing three clients, 40% of revenue, in one weekend) and the early months without signing a client. He bought his first car only this year despite earning tens of millions.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Iman Gadzhi explains why a boring agency is the best first business: low downside, free cash flow, and leverage through hiring. He covers asymmetric bets, building the team before chasing lifestyle, and treating NFTs as a pricing model for memberships. He also says wealth normalizes rather than fulfills.

chunks.heading: Becoming Wealthy Starts With Feeling Deserving of It, and Poverty Plus Proximity to Wealth Gave Iman That
chunks.text:
- Iman grew up with a strange mix: his mom was on government benefits and worked temporary jobs (Harrods, Chelsea and Westminster hospital), his stepdad paid for private school but little else, and he was surrounded by wealthy people.
- For the last four years in that house there was no hot water and no heating. When his stepdad found out he was starting a business, he cut the wifi.
- He built his early business on a 25 pounds a month limited hotspot plan on Three, in 2015.
- He says the wealth around him did not motivate him; it normalized wealth. He argues that most people repel money because they don't feel deserving of it.
- His view: wealthy people are not necessarily smarter, "a lot of times it's just because they feel deserving of it." As a kid he would see a sports car and think "that'll be my reality very soon."
- He sees comfortable middle-class households as a weak spot, with enough comfort to lose the fire but no poverty-level hunger. He says he got "the best of both worlds."
- He started reading Rich Dad Poor Dad and Think and Grow Rich at 14 and calls those books his "phantom mentors."
- Book needs change by stage: Think and Grow Rich and Rich Dad Poor Dad for the start, then denser books like Reality Transurfing from roughly 100k a year toward a million. At the beginning he says it is simply discipline: "just do it like that's it." Mindset and shadow work matter later.

chunks.heading: Fulfillment vs Peace vs Joy: Pick What You Optimize For
chunks.text:
- Iman rejects "happiness" as a goal, calling it "a whole load of [ __ ]". He says he is "not very happy" but doesn't care, because he optimizes for fulfillment.
- His three categories:
  - Fulfillment: doing something really hard (boxing, building a company, running a marathon). Example: after getting beaten up in a fight you don't feel happy, you feel fulfilled.
  - Peace: moving to a farm, walking in the woods.
  - Joy: waking up in Bali with friends, riding mopeds to a waterfall.
- The three conflict: fulfillment usually requires hard things that give neither peace nor joy in the moment, and joy (adventure) conflicts with peace (calm).
- His "terms and conditions" for copying his life: "it comes with not too much joy and pretty much next to zero peace" in this season, but more fulfillment and the things others want.
- Wealth normalizes pleasure. Using a taste analogy: at his level it's like losing your sense of taste, you still go to restaurants but get no pleasure from them. A grinder earning their first 100k gets more satisfaction than he does at eight figures.
- He flies private in Europe and first class long haul because it adds comfort and makes it easier to do bigger, harder things, not because it adds joy. He says he considered flying economy to reset but thinks it isn't sensible.
- He says the first time he buys his own jet with company branding would give him real pleasure, then it normalizes too.
- He tells people to go in "with your eyes open" about what the lifestyle does and doesn't give.

chunks.heading: Why an Agency Is the Best Stepping Stone (and Why Boring Beats Sexy)
chunks.text:
- Iman says an agency should never be the end goal (he finds it a depressing business to run for 30 years) but it is "the best stepping stone possible."
- An agency is leverage: you hire people (contractors first, then full-time) to deliver the service. He compares it to law firms that pay a lawyer around 75 pounds an hour and bill the client 300. Clients prefer the agency because it has the team plus time for systems, operations and client delivery.
- Agencies throw off free cash flow. His example: outgoings of 1,000 a month versus 10,000 turned over. Agency owners talk profit only: "nothing else matters."
- Friends' agencies reach 10k, 20k, up to 100k a month profit, then the owners want e-commerce for the cool factor, while e-commerce owners want the agency's free cash flow.
- E-commerce reality: very low margins, cash fronted to suppliers, constant reinvestment. He knows owners of eight- and nine-figure-valued brands, including one doing about 30 million a year, with little profit and not much cash. His agency's most successful e-commerce clients sell things like glow-in-the-dark teddy bears and radio devices, not the next jewelry or clothing line. Coloured sand is fine: "if coloured sand makes money then who cares."
- His principle: make the business practical, then the life can be whatever you want. Don't chase the lifestyle before the business exists.
- Spotting fakes: look at how opulent someone's lifestyle is. He hired a full-time crypto researcher in September who "maybe has a drink once a month"; a real trader can't be partying because they're the only point of reference for their success. He can party hard because he built infrastructure and a team, whereas he couldn't in his first two or three years when he was the strongest link.
- Working from the beach is "horrendous," he says; sand and sun don't work for laptops.
- His own businesses are boring in practice. In his software company he and his co-founder spend their catch-ups on LTV, churn and bug fixes. "My life is good because of it."

chunks.heading: Starting Small: Low-Downside Businesses and Asymmetric Bets
chunks.text:
- Iman's analogy: Formula One drivers start in go-karts; do not start with a super difficult business.
- He argues against beginners starting real estate, trading, or e-commerce. You can burn 1,500 dollars on ads just to find a product doesn't work, or lose 2,000 trading crypto. His rule: start where you can "fall, scrape your knees, get no's, get losses" with no real downside, "bowling with the bumpers on."
- Core framework: look for asymmetric returns like a chess player or fighter. Always ask what the downside is, aim for lots of upside with as close to zero downside as possible, and keep making those bets.
- To go from 0-10k or under 50k toward 100k and then a million, his first instruction is to increase income:
  - Sell the value you bring at your current job (while recognizing most companies are dead ends), or
  - Start a cash flow business or offer services, or
  - Get a good sales job making 10-30k a month and save 50-60%.
- He says don't be romantic about it: "do whatever you want I don't really care," just increase income first.
- Wealth for stepping into software: he and his co-founder bootstrapped AgencyFlow, an all-in-one platform for online boutique agencies (replacing Slack, Asana, invoicing tools, Pipedrive). It launched publicly in February (2022), received an eight-figure offer he turned down, and they plan to sell for hundreds of millions in three to five years. They were practical from day one and it came from lived agency pain.
- Target positioning: not for 3-person agencies or large traditional agencies. Teams up to roughly 30 can use it, but large sales teams should move to tools like Close or HubSpot. "There's a tool for everyone at their current stage."
- He says the agency experience let him see what the market needs before building software, whereas many people start software without knowing the need.

chunks.heading: Monk Mode and Environment Design
chunks.text:
- Iman's monk mode began in cape Town in spring 2020 during lockdown, when South Africa banned alcohol and cigarettes and travel beyond the supermarket. He then repeated it deliberately for six weeks: no alcohol, 45 minutes of phone screen time a day, strict carnivore diet.
- His general protocol for others: at least 15 minutes of meditation a day, a screen-time cap, and exercise (he omits exercise from his own because it's already ingrained).
- Also no porn or masturbation unless in a relationship. He ranks from worst to best: porn and masturbation, then masturbation with intention/imagination, then sex with a person, then sex with someone you care about. He says "sexual energy is the most powerful energy that man has and most guys just waste it into a tissue."
- Duration: 21 to 90 days. Three weeks is already intense; he doesn't recommend more than 90 days because "you'll go crazy." Afterward blow off steam (sometimes 3-4 days, sometimes up to four months), then do another period.
- Environment is everything: he can't do monk mode in London or Dubai in peak season (December-February) because friends, girls and visitors flood in. That's why he keeps a house in Cape Town to get away from distractions. He picks locations by season, since Cape Town's summer is November-February.
- Suggested locations for starting an agency: Cape Town, Romania, Georgia, Colombia, Brazil, Eastern Europe generally. Half the cost and better quality of life means "you're already earning twice as much money." He prefers time-zone-friendly places and says Bali caused trouble with sales calls for him.
- Slow-mad: stay in a place six to twelve weeks (not four or five days) so you can keep protocols. For people who can't travel: work with what you have, and sell excess stuff (cars, watches) to fund a three-week trip, which he says can cost about 1,500 pounds.
- What holds people back is mostly what they consume, not what they fail to do: news, the YouTube subscription box, junk content, food, drink, and people they associate with. He gives a mild nod that Twitter and TikTok can have good pockets of information.
- Consuming 87 hours of videos without action is pointless. "You got to know what game you're playing."

chunks.heading: Moving to Dubai, Taxes and Wealth Structuring
chunks.text:
- Iman left the UK in January 2021 because the government telling him he couldn't leave his house was his limit. He looked for countries "going in the right direction" and chose Dubai (also cites Miami in the US) because they don't antagonize wealthy people.
- His argument: wealthy people create the jobs and have to provide value in a free market. He dislikes bankers and government but not the wealthy. He says he never villainized the wealthy when his family was on benefits.
- Tax approach (he says "minimize, not avoid"): once you control your income and aren't on earned career income, you may never need to pay personal tax again. One method he mentions: take loans against assets. Companies still pay corporate tax, VAT and employer tax.
- Staying clean with UK tax authorities: he spends under 45 days a year in the UK (allowed 90), owns no UK property, and has no ties, to avoid giving HMRC a reason. He is skeptical of UK landlord rules, such as being unable to deduct loan interest and tenant rules on sales.
- Time-wise he says most of his income reached its current level in 2021-2022, and now earns over ten million a year.
- Dubai property as an investment: his apartment was worth 7.2 million dirhams when he moved in (four bedrooms plus maid's room, beach, sea views) and rent was 600,000 dirhams a year (about 7.5% of value). A year later it is worth 9.2 million and similar apartments rent for around 800,000. He plans to buy mainly Dubai apartments and some houses, and rent them out rather than use Airbnb.
- Seasons: he would never raise a family in Dubai or Cape Town, but they suit this season of life.
- Cost of living: in Cape Town or Bali long-term, 20-30k a month gives a king's life and he struggles to spend over 30k a month there; in London 30k a weekend is easy and 30k a month is not king-level. He says location freedom is a key advantage of agency and software businesses.

chunks.heading: Money Philosophy, Crypto and Investing
chunks.text:
- Iman says he has "no respect for money" in the sense of treating it like scarce air. Money is energy and has to flow: pay suppliers and partners on time, don't hoard, provide value in excess of what you take. People who worship and hoard money usually have little of it.
- He saves and invests 80% of what he makes and spends 20%, which he forces himself to do. He notes you need higher income before that split is possible.
- Crypto story: he put about 1 million dollars into crypto, which grew to over 10 million at the peak. In a video he screen-shared a 6.8 million dollar portfolio, then 3-5 days later it was 3.5 million. The big lesson was taking profits. He says he is not a genius and you can't time tops or bottoms, so dollar cost average out on the way up and in on the way down, using key price ranges and standing orders.
- Current posture (October 2022): about 70% cash, fully out of crypto by April (last sale was Luna), then bought roughly 1 million dollars of Bitcoin with orders at about 20k, 19k and 18k. He expects 16-17k "almost a guarantee" and possibly 14-13k, and says "if Bitcoin goes down to 14 15,000 I'm deploying five million dollars."
- He sees the stock market falling another 20-30% around November, and real estate collapsing about 18 months after stocks, so around 2023. He's stacking cash for that, especially Dubai property. Cash gives "time to think."
- He sees most NFTs as scams but frames NFT as a pricing model: charge more upfront and take royalties (8.5% on resales for his project).
- Watches: his portfolio is around 3.5 million dollars, nearly all bought at retail, and he won't sell because resellers get blacklisted by brands. He picks pieces no longer in mass production and not hype pieces, and he buys Patek, Rolex and others through relationships. Example: a Patek Nautilus 5712 a friend bought for 140,000 pounds in February, which Iman bought pre-owned with box and papers for 77,000. He also holds 300-400k of Hermès-type bags (Birkins and Kellys) as investments.
- Ego-driven mistake: he bought three Bored Apes for a total of 1.2 million dollars as a brand and press play, sold two for about 100-150k loss each, and kept one with a Soviet hat. His lesson: "don't ever make a decision based off of ego."

chunks.heading: Gentlemen's Croquet Club: Memberships as Assets and Vetting for Community Quality
chunks.text:
- Iman co-founded Gentlemen's Croquet Club (GCC), an NFT-based members club of about 700 members out of 975 NFTs. The floor price was once about 16 ETH-equivalent per his figures, about 6.5 more recently. At one point one NFT was worth roughly 50,000 dollars per his words.
- His idea: your seat at the table should be an asset. In clubs like Annabel's or a 10,000 pound a year gym club like Kicks, when you leave you just stop paying; with an NFT you can sell your spot. He wants masterminds structured the same way.
- Why people pay: the price reflects the people in the room, not the facility. He kept a Kicks membership at 10k a year without using the gym, for the meetings and relationships.
- Vetting: members must do a video call application explaining why they deserve to pay 5,000 dollars. He wants no anonymous or ego-driven members, says money doesn't make someone interesting, and has a "no lame people" rule. He lets go of staff who are great at work but lame, with a 60-day or six-year hiring philosophy, and takes 10 team members to visit the schools he builds in Nepal each November.
- Product stack: a custom vault that authenticates via MetaMask; courses on buying watches at retail, investing in crypto and watches, social circles and Instagram; three research reports a week from his crypto researcher (some say "don't do anything"); an upcoming member Rolodex directory so members can see who lives in a city and contact them via Instagram, Twitter or email.
- Gentleman's training: he wants it to teach people to be gentlemen (wine, cigars, conduct) because he is "new money" who had to learn these things, and went skiing for the first time six months earlier.
- A concierge partnership (under NDA) with an extremely selective private membership concierge service, with an app launching in 3-4 months. Members skip an application with a sub-1% acceptance rate. Examples: a private jet leg quoted 16k via the concierge versus 22k via his broker; a Chanel/Hermès-type bag sourced in two days; restaurant reservations at the busiest London spots.
- He deliberately avoids marketing until key features are live ("once we do marketing it's game over").

chunks.heading: Psychedelics and Meditation
chunks.text:
- Iman did LSD at 15, bought with Bitcoin (he says that is not recommended for most people), and later tried mushrooms and ayahuasca.
- His view: psychedelics make sense "when you're lost in life." He hasn't used them in a while because he's in an execution phase where he knows what he needs to do. If he were at a real crossroads he would consider them.
- Meditation is a staple in his routine, and he notes that without it for two or three weeks he feels the difference.
